Bosnia and Herzegovina's [government building](/wiki/Greece%E2%80%93Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_Friendship_Building "Greece–Bosnia and Herzegovina Friendship Building") in [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Hipotekarna_banka_palata_predsjednika.JPG/250px-Hipotekarna_banka_palata_predsjednika.JPG)](/wiki/File:Hipotekarna_banka_palata_predsjednika.JPG)

[Palace of the Republic](/wiki/Palace_of_the_Republic,_Banja_Luka "Palace of the Republic, Banja Luka") in [Banja Luka](/wiki/Banja_Luka "Banja Luka")

The third level of Bosnia and Herzegovina's political subdivision is manifested in [cantons](/wiki/Cantons_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Cantons of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina"). They are unique to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina entity, which consists of ten of them. Each has a cantonal government, which is under the law of the Federation as a whole. Some cantons are ethnically mixed and have special laws to ensure the equality of all constituent people.[[148]](#cite_note-Mansfield_2003_pp._2052–2093-151)

The fourth level of political division in Bosnia and Herzegovina are the [municipalities](/wiki/Municipalities_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina"). The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is divided into 79 municipalities, and Republika Srpska into 64. Municipalities also have their own local government, and are typically based on the most significant city or place in their territory. As such, many municipalities have a long tradition and history with their present boundaries. Some others, however, were only created following the recent war after traditional municipalities were split by the [Inter-Entity Boundary Line](/wiki/Inter-Entity_Boundary_Line "Inter-Entity Boundary Line"). Each canton in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina consists of several municipalities, which are divided into local communities.[[149]](#cite_note-CoR-152)

Besides entities, cantons, and municipalities, Bosnia and Herzegovina also has four "official" cities. These are: [Banja Luka](/wiki/Banja_Luka "Banja Luka"), [Mostar](/wiki/Mostar "Mostar"), [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo") and [East Sarajevo](/wiki/Isto%C4%8Dno_Sarajevo "Istočno Sarajevo"). The territory and government of the cities of Banja Luka and Mostar corresponds to the municipalities of the same name, while the cities of Sarajevo and East Sarajevo officially consist of several municipalities. Cities have their own city government whose power is in between that of the municipalities and cantons (or the entity, in the case of Republika Srpska).

More recently, several central institutions have been established (such as a [defense ministry](/wiki/Defence_minister "Defence minister"), security ministry, state court, [indirect taxation](/wiki/Indirect_tax "Indirect tax") service and so on) in the process of transferring part of the jurisdiction from the entities to the state. The representation of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina is by elites who represent the country's three major groups, with each having a guaranteed share of power.

The [Chair](/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Presidency_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina") of the [Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Presidency_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina") rotates among three members ([Bosniak](/wiki/Bosniaks "Bosniaks"), [Serb](/wiki/Serbs "Serbs"), [Croat](/wiki/Croats "Croats")), each elected as the chair for an eight-month term within their four-year term as a member. The three members of the Presidency are elected directly by the people, with Federation voters voting for the Bosniak and the Croat and the Republika Srpska voters voting for the Serb.

The [Chair of the Council of Ministers](/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Council_of_Ministers_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Chairman of the Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina") is nominated by the Presidency and approved by the parliamentary [House of Representatives](/wiki/House_of_Representatives_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "House of Representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina"). The Chair of the Council of Ministers is then responsible for appointing a Foreign Minister, Minister of Foreign Trade and others as appropriate.

The Parliamentary Assembly is the lawmaking body in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It consists of two houses: the [House of Peoples](/wiki/House_of_Peoples_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "House of Peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina") and the House of Representatives. The House of Peoples has 15 delegates chosen by parliaments of the entities, two-thirds of which come from the Federation (5 Bosniaks and 5 Croats) and one-third from the Republika Srpska (5 Serbs). The House of Representatives is composed of 42 Members elected by the people under a form of proportional representation, two-thirds elected from the Federation and one-third elected from Republika Srpska.[[150]](#cite_note-Heath-Brown_2017_p._221-153)

The [Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina") is the supreme, final arbiter of legal matters. It is composed of nine members: four members are selected by the [Federal House of Representatives](/wiki/House_of_Representatives_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "House of Representatives of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina"), two by the [National Assembly of Republika Srpska](/wiki/National_Assembly_(Republika_Srpska) "National Assembly (Republika Srpska)") and three by the President of the [European Court of Human Rights](/wiki/European_Court_of_Human_Rights "European Court of Human Rights") after consultation with the Presidency, who cannot be Bosnian citizens.[[151]](#cite_note-154)

However, the highest political authority in the country is the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, the chief [executive officer](/wiki/Executive_officer "Executive officer") for the international civilian presence in the country and is selected by the [European Union](/wiki/European_Union "European Union"). Since 1995, the High Representative has been able to bypass the elected parliamentary assembly, and since 1997 has been able to remove elected officials. The methods selected by the High Representative have been criticized as undemocratic.[[152]](#cite_note-155) International supervision [is to end when the country is deemed politically and democratically stable and self-sustaining](/wiki/High_Representative_for_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina#Conditions_for_closure_of_the_Office_of_the_High_Representative "High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina").

### Foreign relations

Main article: [Foreign relations of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Foreign_relations_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Foreign relations of Bosnia and Herzegovina")

See also: [Accession of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the European Union](/wiki/Accession_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_to_the_European_Union "Accession of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the European Union")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Secretary_Clinton_Meets_With_President_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_Zeljko_Komsic_%286507403825%29.jpg/250px-Secretary_Clinton_Meets_With_President_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_Zeljko_Komsic_%286507403825%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Secretary_Clinton_Meets_With_President_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_Zeljko_Komsic_(6507403825).jpg)

[Željko Komšić](/wiki/%C5%BDeljko_Kom%C5%A1i%C4%87 "Željko Komšić"), Croat member of the [Bosnian Presidency](/wiki/Presidency_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina"), and [Hillary Clinton](/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton"), U.S. Secretary of State, 13 December 2011

[European Union integration](/wiki/Accession_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_to_the_European_Union "Accession of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the European Union") is one of the main political objectives of Bosnia and Herzegovina; it initiated the [Stabilisation and Association Process](/wiki/Stabilisation_and_Association_Process "Stabilisation and Association Process") in 2007. Countries participating in the SAP have been offered the possibility to become, once they fulfill the necessary conditions, Member States of the EU.[[153]](#cite_note-156) Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate country for EU accession since December 2022.[[129]](#cite_note-sarajevotimes-132) Accession talks are set to begin following the impeding of more reforms.[[154]](#cite_note-157)

The implementation of the [Dayton Agreement](/wiki/Dayton_Agreement "Dayton Agreement") in 1995 has focused the efforts of policymakers in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the international community, on regional stabilization in the countries-successors of the [former Yugoslavia](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia").[[155]](#cite_note-Usa_2012_p._269-158)

Within Bosnia and Herzegovina, relations with its neighbors of [Croatia](/wiki/Croatia "Croatia"), [Serbia](/wiki/Serbia "Serbia") and [Montenegro](/wiki/Montenegro "Montenegro") have been fairly stable since the signing of the Dayton Agreement. On 23 April 2010, Bosnia and Herzegovina received the [Membership Action Plan](/wiki/Enlargement_of_NATO#Membership_Action_Plan "Enlargement of NATO") from [NATO](/wiki/NATO "NATO"), which is the last step before full membership in the alliance. Full membership was initially expected in 2014 or 2015, depending on the progress of reforms.[[156]](#cite_note-159) In December 2018, NATO approved a Bosnian Membership Action Plan.[[157]](#cite_note-160)

Bosnia and Herzegovina is the 61st most peaceful country in the world, according to the 2024 [Global Peace Index](/wiki/Global_Peace_Index "Global Peace Index").[[158]](#cite_note-161)

### Military

The [Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina") (OSBiH) were unified into a single entity in 2005, with the merger of the [Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Army_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina") and the [Army of Republika Srpska](/wiki/Army_of_Republika_Srpska "Army of Republika Srpska"), which had defended their respective regions.[[159]](#cite_note-Lobjakas_2005-162) The [Ministry of Defence](/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_(Bosnia_and_Herzegovina) "Ministry of Defence (Bosnia and Herzegovina)") was formed in 2004.[[160]](#cite_note-NATO_2004-163)

The Bosnian military consists of the [Bosnian Ground Forces](/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina") and [Air Force and Air Defense](/wiki/Air_Force_and_Anti-Aircraft_Defence_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Air Force and Anti-Aircraft Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina").[[161]](#cite_note-European_Western_Balkans_2017-164) The Ground Forces number 7,200 active and 5,000 reserve personnel.[[162]](#cite_note-mod.gov.ba_2016-165) They are armed with a mix of American, Yugoslav, Soviet, and European-made weaponry, vehicles, and military equipment. The Air Force and Air Defense Forces have 1,500 personnel and about 62 aircraft. The Air Defense Forces operate [MANPADS](/wiki/Man-portable_air-defense_system "Man-portable air-defense system") hand-held missiles, [surface-to-air missile](/wiki/Surface-to-air_missile "Surface-to-air missile") (SAM) batteries, anti-aircraft cannons, and radar. The Army has recently adopted remodeled [MARPAT](/wiki/MARPAT "MARPAT") uniforms, used by Bosnian soldiers serving with the [International Security Assistance Force](/wiki/International_Security_Assistance_Force "International Security Assistance Force") (ISAF) in [Afghanistan](/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan"). A domestic production program is now underway to ensure that army units are equipped with the correct ammunition.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Beginning in 2007, the Ministry of Defence undertook the army's first ever international assistance mission, enlisting the military to serve with ISAF peace missions to Afghanistan, [Iraq](/wiki/Iraq "Iraq") and the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo") in 2007. Five officers, acting as officers/advisors, served in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. 45 soldiers, mostly acting as base security and medical assistants, served in Afghanistan. 85 Bosnian soldiers served as base security in Iraq, occasionally conducting infantry patrols there as well. All three deployed groups have been commended by their respective international forces as well as the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The international assistance operations are still ongoing.[[163]](#cite_note-NATO_2015-166)

The Air Force and Anti-Aircraft Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed when elements of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the [Republika Srpska Air Force](/wiki/Republika_Srpska_Air_Force "Republika Srpska Air Force") were merged in 2006. The Air Force has seen improvements in the last few years with added funds for aircraft repairs and improved cooperation with the [Ground Forces](/wiki/Army "Army") as well as to the citizens of the country. The Ministry of Defence is pursuing the acquisition of new aircraft including helicopters and perhaps even fighter jets.[[164]](#cite_note-167)

Economy
-------

Main article: [Economy of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Economy_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Economy of Bosnia and Herzegovina")

See also: [List of companies of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/List_of_companies_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "List of companies of Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/GDP_per_capita_development_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina.svg/250px-GDP_per_capita_development_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina.svg.png)](/wiki/File:GDP_per_capita_development_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina.svg)

Estimated development of real GDP per capita of Bosnia and Herzegovina, since 1952

During the [Bosnian War](/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War"), the economy suffered €200 billion in material damages, roughly €356.80 billion in 2025 (inflation adjusted).[[165]](#cite_note-168)[[166]](#cite_note-169) Bosnia and Herzegovina faces the dual-problem of rebuilding a war-torn country and introducing transitional liberal market reforms to its formerly mixed economy. One legacy of the previous era is a strong industry; under former republic president [Džemal Bijedić](/wiki/D%C5%BEemal_Bijedi%C4%87 "Džemal Bijedić") and [Yugoslav](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia") President [Josip Broz Tito](/wiki/Josip_Broz_Tito "Josip Broz Tito"), metal industries were promoted in the republic, resulting in the development of a large share of Yugoslavia's plants; [SR Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Socialist_Republic_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina") had a very strong industrial export oriented economy in the 1970s and 1980s, with large scale exports worth millions of [US$](/wiki/USD "USD").

For most of Bosnia's history, agriculture has been conducted on privately owned farms; Fresh food has traditionally been exported from the republic.[[167]](#cite_note-170)

The war in the 1990s, caused a dramatic change in the Bosnian economy.[[168]](#cite_note-171) GDP fell by 60% and the destruction of physical infrastructure devastated the economy.[[169]](#cite_note-172) With much of the production capacity unrestored, the Bosnian economy still faces considerable difficulties. Figures show GDP and per capita income increased 10% from 2003 to 2004; this and Bosnia's shrinking [national debt](/wiki/Government_debt "Government debt") being negative trends, and high unemployment 38.7% and a large [trade deficit](/wiki/Balance_of_trade "Balance of trade") remain cause for concern.

The national currency is the (Euro-pegged) [convertible mark](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_convertible_mark "Bosnia and Herzegovina convertible mark") (KM), controlled by the [currency board](/wiki/Currency_board "Currency board"). Annual inflation is the lowest relative to other countries in the region at 1.9% in 2004.[[170]](#cite_note-173) The international debt was $5.1 billion (as of 31 December 2014). [Real GDP](/wiki/Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") growth rate was 5% for 2004 according to the [Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Central_Bank_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina") and Statistical Office of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Bosnia and Herzegovina has displayed positive progress in the previous years, which decisively moved its place from the lowest income equality rank of [income equality rankings](/wiki/List_of_countries_by_income_equality "List of countries by income equality") fourteen out of 193 nations.[[171]](#cite_note-174)

According to [Eurostat](/wiki/Eurostat "Eurostat") data, Bosnia and Herzegovina's PPS GDP per capita stood at 29 per cent of the EU average in 2010.[[172]](#cite_note-175)

The [International Monetary Fund](/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") (IMF) announced a loan to Bosnia worth US$500 million to be delivered by [Stand-By Arrangement](/wiki/IMF_Stand-By_Arrangement "IMF Stand-By Arrangement"). This was scheduled to be approved in September 2012.[[173]](#cite_note-176)

The [United States Embassy](/wiki/Embassy_of_the_United_States,_Sarajevo "Embassy of the United States, Sarajevo") in [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo") produces the Country Commercial Guide – an annual report that delivers a comprehensive look at Bosnia and Herzegovina's commercial and economic environment, using economic, political, and market analysis.

By some estimates, [grey economy](/wiki/Informal_economy "Informal economy") is 25.5% of GDP.[[174]](#cite_note-177)

In 2017, exports grew by 17% when compared to the previous year, totaling €5.65 billion.[[175]](#cite_note-178) The total volume of [foreign trade](/wiki/International_trade "International trade") in 2017 amounted to €14.97 billion and increased by 14% compared to the previous year. Imports of goods increased by 12% and amounted to €9.32 billion. The [coverage of imports by exports](/wiki/Balance_of_trade "Balance of trade") increased by 3% compared to the previous year and now it is 61 percent. In 2017, Bosnia and Herzegovina mostly exported [car seats](/wiki/Car_seat "Car seat"), [electricity](/wiki/Electricity "Electricity"), [processed wood](/wiki/Wood_processing "Wood processing"), [aluminium](/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium") and [furniture](/wiki/Furniture "Furniture"). In the same year, it mostly imported [crude oil](/wiki/Petroleum "Petroleum"), [automobiles](/wiki/Car "Car"), [motor oil](/wiki/Motor_oil "Motor oil"), [coal](/wiki/Coal "Coal") and [briquettes](/wiki/Briquette "Briquette").[[176]](#cite_note-179)

The unemployment rate in 2017 was 20.5%, but [The Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies](/wiki/The_Vienna_Institute_for_International_Economic_Studies "The Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies") is predicting falling unemployment rate for the next few years. In 2018, the unemployment should be 19.4% and it should further fall to 18.8% in 2019. In 2020, the unemployment rate should go down to 18.3%.[[177]](#cite_note-180)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/a8/Avaz_Twist_Tower_in_Sarajevo_2014.jpg/250px-Avaz_Twist_Tower_in_Sarajevo_2014.jpg)](/wiki/File:Avaz_Twist_Tower_in_Sarajevo_2014.jpg)

The [Avaz Twist Tower](/wiki/Avaz_Twist_Tower "Avaz Twist Tower") in [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo"), the tallest building in Bosnia and Herzegovina

On 31 December 2017, the [Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Council_of_Ministers_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina") issued the report on public debt of Bosnia and Herzegovina, stating the public debt was reduced by €389.97 million, or by more than 6% when compared to 31 December 2016. By the end of 2017, public debt was €5.92 billion, which amounted to 35.6 percent of GDP.[[178]](#cite_note-181)

As of 31 December 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bosnia_and_Herzegovina&action=edit), there were 32,292 registered companies in the country, which together had revenues of €33.572 billion that same year.[[179]](#cite_note-182)

In 2017, the country received €397.35 million in [foreign direct investment](/wiki/Foreign_direct_investment "Foreign direct investment"), which equals to 2.5% of the GDP.[[180]](#cite_note-183)

In 2017, Bosnia and Herzegovina ranked third in the world in terms of the number of new jobs created by foreign investment, relative to the number of inhabitants.[[181]](#cite_note-184)[[182]](#cite_note-185)

In 2018, Bosnia and Herzegovina exported goods worth 11.9 billion KM (€6.07 billion), which is 7.43% higher than in the same period in 2017, while imports amounted to 19.27 billion KM (€9.83 billion), which is 5.47% higher.[[183]](#cite_note-186)

The average price of new apartments sold in the country in the first six months of 2018 is 1,639 km (€886.31) per square metre. This represents a jump of 3.5% from the previous year.[[184]](#cite_note-187)

On 30 June 2018, public debt of Bosnia and Herzegovina amounted to about €6.04 billion, of which external debt is 70.56 percent, while the internal debt is 29.4 percent of total public indebtedness. The share of public debt in gross domestic product is 34.92 percent.[[185]](#cite_note-188)

In the first 7 months of 2018, 811,660 tourists visited the country, a 12.2% jump when compared to the first 7 months of 2017.[[186]](#cite_note-189) In the first 11 months of 2018, 1,378,542 tourists visited Bosnia-Herzegovina, an increase of 12.6%, and had 2,871,004 overnight hotel stays, a 13.8% increase from the previous year. Also, 71.8% of the tourists came from foreign countries.[[187]](#cite_note-klix.ba-190) In the first seven months of 2019, 906,788 tourists visited the country, an 11.7% jump from the previous year.[[188]](#cite_note-191)

In 2018, the total value of [mergers and acquisitions](/wiki/Mergers_and_acquisitions "Mergers and acquisitions") in Bosnia and Herzegovina amounted to €404.6 million.[[189]](#cite_note-192)

In 2018, 99.5 percent of enterprises in Bosnia and Herzegovina used computers in their business, while 99.3 percent had internet connections, according to a survey conducted by the Bosnia and Herzegovina Statistics Agency.[[190]](#cite_note-193)

In 2018, Bosnia and Herzegovina received 783.4 million KM (€400.64 million) in [direct foreign investment](/wiki/Direct_foreign_investment "Direct foreign investment"), which was equivalent to 2.3% of GDP.[[191]](#cite_note-194)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Sarajevo_Tram-Stop_Banka_2011-10-28_%282%29.jpg/250px-Sarajevo_Tram-Stop_Banka_2011-10-28_%282%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Sarajevo_Tram-Stop_Banka_2011-10-28_(2).jpg)

The [Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Central_Bank_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina") in Sarajevo

In 2018, the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina made a profit of 8,430,875 km (€4,306,347).[[192]](#cite_note-195)

The [World Bank](/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank") predicted that the economy would grow 3.4% in 2019.[[193]](#cite_note-196)

Bosnia and Herzegovina was placed 83rd on the [Index of Economic Freedom](/wiki/Index_of_Economic_Freedom "Index of Economic Freedom") for 2019. The total rating for Bosnia and Herzegovina is 61.9. This position represents some progress relative to the 91st place in 2018. This result is below the regional level, but still above the global average, making Bosnia and Herzegovina a "moderately free" country.[[194]](#cite_note-197)

On 31 January 2019, total deposits in Bosnian banks were KM 21.9 billion (€11.20 billion), which represents 61.15% of nominal GDP.[[195]](#cite_note-198)

In the second quarter of 2019, the average price of new apartments sold in Bosnia and Herzegovina was 1,606 km (€821.47) per square metre.[[196]](#cite_note-199)

In the first six months of 2019, exports amounted to 5.829 billion KM (€2.98 billion), which is 0.1% less than in the same period of 2018, while imports amounted to 9.779 billion KM (€5.00 billion), which is by 4.5% more than in the same period of the previous year.[[197]](#cite_note-200)

In the first six months of 2019, foreign direct investment amounted to 650.1 million KM (€332.34 million).[[198]](#cite_note-201)

Bosnia and Herzegovina was ranked 80th in the [Global Innovation Index](/wiki/Global_Innovation_Index "Global Innovation Index") in 2024,[[199]](#cite_note-202) but its ranking dropped to 92nd in 2025.[[200]](#cite_note-203)

As of 30 November 2023, Bosnia and Herzegovina had 1.3 million registered motor vehicles.[[201]](#cite_note-204)

According to projections by the [World Tourism Organization](/wiki/World_Tourism_Organization "World Tourism Organization"), Bosnia and Herzegovina had the third highest tourism growth rate in the world between 1995 and 2020.[[202]](#cite_note-Traveloholic_Tours-205)[[203]](#cite_note-Travel_Talk_Tours_2017-206)

In 2017, 1,307,319 tourists visited Bosnia and Herzegovina, an increase of 13.7%, and had 2,677,125 overnight hotel stays, a 12.3% increase from the previous year. 71.5% of the tourists came from foreign countries.[[204]](#cite_note-207)

In 2018, 1.883.772 tourists visited Bosnia and Herzegovina, an increase of 44,1%, and had 3.843.484 overnight hotel stays, a 43.5% increase from the previous year. Also, 71.2% of the tourists came from foreign countries.[[205]](#cite_note-208)

In 2006, when ranking the best cities in the world, [Lonely Planet](/wiki/Lonely_Planet "Lonely Planet") placed [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo"), the [national capital](/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city")[[1]](#cite_note-Constitution-1) and host of the [1984 Winter Olympics](/wiki/1984_Winter_Olympics "1984 Winter Olympics"), as #43 on the list.[[206]](#cite_note-209) Tourism in Sarajevo is chiefly focused on historical, religious, and cultural aspects. In 2010, Lonely Planet's "Best in Travel" nominated it as one of the top ten cities to visit that year.[[207]](#cite_note-210) Sarajevo also won travel blog Foxnomad's "Best City to Visit" competition in 2012, beating more than one hundred other cities around the entire world.[[208]](#cite_note-211)

[Međugorje](/wiki/Medjugorje "Medjugorje") has become one of the most popular pilgrimage sites for [Catholics](/wiki/Catholics "Catholics") from around the world and has turned into Europe's third most important religious place, where each year more than 1 million people visit.[[209]](#cite_note-212) It has been estimated that 30 million pilgrims have come to Međugorje since the reputed apparitions began in 1981.[[210]](#cite_note-reuters-213) Since 2019, pilgrimages to Međugorje have been officially authorized and organized by the [Vatican](/wiki/Holy_See "Holy See").[[211]](#cite_note-Vatican_News_2019-214)

Bosnia has also become an increasingly popular skiing and [Ecotourism](/wiki/Ecotourism "Ecotourism") destination. The mountains that hosted the winter olympic games of [Bjelašnica](/wiki/Bjela%C5%A1nica "Bjelašnica"), [Jahorina](/wiki/Jahorina "Jahorina") and [Igman](/wiki/Igman "Igman") are the most visited skiing mountains in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina remains one of the last undiscovered natural regions of the southern area of the [Alps](/wiki/Alps "Alps"), with vast tracts of wild and untouched nature attracting adventurers and nature lovers. *[National Geographic](/wiki/National_Geographic "National Geographic")* named Bosnia and Herzegovina as the best mountain biking adventure destination for 2012.[[212]](#cite_note-test-215) The central [Bosnian Dinaric Alps](/wiki/Dinaric_Alps "Dinaric Alps") are favored by hikers and mountaineers, as they contain both [Mediterranean](/wiki/Mediterranean_climate "Mediterranean climate") and [Alpine](/wiki/Alpine_climate "Alpine climate") climates. [Whitewater rafting](/wiki/Rafting "Rafting") has become somewhat of a [national pastime](/wiki/National_sport "National sport") in Bosnia and Herzegovina.[[213]](#cite_note-Zuvela_2007-216) The primary rivers used for whitewater rafting in the country include the [Vrbas](/wiki/Vrbas_(river) "Vrbas (river)"), [Tara](/wiki/Tara_(Drina) "Tara (Drina)"), [Drina](/wiki/Drina "Drina"), [Neretva](/wiki/Neretva "Neretva") and [Una](/wiki/Una_(Sava) "Una (Sava)").[[214]](#cite_note-All_about_buses_2018-217) Meanwhile, the most prominent rivers are the Vrbas and Tara, as they both hosted [The 2009 World Rafting Championship](/wiki/International_Rafting_Federation "International Rafting Federation").[[215]](#cite_note-IRF_admin_2010-218)[[216]](#cite_note-Sito-Sucic_2009-219) The reason the Tara river is immensely popular for whitewater rafting is because it contains the deepest [river canyon](/wiki/Canyon "Canyon") in Europe, the [Tara River Canyon](/wiki/Tara_River_Canyon "Tara River Canyon").[[217]](#cite_note-Tara_Sport_2019-220)[[218]](#cite_note-The_Telegraph_2016-221)

Most recently, the *[Huffington Post](/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")* named Bosnia and Herzegovina the "9th Greatest Adventure in the World for 2013", adding that the country boasts "the cleanest water and air in Europe; the greatest untouched forests; and the most wildlife. The best way to experience is the three rivers trip, which purls through the best the Balkans have to offer."[[219]](#cite_note-222)

### Transport

Main article: [Transport in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Transport_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Transport in Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Sarajevo_Airport_1_2024.jpg/250px-Sarajevo_Airport_1_2024.jpg)](/wiki/File:Sarajevo_Airport_1_2024.jpg)

[Sarajevo International Airport](/wiki/Sarajevo_International_Airport "Sarajevo International Airport")

[Sarajevo International Airport](/wiki/Sarajevo_International_Airport "Sarajevo International Airport"), also known as Butmir Airport, is the main [international airport](/wiki/International_airport "International airport") in Bosnia and Herzegovina, located 3.3 [NM](/wiki/Nautical_mile "Nautical mile") (6.1 km; 3.8 mi) southwest of the [Sarajevo main railway station](/wiki/Sarajevo_main_railway_station "Sarajevo main railway station")[[220]](#cite_note-AIP-223) in the city of [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo") in the suburb of [Butmir](/wiki/Butmir "Butmir").

Railway operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina are successors of the [Yugoslav Railways](/wiki/Yugoslav_Railways "Yugoslav Railways") within the country boundaries following independence from the [former Yugoslavia](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia") in 1992. Today, they are operated by the [Railways of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Railways_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Railways of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina") (ŽFBiH) in the [Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina") and by [Republika Srpska Railways](/wiki/Republika_Srpska_Railways "Republika Srpska Railways") (ŽRS) in [Republika Srpska](/wiki/Republika_Srpska "Republika Srpska").

### Telecommunications

Main article: [Telecommunications in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Telecommunications_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Telecommunications in Bosnia and Herzegovina")

The Bosnian communications market was fully [liberalised](/wiki/Economic_liberalization "Economic liberalization") in January 2006. The three [landline](/wiki/Landline "Landline") telephone operators predominantly provide services in their operating areas but have nationwide licenses for domestic and international calls. Mobile data services are also available, including high-speed [EDGE](/wiki/Enhanced_Data_rates_for_GSM_Evolution "Enhanced Data rates for GSM Evolution"), [3G](/wiki/3G "3G") and [4G](/wiki/4G "4G") services.[[221]](#cite_note-224)

*[Oslobođenje](/wiki/Oslobo%C4%91enje "Oslobođenje")* (Liberation), founded in 1943, is one of the country's longest running continuously circulating newspapers. There are many national publications, including the *[Dnevni avaz](/wiki/Dnevni_avaz "Dnevni avaz")* (Daily Voice), founded in 1995, and *Jutarnje Novine* (Morning News), to name but a few in circulation in Sarajevo.[[222]](#cite_note-225) Other local periodicals include the Croatian *[Hrvatska riječ](/wiki/Hrvatska_rije%C4%8D "Hrvatska riječ")* newspaper and Bosnian *[Start](/w/index.php?title=Start_(Bosnian_magazine)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Start (Bosnian magazine) (page does not exist)")* magazine, as well as *Slobodna Bosna* (*Free Bosnia*) and *BH Dani* (*BH Days*) weekly newspapers. *[Novi Plamen](/wiki/Novi_Plamen "Novi Plamen")*, a monthly magazine, was the most left-wing publication. International news station [Al Jazeera](/wiki/Al_Jazeera_Media_Network "Al Jazeera Media Network") maintains a [sister channel](/wiki/Sister_channel "Sister channel") catering to the [Balkan](/wiki/Balkans "Balkans") region, [Al Jazeera Balkans](/wiki/Al_Jazeera_Balkans "Al Jazeera Balkans"), broadcasting out of and based in Sarajevo.[[223]](#cite_note-226) Since 2014, the [N1 platform](/wiki/N1_(TV_channel) "N1 (TV channel)") has broadcast as an affiliate of [CNN International](/wiki/CNN_International "CNN International"), with offices in Sarajevo, [Zagreb](/wiki/Zagreb "Zagreb") and [Belgrade](/wiki/Belgrade "Belgrade").[[224]](#cite_note-227)

As of 2021, Bosnia and Herzegovina ranked second highest in [press freedom](/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press "Freedom of the press") in the region, after [Croatia](/wiki/Croatia "Croatia"), and is placed 58th internationally.[[225]](#cite_note-228)

As of December 2021[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bosnia_and_Herzegovina&action=edit), there are 3,374,094 internet users in the country, or 95.55% of the entire population.[[226]](#cite_note-229)

Demographics
------------

Main articles: [Demographics of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Demographics_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Demographics of Bosnia and Herzegovina") and [Bosnians](/wiki/Bosnians "Bosnians")

See also: [Demographic history of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Demographic_history_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Demographic history of Bosnia and Herzegovina")

According to the [1991 census](/wiki/1991_population_census_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "1991 population census in Bosnia and Herzegovina"), Bosnia and Herzegovina had a population of 4,369,319, while the 1996 World Bank Group census showed a decrease to 3,764,425.[[227]](#cite_note-230) Large population migrations during the [Yugoslav Wars](/wiki/Yugoslav_Wars "Yugoslav Wars") in the 1990s have caused demographic shifts in the country. Between 1991 and 2013, political disagreements made it impossible to organize a census. A census had been planned for 2011,[[228]](#cite_note-231) and then for 2012,[[229]](#cite_note-232) but was delayed until October 2013. The [2013 census](/wiki/2013_population_census_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "2013 population census in Bosnia and Herzegovina") found a total population of 3,531,159 people,[[5]](#cite_note-Popis2013-5) a drop of approximately 20% since 1991.[[230]](#cite_note-233) The 2013 census figures include non-permanent Bosnian residents and for this reason are contested by Republika Srpska officials and Serb politicians (see Ethnic groups below).[[231]](#cite_note-WithoutSerbAgreement-234)

According to [United Nations Population Fund](/wiki/United_Nations_Population_Fund "United Nations Population Fund"), between 2013 and 2020, Bosnia and Herzegovina was losing 25,000 people yearly. The demographic expert Stevo Palašić concluded that between 1991 and 2023, Bosnia and Herzegovina lost 1.4 million people or one-third of its population. [Tim Judah](/wiki/Tim_Judah "Tim Judah") considers the 2022 state agency estimate of 3.4 million inhabitants "extremely optimistic" and wrongly based on the 2013 census. Pašalić, who based his calculation on the official data, estimates the number to 2.9 million. Other demographic experts from Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Miodrag Pantović and Nermin Oruč, estimate that the total population in Bosnia and Herzegovina is slightly below 1.5 million.[[11]](#cite_note-Vecernji-12)

### Urban areas

Main article: [List of cities in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "List of cities in Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo") is home to 419,957 inhabitants in its urban area which comprises the [City of Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo#Municipalities_and_city_government "Sarajevo") as well as the municipalities of [Ilidža](/wiki/Ilid%C5%BEa "Ilidža"), [Vogošća](/wiki/Vogo%C5%A1%C4%87a "Vogošća"), [Istočna Ilidža](/wiki/Isto%C4%8Dna_Ilid%C5%BEa "Istočna Ilidža"), [Istočno Novo Sarajevo](/wiki/Isto%C4%8Dno_Novo_Sarajevo "Istočno Novo Sarajevo") and [Istočni Stari Grad](/wiki/Isto%C4%8Dni_Stari_Grad "Istočni Stari Grad").[[232]](#cite_note-235) The [metro area](/wiki/Sarajevo_metropolitan_area "Sarajevo metropolitan area") has a population of 555,210 and includes [Sarajevo Canton](/wiki/Sarajevo_Canton "Sarajevo Canton"), [East Sarajevo](/wiki/Isto%C4%8Dno_Sarajevo "Istočno Sarajevo") and the municipalities of [Breza](/wiki/Breza,_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Breza, Bosnia and Herzegovina"), [Kiseljak](/wiki/Kiseljak "Kiseljak"), [Kreševo](/wiki/Kre%C5%A1evo "Kreševo") and [Visoko](/wiki/Visoko "Visoko").[[233]](#cite_note-236)

### Ethnic groups

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/BiH_-_Etnicki_sastav_po_opstinama_2013_1.gif/250px-BiH_-_Etnicki_sastav_po_opstinama_2013_1.gif)](/wiki/File:BiH_-_Etnicki_sastav_po_opstinama_2013_1.gif)

Ethnic composition in Bosnia and Herzegovina as of 2013:[[5]](#cite_note-Popis2013-5)

1. [Bosniaks](/wiki/Bosniaks "Bosniaks") (50.1%)
2. [Serbs](/wiki/Serbs_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina") (30.8%)

Bosnia and Herzegovina is home to three ethnic "[constituent peoples](/wiki/Ethnic_groups_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina")", namely [Bosniaks](/wiki/Bosniaks "Bosniaks"), [Serbs](/wiki/Serbs "Serbs") and [Croats](/wiki/Croats "Croats"), plus a number of smaller groups including [Jews](/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "History of the Jews in Bosnia and Herzegovina") and [Roma](/wiki/Romani_people_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Romani people in Bosnia and Herzegovina").[[234]](#cite_note-237) According to data from the 2013 census published by the [Agency for Statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Statistical_system_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina#The_Agency_for_Statistics_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_(BHAS) "Statistical system of Bosnia and Herzegovina"), Bosniaks constitute 50.1% of the population, Serbs 30.8%, Croats 15.5% and others 2.7%, with the remaining respondents not declaring their ethnicity or not answering.[[5]](#cite_note-Popis2013-5) The census results are contested by the [Republika Srpska](/wiki/Republika_Srpska "Republika Srpska") statistical office and by [Bosnian Serb](/wiki/Serbs_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina") politicians.[[235]](#cite_note-238) The dispute over the census concerns the inclusion of non-permanent Bosnian residents in the figures, which Republika Srpska officials oppose.[[231]](#cite_note-WithoutSerbAgreement-234) The [European Union](/wiki/European_Union "European Union")'s statistics office, [Eurostat](/wiki/Eurostat "Eurostat"), concluded in May 2016 that the census methodology used by the Bosnian statistical agency is in line with international recommendations.[[236]](#cite_note-239)

### Languages

Bosnia's constitution does not specify any official languages.[[237]](#cite_note-240)[[238]](#cite_note-241)[[4]](#cite_note-Footitt-4) However, academics Hilary Footitt and Michael Kelly note the [Dayton Agreement](/wiki/Dayton_Agreement "Dayton Agreement") states it[*[clarification needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*] is "done in [Bosnian](/wiki/Bosnian_language "Bosnian language"), [Croatian](/wiki/Croatian_language "Croatian language"), English and [Serbian](/wiki/Serbian_language "Serbian language")", and they describe this as the "de facto recognition of three official languages" at the state level. The equal status of Bosnian, Serbian and Croatian was verified by the [Constitutional Court](/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina") in 2000.[[4]](#cite_note-Footitt-4) It ruled the provisions of the [Federation](/wiki/Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina") and Republika Srpska constitutions on language were incompatible with the state constitution, since they only recognised Bosnian and Croatian (in the case of the Federation) and Serbian (in the case of Republika Srpska) as official languages at the entity level. As a result, the wording of the entity constitutions was changed and all three languages were made official in both entities.[[4]](#cite_note-Footitt-4) The three [standard languages](/wiki/Standard_language "Standard language") are fully [mutually intelligible](/wiki/Mutual_intelligibility "Mutual intelligibility") and are known collectively under the appellation of [Serbo-Croatian](/wiki/Serbo-Croatian "Serbo-Croatian"), despite this term not being formally recognized in the country. Use of one of the three languages has become a marker of ethnic identity.[[239]](#cite_note-242) Michael Kelly and Catherine Baker argue: "The three official languages of today's Bosnian state...represent the symbolic assertion of national identity over the pragmatism of mutual intelligibility".[[240]](#cite_note-243)

According to the 1992 [European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages](/wiki/European_Charter_for_Regional_or_Minority_Languages "European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages") (ECRML), Bosnia and Herzegovina recognizes the following minority languages: [Albanian](/wiki/Albanian_language "Albanian language"), [Montenegrin](/wiki/Montenegrin_language "Montenegrin language"), [Czech](/wiki/Czech_language "Czech language"), [Italian](/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language"), [Hungarian](/wiki/Hungarian_language "Hungarian language"), [Macedonian](/wiki/Macedonian_language "Macedonian language"), [German](/wiki/German_language "German language"), [Polish](/wiki/Polish_language "Polish language"), [Romani](/wiki/Romani_language "Romani language"), [Romanian](/wiki/Romanian_language "Romanian language"), [Rusyn](/wiki/Rusyn_language "Rusyn language"), [Slovak](/wiki/Slovak_language "Slovak language"), [Slovene](/wiki/Slovene_language "Slovene language"), [Turkish](/wiki/Turkish_language "Turkish language"), [Ukrainian](/wiki/Ukrainian_language "Ukrainian language") and Jewish ([Yiddish](/wiki/Yiddish "Yiddish") and [Ladino](/wiki/Judaeo-Spanish "Judaeo-Spanish")).[[241]](#cite_note-charter-ratifications-244)

The German minority in Bosnia and Herzegovina are mostly remnants of [Danube Swabians](/wiki/Danube_Swabians "Danube Swabians"), who settled in the area after the [Habsburg monarchy](/wiki/Austrian_Empire "Austrian Empire") claimed the Balkans from the [Ottoman Empire](/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"). Due to [expulsions](/wiki/Flight_and_expulsion_of_Germans_(1944%E2%80%931950) "Flight and expulsion of Germans (1944–1950)") and [(forced) assimilation](/wiki/Persecution_of_Germans "Persecution of Germans") after the two [World wars](/wiki/World_war "World war"), the number of ethnic Germans in Bosnia and Herzegovina was drastically diminished.[[242]](#cite_note-245)

In the 2013 census, 52.86% of the population consider their mother tongue Bosnian, 30.76% Serbian, 14.6% Croatian and 1.57% another language, with 0.21% not giving an answer.[[5]](#cite_note-Popis2013-5)

### Education

Main article: [Education in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Education_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Education in Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Sarajevo_University_building.JPG/250px-Sarajevo_University_building.JPG)](/wiki/File:Sarajevo_University_building.JPG)

The [University of Sarajevo](/wiki/University_of_Sarajevo "University of Sarajevo")'s [Faculty of Law](/wiki/Faculty_of_Law,_University_of_Sarajevo "Faculty of Law, University of Sarajevo")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Mostar_gimnasium.jpg/250px-Mostar_gimnasium.jpg)](/wiki/File:Mostar_gimnasium.jpg)

[Gimnazija Mostar](/wiki/Gimnazija_Mostar "Gimnazija Mostar") in [Mostar](/wiki/Mostar "Mostar")

Primary schooling lasts for nine years. Secondary education is provided by general and technical secondary schools (typically [Gymnasiums](/wiki/Gymnasium_(school) "Gymnasium (school)")) where studies typically last for four years. All forms of secondary schooling include an element of [vocational training](/wiki/Vocational_education "Vocational education"). Pupils graduating from general secondary schools obtain the *[Matura](/wiki/Matura "Matura")* and can enroll in any tertiary educational institution or academy by passing a qualification examination prescribed by the governing body or institution. Students graduating technical subjects obtain a [Diploma](/wiki/Diploma "Diploma").[[244]](#cite_note-247)

The first bespoke higher-education institution was a school of [Sufi](/wiki/Sufism "Sufism") philosophy established by [Gazi Husrev-beg](/wiki/Gazi_Husrev_Bey "Gazi Husrev Bey") in 1531. Numerous other religious schools then followed. In 1887, under the [Austro-Hungarian Empire](/wiki/Austria-Hungary "Austria-Hungary"), a [Sharia](/wiki/Sharia "Sharia") law school began a five-year program.[[245]](#cite_note-248)

In the 1940s, the [University of Sarajevo](/wiki/University_of_Sarajevo "University of Sarajevo") became the city's first secular higher education institute. In the 1950s, post-baccalaurate graduate degrees became available.[[246]](#cite_note-249) Severely damaged during the [war](/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War"), it was recently rebuilt in partnership with more than 40 other universities. There are various other institutions of higher education, including: [University Džemal Bijedić of Mostar](/wiki/University_D%C5%BEemal_Bijedi%C4%87_of_Mostar "University Džemal Bijedić of Mostar"), [University of Banja Luka](/wiki/University_of_Banja_Luka "University of Banja Luka"), [University of Mostar](/wiki/University_of_Mostar "University of Mostar"), [University of East Sarajevo](/wiki/University_of_East_Sarajevo "University of East Sarajevo"), [University of Tuzla](/wiki/University_of_Tuzla "University of Tuzla"), [American University in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/American_University_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "American University in Bosnia and Herzegovina") and the [Academy of Sciences and Arts of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_and_Arts_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Academy of Sciences and Arts of Bosnia and Herzegovina").

Also, Bosnia and Herzegovina is home to several private and international higher education institutions, some of which are:

* [Sarajevo School of Science and Technology](/wiki/Sarajevo_School_of_Science_and_Technology "Sarajevo School of Science and Technology")
* [International University of Sarajevo](/wiki/International_University_of_Sarajevo "International University of Sarajevo")
* [American University in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/American_University_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "American University in Bosnia and Herzegovina")
* [Sarajevo Graduate School of Business](/wiki/Sarajevo_Graduate_School_of_Business "Sarajevo Graduate School of Business")
* [International Burch University](/wiki/International_Burch_University "International Burch University")
* [United World College in Mostar](/wiki/United_World_College_in_Mostar "United World College in Mostar")

### Architecture

Main article: [Architecture of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Architecture_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Architecture of Bosnia and Herzegovina")

The [architecture of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Architecture_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Architecture of Bosnia and Herzegovina") is largely influenced by four major periods where political and social changes influenced the creation of distinct cultural and architectural habits of the population. ### Media

Main article: [Mass media in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Mass_media_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Mass media in Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/d6/Radio_and_Television_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_%28BHRT%29_building%2C_Sarajevo.jpg/250px-Radio_and_Television_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_%28BHRT%29_building%2C_Sarajevo.jpg)](/wiki/File:Radio_and_Television_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_(BHRT)_building,_Sarajevo.jpg)

[BHRT](/wiki/Radio_and_Television_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Radio and Television of Bosnia and Herzegovina") headquarters in Sarajevo

Some television, magazines, and newspapers in Bosnia and Herzegovina are state-owned, and some are for-profit corporations funded by [advertising](/wiki/Advertising "Advertising"), [subscription](/wiki/Subscription_business_model "Subscription business model"), and other sales-related revenues. The [Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Constitution_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina") guarantees [freedom of speech](/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech").

As a [country in transition](/wiki/Transition_economy "Transition economy") with a post-war legacy and a [complex domestic political structure](/wiki/Politics_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Politics of Bosnia and Herzegovina"), Bosnia and Herzegovina's media system is under transformation. In the early post-war period (1995–2005), media development was guided mainly by international donors and cooperation agencies, who invested to help reconstruct, diversify, democratize and professionalize media outlets.[[248]](#cite_note-251)[[249]](#cite_note-EJC-252)

Post-war developments included the establishment of an independent Communication Regulatory Agency, the adoption of a Press Code, the establishment of the Press Council, the decriminalization of libel and defamation, the introduction of a rather advanced Freedom of Access to Information Law, and the creation of a Public Service Broadcasting System from the formerly state-owned broadcaster.
Yet, internationally backed positive developments have been often obstructed by domestic elites, and the professionalisation of media and journalists has proceeded only slowly. High levels of partisanship and linkages between the media and the political systems hinder the adherence to professional code of conducts.[[249]](#cite_note-EJC-252)

### Literature

Main article: [Literature of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Literature_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Literature of Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/S._Kragujevic%2C_Andric_na_vest_o_N._nagradi_1961.JPG/250px-S._Kragujevic%2C_Andric_na_vest_o_N._nagradi_1961.JPG)](/wiki/File:S._Kragujevic,_Andric_na_vest_o_N._nagradi_1961.JPG)

[Ivo Andrić](/wiki/Ivo_Andri%C4%87 "Ivo Andrić") with his wife [Milica](/wiki/Milica_Babi%C4%87-Jovanovi%C4%87 "Milica Babić-Jovanović"), upon learning he had won the [Nobel Prize in Literature](/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature")

Bosnia and Herzegovina has a rich literature, including the [Nobel Prize](/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize") winner [Ivo Andrić](/wiki/Ivo_Andri%C4%87 "Ivo Andrić") and poets such as [Antun Branko Šimić](/wiki/Antun_Branko_%C5%A0imi%C4%87 "Antun Branko Šimić"), [Aleksa Šantić](/wiki/Aleksa_%C5%A0anti%C4%87 "Aleksa Šantić"), [Jovan Dučić](/wiki/Jovan_Du%C4%8Di%C4%87 "Jovan Dučić") and [Mak Dizdar](/wiki/Mak_Dizdar "Mak Dizdar"), writers such as [Zlatko Topčić](/wiki/Zlatko_Top%C4%8Di%C4%87 "Zlatko Topčić"), [Meša Selimović](/wiki/Me%C5%A1a_Selimovi%C4%87 "Meša Selimović"), [Semezdin Mehmedinović](/wiki/Semezdin_Mehmedinovi%C4%87 "Semezdin Mehmedinović"), [Miljenko Jergović](/wiki/Miljenko_Jergovi%C4%87 "Miljenko Jergović"), [Isak Samokovlija](/wiki/Isak_Samokovlija "Isak Samokovlija"), [Safvet-beg Bašagić](/wiki/Safvet-beg_Ba%C5%A1agi%C4%87 "Safvet-beg Bašagić"), [Abdulah Sidran](/wiki/Abdulah_Sidran "Abdulah Sidran"), [Petar Kočić](/wiki/Petar_Ko%C4%8Di%C4%87 "Petar Kočić"), [Aleksandar Hemon](/wiki/Aleksandar_Hemon "Aleksandar Hemon"), [Mehmed Begić](/wiki/Mehmed_Begi%C4%87 "Mehmed Begić") and [Nedžad Ibrišimović](/wiki/Ned%C5%BEad_Ibri%C5%A1imovi%C4%87 "Nedžad Ibrišimović").

The [National Theater](/wiki/Sarajevo_National_Theatre "Sarajevo National Theatre") was founded in 1919 in [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo") and its first director was dramatist [Branislav Nušić](/wiki/Branislav_Nu%C5%A1i%C4%87 "Branislav Nušić"). Magazines such as *[Novi Plamen](/wiki/Novi_Plamen "Novi Plamen")* or *Sarajevske sveske* are some of the more prominent publications covering cultural and literary themes.

By the late 1950s, Ivo Andrić's works had been translated into a number of languages. In 1958, the [Association of Writers of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Association_of_Writers_of_Yugoslavia "Association of Writers of Yugoslavia") nominated Andrić as its first ever candidate for the [Nobel Prize in Literature](/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature")

### Art

Main article: [Bosnian and Herzegovinan art](/wiki/Bosnian_and_Herzegovinan_art "Bosnian and Herzegovinan art")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Bosniangraves_bosniska_gravar_februari_2007_stecak_stecci5.jpg/250px-Bosniangraves_bosniska_gravar_februari_2007_stecak_stecci5.jpg)](/wiki/File:Bosniangraves_bosniska_gravar_februari_2007_stecak_stecci5.jpg)

[Stećci](/wiki/Ste%C4%87ak "Stećak") from [Radimlja](/wiki/Ste%C4%87ak_necropolis_Radimlja "Stećak necropolis Radimlja"), near [Stolac](/wiki/Stolac "Stolac") (13th century)

The [art of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_art "Bosnia and Herzegovina art") was always evolving and ranged from the original medieval tombstones called [Stećci](/wiki/Ste%C4%87ak "Stećak") to paintings in [Kotromanić](/wiki/Kotromani%C4%87_dynasty "Kotromanić dynasty") court. Twenty stećak necropolis sites in Bosnia and Herzegovina were added on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2006.[[250]](#cite_note-253) However, only with the arrival of [Austro-Hungarians](/wiki/Austria-Hungary "Austria-Hungary") did the painting renaissance in Bosnia really begin to flourish. The first educated artists from European academies appeared with the beginning of the 20th century. Among those are: [Gabrijel Jurkić](/wiki/Gabrijel_Jurki%C4%87 "Gabrijel Jurkić"), [Petar Šain](/wiki/Petar_%C5%A0ain "Petar Šain"), [Roman Petrović](/wiki/Roman_Petrovi%C4%87 "Roman Petrović") and [Lazar Drljača](/wiki/Lazar_Drlja%C4%8Da "Lazar Drljača").
After [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), artists like [Mersad Berber](/wiki/Mersad_Berber "Mersad Berber") and [Safet Zec](/wiki/Safet_Zec "Safet Zec") rose in popularity. In 2007, [Ars Aevi](/wiki/Ars_Aevi "Ars Aevi"), a museum of contemporary art that includes works by renowned world artists, was founded in Sarajevo.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

### Music

Main article: [Music of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Music_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Music of Bosnia and Herzegovina")

See also: [List of Bosnia and Herzegovina patriotic songs](/wiki/List_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_patriotic_songs "List of Bosnia and Herzegovina patriotic songs") and [Bosnian root music](/wiki/Bosnian_root_music "Bosnian root music")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/43._TKB_-_Seljo_z_Sarajewa_%28Bo%C5%9Bnia_i_Hercegowina%29_10.JPG/250px-43._TKB_-_Seljo_z_Sarajewa_%28Bo%C5%9Bnia_i_Hercegowina%29_10.JPG)](/wiki/File:43._TKB_-_Seljo_z_Sarajewa_(Bo%C5%9Bnia_i_Hercegowina)_10.JPG)

[Bosniaks](/wiki/Bosniaks "Bosniaks") dancing a traditional [kolo](/wiki/Kolo_(dance) "Kolo (dance)")

Typical Bosnian songs are *[ganga](/wiki/Ganga_(music) "Ganga (music)"), rera*, and the traditional Slavic music for the folk dances such as *[kolo](/wiki/Kolo_(dance) "Kolo (dance)")*, while from the Ottoman era the most popular is [Sevdalinka](/wiki/Sevdalinka "Sevdalinka"). Pop and Rock music has a tradition here as well, with the more famous musicians including [Dino Zonić](/wiki/Dino_Zoni%C4%87 "Dino Zonić"), [Goran Bregović](/wiki/Goran_Bregovi%C4%87 "Goran Bregović"), [Davorin Popović](/wiki/Davorin_Popovi%C4%87 "Davorin Popović"), [Kemal Monteno](/wiki/Kemal_Monteno "Kemal Monteno"), [Zdravko Čolić](/wiki/Zdravko_%C4%8Coli%C4%87 "Zdravko Čolić"), [Elvir Laković Laka](/wiki/Elvir_Lakovi%C4%87_Laka "Elvir Laković Laka"), [Edo Maajka](/wiki/Edo_Maajka "Edo Maajka"), [Hari Varešanović](/wiki/Hari_Vare%C5%A1anovi%C4%87 "Hari Varešanović"), [Dino Merlin](/wiki/Dino_Merlin "Dino Merlin"), [Mladen Vojičić Tifa](/wiki/Mladen_Voji%C4%8Di%C4%87_Tifa "Mladen Vojičić Tifa"), [Željko Bebek](/wiki/%C5%BDeljko_Bebek "Željko Bebek"), etc. Other composers such as [Đorđe Novković](/wiki/%C4%90or%C4%91e_Novkovi%C4%87 "Đorđe Novković"), [Al' Dino](/wiki/Al%27_Dino "Al' Dino"), [Haris Džinović](/wiki/Haris_D%C5%BEinovi%C4%87 "Haris Džinović"), [Kornelije Kovač](/wiki/Kornelije_Kova%C4%8D "Kornelije Kovač"), and many [rock and pop bands](/wiki/Musical_ensemble#Rock_and_pop_bands "Musical ensemble"), for example, [Bijelo Dugme](/wiki/Bijelo_Dugme "Bijelo Dugme"), [Crvena jabuka](/wiki/Crvena_jabuka "Crvena jabuka"), [Divlje jagode](/wiki/Divlje_jagode "Divlje jagode"), [Indexi](/wiki/Indexi "Indexi"), [Plavi orkestar](/wiki/Plavi_orkestar "Plavi orkestar"), [Zabranjeno Pušenje](/wiki/Zabranjeno_Pu%C5%A1enje "Zabranjeno Pušenje"), [Ambasadori](/wiki/Ambasadori "Ambasadori"), [Dubioza kolektiv](/wiki/Dubioza_kolektiv "Dubioza kolektiv"), who were among the leading ones in the former Yugoslavia. Bosnia is home to the composer [Dušan Šestić](/wiki/Du%C5%A1an_%C5%A0esti%C4%87 "Dušan Šestić"), the creator of the [National Anthem of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/National_Anthem_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "National Anthem of Bosnia and Herzegovina") and father of singer [Marija Šestić](/wiki/Marija_%C5%A0esti%C4%87 "Marija Šestić"), to the jazz musician, educator and Bosnian jazz ambassador [Sinan Alimanović](/wiki/Sinan_Alimanovi%C4%87 "Sinan Alimanović"), composer [Saša Lošić](/wiki/Sa%C5%A1a_Lo%C5%A1i%C4%87 "Saša Lošić") and pianist [Saša Toperić](/wiki/Sa%C5%A1a_Toperi%C4%87 "Saša Toperić"). In the villages, especially in [Herzegovina](/wiki/Herzegovina "Herzegovina"), Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats play the ancient [gusle](/wiki/Gusle "Gusle"). The gusle is used mainly to recite epic poems in a usually dramatic tone.

Probably the most distinctive and identifiably "Bosnian" of music, Sevdalinka is a kind of emotional, melancholic folk song that often describes sad subjects such as love and loss, the death of a dear person or heartbreak.[[251]](#cite_note-254) Sevdalinkas were traditionally performed with a [saz](/wiki/Ba%C4%9Flama "Bağlama"), a Turkish string instrument, which was later replaced by the accordion.[[252]](#cite_note-255) However the more modern arrangement is typically a vocalist accompanied by the accordion along with snare drums, upright bass, guitars, clarinets and violins.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/Ensemble_%22Kolo%22%2C_%C4%90ur%C4%91evdan_customs_from_Podgrme%C4%8D.jpg/250px-Ensemble_%22Kolo%22%2C_%C4%90ur%C4%91evdan_customs_from_Podgrme%C4%8D.jpg)](/wiki/File:Ensemble_%22Kolo%22,_%C4%90ur%C4%91evdan_customs_from_Podgrme%C4%8D.jpg)

[Serbs](/wiki/Serbs_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina") from [Bosanska Krajina](/wiki/Bosanska_Krajina "Bosanska Krajina") in traditional clothing

Rural folk traditions in Bosnia and Herzegovina include the shouted, [polyphonic](/wiki/Polyphony "Polyphony") ganga and "ravne pjesme" (*flat song*) styles, as well as instruments like a droneless [bagpipe](/wiki/Bagpipes "Bagpipes"), wooden [flute](/wiki/Flute "Flute") and [šargija](/wiki/%C5%A0argija "Šargija"). The gusle, an instrument found throughout the [Balkans](/wiki/Balkans "Balkans"), is also used to accompany ancient [Slavic](/wiki/Slavs "Slavs") [epic](/wiki/Epic_poetry "Epic poetry") [poems](/wiki/Poetry "Poetry"). There are also Bosnian folk songs in the [Ladino](/wiki/Judaeo-Spanish "Judaeo-Spanish") language, derived from the area's Jewish population.

*Bosnian roots music* came from [Central Bosnia](/wiki/Central_Bosnia "Central Bosnia"), [Posavina](/wiki/Posavina "Posavina"), the [Drina](/wiki/Drina "Drina") valley and [Kalesija](/wiki/Kalesija "Kalesija"). It is usually performed by singers with two violinists and a šargija player. These bands first appeared around [World War I](/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and became popular in the 1960s. This is the third oldest music after the Sevdalinka and [ilahija](/wiki/Nasheed "Nasheed"). Self-taught people, mostly in two or three members of the different choices of old instruments, mostly in the violin, sacking, saz, drums, flutes (*zurle*) or wooden flute, as others have already called, the original performers of Bosnian music that can not be written notes, transmitted by ear from generation to generation, family is usually hereditary. It is thought to be brought from Persia-Kalesi tribe that settled in the area of the present Sprečanski valleys and hence probably the name Kalesija. In this part of Bosnia, it is the most common. This kind of music was enjoyed by all three peoples in Bosnia, Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats, and it contributed a lot to reconcile people socializing, entertainment and other organizations through festivals. In Kalesija, it is maintained each year with the original Bosnian Festival music.

### Cinema and theatre

Main article: [List of Bosnia and Herzegovina films](/wiki/List_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_films "List of Bosnia and Herzegovina films")

Sarajevo is internationally renowned for its eclectic and diverse selection of festivals. The [Sarajevo Film Festival](/wiki/Sarajevo_Film_Festival "Sarajevo Film Festival") was established in 1995, during the [Bosnian War](/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War") and has become the premier and largest film festival in the Balkans and [Southeast Europe](/wiki/Southeast_Europe "Southeast Europe").

Bosnia has a rich cinematic and film heritage, dating back to the [Kingdom of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Yugoslavia "Kingdom of Yugoslavia"); many Bosnian filmmakers have achieved international prominence and some have won international awards ranging from the [Academy Awards](/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") to multiple [Palme d'Ors](/wiki/Palme_d%27Or "Palme d'Or") and [Golden Bears](/wiki/Golden_Bear "Golden Bear"). Some notable Bosnian screenwriters, directors and producers are [Danis Tanović](/wiki/Danis_Tanovi%C4%87 "Danis Tanović") (known for the Academy Award and [Golden Globe Award](/wiki/Golden_Globe_Awards "Golden Globe Awards") winning 2001 film *[No Man's Land](/wiki/No_Man%27s_Land_(2001_film) "No Man's Land (2001 film)")* and [Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize](/wiki/Silver_Bear_Grand_Jury_Prize "Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize") winning 2016 film *[Death in Sarajevo](/wiki/Death_in_Sarajevo "Death in Sarajevo")*),[[253]](#cite_note-256) [Jasmila Žbanić](/wiki/Jasmila_%C5%BDbani%C4%87 "Jasmila Žbanić") (won Golden Bear, Academy Award and [BAFTA](/wiki/British_Academy_Film_Awards "British Academy Film Awards") nominated 2020 film *[Quo Vadis, Aida?](/wiki/Quo_Vadis,_Aida%3F "Quo Vadis, Aida?")*), [Emir Kusturica](/wiki/Emir_Kusturica "Emir Kusturica") (won two Palme d'Ors at [Cannes](/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival")), [Zlatko Topčić](/wiki/Zlatko_Top%C4%8Di%C4%87 "Zlatko Topčić"), [Ademir Kenović](/wiki/Ademir_Kenovi%C4%87 "Ademir Kenović"), [Ahmed Imamović](/wiki/Ahmed_Imamovi%C4%87 "Ahmed Imamović"), [Pjer Žalica](/wiki/Pjer_%C5%BDalica "Pjer Žalica"), [Aida Begić](/wiki/Aida_Begi%C4%87 "Aida Begić"), etc.

### Cuisine

Main article: [Bosnia and Herzegovina cuisine](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_cuisine "Bosnia and Herzegovina cuisine")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Bosnian_meat_platter.JPG/250px-Bosnian_meat_platter.JPG)](/wiki/File:Bosnian_meat_platter.JPG)

Bosnian meat platter that contains, among other things, [ćevapi](/wiki/%C4%86evapi "Ćevapi"), which is considered the [national dish](/wiki/National_dish "National dish") of Bosnia and Herzegovina

Bosnian cuisine uses many spices, in moderate quantities. Most dishes are light, as they are boiled; the sauces are fully natural, consisting of little more than the natural juices of the vegetables in the dish. Typical ingredients include tomatoes, potatoes, onions, [garlic](/wiki/Garlic "Garlic"), [peppers](/wiki/Capsicum "Capsicum"), [cucumbers](/wiki/Cucumber "Cucumber"), carrots, [cabbage](/wiki/Cabbage "Cabbage"), [mushrooms](/wiki/Mushroom "Mushroom"), [spinach](/wiki/Spinach "Spinach"), [zucchini](/wiki/Zucchini "Zucchini"), [dried beans](/wiki/Bean "Bean"), fresh beans, [plums](/wiki/Plum "Plum"), milk, [paprika](/wiki/Paprika "Paprika") and cream called [pavlaka](/wiki/Smetana_(dairy_product) "Smetana (dairy product)"). Bosnian cuisine is balanced between [Western](/wiki/Western_culture "Western culture") and [Eastern](/wiki/Eastern_world "Eastern world") influences. As a result of the [Ottoman](/wiki/Turkish_cuisine "Turkish cuisine") administration for almost 500 years, Bosnian food is closely related to Turkish, [Greek](/wiki/Greek_cuisine "Greek cuisine") and other former Ottoman and [Mediterranean](/wiki/Mediterranean_cuisine "Mediterranean cuisine") cuisines. However, due to Austrian rule, there are many influences from [Central Europe](/wiki/Central_European_cuisine "Central European cuisine"). Typical meat dishes include primarily beef and [lamb](/wiki/Lamb_and_mutton "Lamb and mutton"). Some local specialties are [ćevapi](/wiki/%C4%86evapi "Ćevapi"), [burek](/wiki/B%C3%B6rek "Börek"), [dolma](/wiki/Dolma "Dolma"), [sarma](/wiki/Sarma_(food) "Sarma (food)"), [pilav](/wiki/Pilaf "Pilaf"), [goulash](/wiki/Goulash "Goulash"), [ajvar](/wiki/Ajvar "Ajvar") and a whole range of Eastern sweets. Ćevapi is a grilled dish of minced meat, a type of [kebab](/wiki/Kebab "Kebab"), popular in former Yugoslavia and considered a national dish in Bosnia and Herzegovina[[254]](#cite_note-257) and [Serbia](/wiki/Serbia "Serbia").[[255]](#cite_note-258)[[256]](#cite_note-259)[[257]](#cite_note-260)

Local wines come from [Herzegovina](/wiki/Herzegovina "Herzegovina") where the climate is suitable for growing grapes. Herzegovinian *loza* (similar to Italian [Grappa](/wiki/Grappa "Grappa") but less sweet) is very popular. Plum (*rakija*) or apple (*jabukovača*) alcohol beverages are produced in the north. In the south, distilleries used to produce vast quantities of [brandy](/wiki/Brandy "Brandy") and supply all of ex-Yugoslav alcohol factories (brandy is the base of most [alcoholic drinks](/wiki/Alcoholic_drink "Alcoholic drink")).

Coffeehouses, where [Bosnian coffee](/wiki/Turkish_coffee "Turkish coffee") is served in [džezva](/wiki/Cezve "Cezve") with [rahat lokum](/wiki/Turkish_delight "Turkish delight") and [sugar cubes](/wiki/Cube_sugar "Cube sugar"), are common in [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo") and every city in the country. Coffee drinking is a favorite Bosnian pastime and part of the culture. Bosnia and Herzegovina is the ninth country in the entire world by per capita coffee consumption.[[258]](#cite_note-261)

Bosnia and Herzegovina regularly qualifies for the [European Championship in Basketball](/wiki/EuroBasket "EuroBasket"), with players including [Mirza Teletović](/wiki/Mirza_Teletovi%C4%87 "Mirza Teletović"), [Nihad Đedović](/wiki/Nihad_%C4%90edovi%C4%87 "Nihad Đedović") and [Jusuf Nurkić](/wiki/Jusuf_Nurki%C4%87 "Jusuf Nurkić"). The [Bosnia and Herzegovina national under-16 team](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_men%27s_national_under-16_and_under-17_basketball_team "Bosnia and Herzegovina men's national under-16 and under-17 basketball team") won two gold medals in 2015, winning both [2015 European Youth Summer Olympic Festival](/wiki/Basketball_at_the_2015_European_Youth_Summer_Olympic_Festival "Basketball at the 2015 European Youth Summer Olympic Festival") as well as the [2015 FIBA Europe Under-16 Championship](/wiki/2015_FIBA_Europe_Under-16_Championship "2015 FIBA Europe Under-16 Championship").

Women's basketball club [Jedinstvo Aida](/wiki/%C5%BDKK_Jedinstvo_Tuzla "ŽKK Jedinstvo Tuzla") from [Tuzla](/wiki/Tuzla "Tuzla") won the [Women's European Club Championship](/wiki/EuroLeague_Women "EuroLeague Women") in 1989 and went to the [Ronchetti Cup](/wiki/Ronchetti_Cup "Ronchetti Cup") final in 1990, led by [Razija Mujanović](/wiki/Razija_Mujanovi%C4%87 "Razija Mujanović").[[262]](#cite_note-265)

The Bosnian [chess](/wiki/Chess "Chess") team was [Champion of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Yugoslav_Chess_Championship "Yugoslav Chess Championship") seven times, in addition to club [ŠK Bosna](/wiki/%C5%A0K_Bosna "ŠK Bosna") winning four [European Chess Club Cups](/wiki/European_Chess_Club_Cup "European Chess Club Cup"). Chess grandmaster [Borki Predojević](/wiki/Borki_Predojevi%C4%87 "Borki Predojević") has also won two European Championships. The most impressive success of Bosnian Chess was a runner-up position at the [31st Chess Olympiad](/wiki/31st_Chess_Olympiad "31st Chess Olympiad") in 1994 in [Moscow](/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"), featuring Grandmasters [Predrag Nikolić](/wiki/Predrag_Nikoli%C4%87 "Predrag Nikolić"), [Ivan Sokolov](/wiki/Ivan_Sokolov_(chess_player) "Ivan Sokolov (chess player)") and [Bojan Kurajica](/wiki/Bojan_Kurajica "Bojan Kurajica").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Middle-weight [boxer](/wiki/Boxing "Boxing") [Marijan Beneš](/wiki/Marijan_Bene%C5%A1 "Marijan Beneš") has won several Championships of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Yugoslav Championships and the [European Championship](/wiki/European_Amateur_Boxing_Championships "European Amateur Boxing Championships").[[263]](#cite_note-nezavisne-266) In 1978, he won the World Title against [Elisha Obed](/wiki/Elisha_Obed "Elisha Obed") from [The Bahamas](/wiki/The_Bahamas "The Bahamas").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/20150331_2219_AUT_BIH_2704.jpg/250px-20150331_2219_AUT_BIH_2704.jpg)](/wiki/File:20150331_2219_AUT_BIH_2704.jpg)

[Edin Džeko](/wiki/Edin_D%C5%BEeko "Edin Džeko") playing for [Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_national_football_team "Bosnia and Herzegovina national football team") in 2015

[Association football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") is the most popular sport in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It dates from 1903, but its popularity grew significantly after [World War I](/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). Bosnian clubs [FK Sarajevo](/wiki/FK_Sarajevo "FK Sarajevo") and [Željezničar](/wiki/FK_%C5%BDeljezni%C4%8Dar_Sarajevo "FK Željezničar Sarajevo") won the [Yugoslav Championship](/wiki/Yugoslav_First_League "Yugoslav First League"), while the [Yugoslav national football team](/wiki/Yugoslavia_national_football_team "Yugoslavia national football team") included Bosnian players of all ethnic backgrounds and generations, such as [Safet Sušić](/wiki/Safet_Su%C5%A1i%C4%87 "Safet Sušić"), [Zlatko Vujović](/wiki/Zlatko_Vujovi%C4%87 "Zlatko Vujović"), [Mehmed Baždarević](/wiki/Mehmed_Ba%C5%BEdarevi%C4%87 "Mehmed Baždarević"), [Davor Jozić](/wiki/Davor_Jozi%C4%87 "Davor Jozić"), [Faruk Hadžibegić](/wiki/Faruk_Had%C5%BEibegi%C4%87 "Faruk Hadžibegić"), [Predrag Pašić](/wiki/Predrag_Pa%C5%A1i%C4%87 "Predrag Pašić"), [Blaž Slišković](/wiki/Bla%C5%BE_Sli%C5%A1kovi%C4%87 "Blaž Slišković"), [Vahid Halilhodžić](/wiki/Vahid_Halilhod%C5%BEi%C4%87 "Vahid Halilhodžić"), [Dušan Bajević](/wiki/Du%C5%A1an_Bajevi%C4%87 "Dušan Bajević"), [Ivica Osim](/wiki/Ivica_Osim "Ivica Osim"), [Josip Katalinski](/wiki/Josip_Katalinski "Josip Katalinski"), [Tomislav Knez](/wiki/Tomislav_Knez "Tomislav Knez"), [Velimir Sombolac](/wiki/Velimir_Sombolac "Velimir Sombolac") and numerous others.

The [Bosnia and Herzegovina national football team](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_national_football_team "Bosnia and Herzegovina national football team") played at the [2014 FIFA World Cup](/wiki/2014_FIFA_World_Cup "2014 FIFA World Cup"), its first major tournament.[[264]](#cite_note-267) Players on the team again includes notable players of all country's ethnic background, such as then and now captains [Emir Spahić](/wiki/Emir_Spahi%C4%87 "Emir Spahić"), [Zvjezdan Misimović](/wiki/Zvjezdan_Misimovi%C4%87 "Zvjezdan Misimović") and [Edin Džeko](/wiki/Edin_D%C5%BEeko "Edin Džeko"), defenders like [Ognjen Vranješ](/wiki/Ognjen_Vranje%C5%A1 "Ognjen Vranješ"), [Sead Kolašinac](/wiki/Sead_Kola%C5%A1inac "Sead Kolašinac") and [Toni Šunjić](/wiki/Toni_%C5%A0unji%C4%87 "Toni Šunjić"), midfielders like [Miralem Pjanić](/wiki/Miralem_Pjani%C4%87 "Miralem Pjanić") and [Senad Lulić](/wiki/Senad_Luli%C4%87 "Senad Lulić"), striker [Vedad Ibišević](/wiki/Vedad_Ibi%C5%A1evi%C4%87 "Vedad Ibišević"), etc. Former Bosnian footballers include [Hasan Salihamidžić](/wiki/Hasan_Salihamid%C5%BEi%C4%87 "Hasan Salihamidžić"), who became only the second Bosnian to ever win a [UEFA Champions League](/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League "UEFA Champions League") trophy, after [Elvir Baljić](/wiki/Elvir_Balji%C4%87 "Elvir Baljić"). He made 234 appearances and scored 31 goals for German club [FC Bayern Munich](/wiki/FC_Bayern_Munich "FC Bayern Munich"). [Sergej Barbarez](/wiki/Sergej_Barbarez "Sergej Barbarez"), who played for several clubs in the German [Bundesliga](/wiki/Bundesliga "Bundesliga"). including [Borussia Dortmund](/wiki/Borussia_Dortmund "Borussia Dortmund"), [Hamburger SV](/wiki/Hamburger_SV "Hamburger SV") and [Bayer Leverkusen](/wiki/Bayer_04_Leverkusen "Bayer 04 Leverkusen") was joint-top scorer in the [2000–01 Bundesliga](/wiki/2000%E2%80%9301_Bundesliga "2000–01 Bundesliga") season with 22 goals. [Meho Kodro](/wiki/Meho_Kodro "Meho Kodro") spent most of his career playing in Spain, most notably with [Real Sociedad](/wiki/Real_Sociedad "Real Sociedad") and [FC Barcelona](/wiki/FC_Barcelona "FC Barcelona"). [Elvir Rahimić](/wiki/Elvir_Rahimi%C4%87 "Elvir Rahimić") made 302 appearances for Russian club [CSKA Moscow](/wiki/PFC_CSKA_Moscow "PFC CSKA Moscow") with whom he won the [UEFA Cup](/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League "UEFA Europa League") in [2005](/wiki/2005_UEFA_Cup_Final "2005 UEFA Cup Final").
[Milena Nikolić](/wiki/Milena_Nikoli%C4%87 "Milena Nikolić"), member of the [women's national team](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_women%27s_national_football_team "Bosnia and Herzegovina women's national football team"), was the [2013–14 UEFA Women's Champions League](/wiki/2013%E2%80%9314_UEFA_Women%27s_Champions_League "2013–14 UEFA Women's Champions League") [top scorer](/wiki/UEFA_Women%27s_Champions_League#Top_scorers_by_tournament "UEFA Women's Champions League").[[265]](#cite_note-uefa.com-nikolic-scorer-268)

Bosnia and Herzegovina was the world champion of [volleyball at the 2004 Summer Paralympics](/wiki/Volleyball_at_the_2004_Summer_Paralympics "Volleyball at the 2004 Summer Paralympics") and [volleyball at the 2012 Summer Paralympics](/wiki/Volleyball_at_the_2012_Summer_Paralympics "Volleyball at the 2012 Summer Paralympics"). Many among those on the team lost their legs in the [Bosnian War](/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War"). Its [national sitting volleyball team](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_national_sitting_volleyball_team "Bosnia and Herzegovina national sitting volleyball team") is one of the dominant forces in [the sport](/wiki/Sitting_volleyball "Sitting volleyball") worldwide, winning nine European Championships, three World Championships and two [Paralympic](/wiki/Volleyball_at_the_Summer_Paralympics "Volleyball at the Summer Paralympics") gold medals.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

[Tennis](/wiki/Tennis "Tennis") is also gaining a lot of popularity after the recent successes of [Damir Džumhur](/wiki/Damir_D%C5%BEumhur "Damir Džumhur") and [Mirza Bašić](/wiki/Mirza_Ba%C5%A1i%C4%87 "Mirza Bašić") at [Grand Slam](/wiki/Grand_Slam_(tennis) "Grand Slam (tennis)") level. Other notable tennis players who have represented Bosnia and Herzegovina are [Tomislav Brkić](/wiki/Tomislav_Brki%C4%87 "Tomislav Brkić"), [Amer Delić](/wiki/Amer_Deli%C4%87 "Amer Delić") and [Mervana Jugić-Salkić](/wiki/Mervana_Jugi%C4%87-Salki%C4%87 "Mervana Jugić-Salkić").
