**Bosnia and Herzegovina**,[[a]](#cite_note-18)[[b]](#cite_note-19) often referred to as **Bosnia-Herzegovina** or simply as **Bosnia**, is a country in [Southeast Europe](/wiki/Southeast_Europe "Southeast Europe"). Situated on the [Balkan Peninsula](/wiki/Balkans "Balkans"), it borders [Serbia](/wiki/Serbia "Serbia") to the east, [Montenegro](/wiki/Montenegro "Montenegro") to the southeast, and [Croatia](/wiki/Croatia "Croatia") to the north and southwest, with a 20-kilometre-long (12-mile) coast on the [Adriatic Sea](/wiki/Adriatic_Sea "Adriatic Sea") in the south. [Bosnia](/wiki/Bosnia_(region) "Bosnia (region)") has a moderate [continental climate](/wiki/Continental_climate "Continental climate") with hot summers and cold, snowy winters. Its geography is largely mountainous, particularly in the central and eastern regions, which are dominated by the [Dinaric Alps](/wiki/Dinaric_Alps "Dinaric Alps"). [Herzegovina](/wiki/Herzegovina "Herzegovina"), the smaller, southern region, has a [Mediterranean climate](/wiki/Mediterranean_climate "Mediterranean climate") and is mostly mountainous. [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo") is the capital and the largest city.

The area has been inhabited since at least the [Upper Palaeolithic](/wiki/Upper_Palaeolithic "Upper Palaeolithic"), with permanent human settlement traced to the [Neolithic](/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") cultures of [Butmir](/wiki/Butmir_culture "Butmir culture"), [Kakanj](/wiki/Kakanj_culture "Kakanj culture"), and [Vučedol](/wiki/Vu%C4%8Dedol_culture "Vučedol culture"). After the arrival of the first [Indo-Europeans](/wiki/Proto-Indo-Europeans "Proto-Indo-Europeans"), the area was populated by several [Illyrian](/wiki/Illyria "Illyria") and [Celtic](/wiki/Celts "Celts") civilisations. Most of modern Bosnia was incorporated into the [Roman province of Dalmatia](/wiki/Dalmatia_(Roman_province) "Dalmatia (Roman province)") by the mid-first century BCE. The [ancestors of the modern South Slavic peoples](/wiki/Early_Slavs "Early Slavs") arrived between the sixth and ninth centuries. In the 12th century, the [Banate of Bosnia](/wiki/Banate_of_Bosnia "Banate of Bosnia") was established as the first independent Bosnian [polity](/wiki/Polity "Polity").[[17]](#cite_note-:0-20) It gradually evolved and expanded into the [Kingdom of Bosnia](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Bosnia "Kingdom of Bosnia"), which became the most powerful state in the western Balkans by the 14th century.[[17]](#cite_note-:0-20) The [Ottoman Empire](/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") [annexed the region](/wiki/Ottoman_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Ottoman Bosnia and Herzegovina") in 1463 and introduced [Islam](/wiki/Islam_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Islam in Bosnia and Herzegovina"). From the late 19th century until [World War I](/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), the country was [annexed into the Austro-Hungarian monarchy](/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_rule_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Austro-Hungarian rule in Bosnia and Herzegovina"). In the [interwar period](/wiki/Interwar_period "Interwar period"), Bosnia and Herzegovina was part of the [Kingdom of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Yugoslavia "Kingdom of Yugoslavia"). After [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), it was granted full republic status in the newly formed [Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia"). In 1992, following the [breakup of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Breakup_of_Yugoslavia "Breakup of Yugoslavia"), [the republic proclaimed independence](/wiki/1992_Bosnian_independence_referendum "1992 Bosnian independence referendum"). This was followed by the [Bosnian War](/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War"), which lasted until late 1995 and ended with the signing of the [Dayton Agreement](/wiki/Dayton_Agreement "Dayton Agreement").

Bosnia and Herzegovina has roughly 2.9 million inhabitants based on the current estimates, composed chiefly of [three main ethnic groups](/wiki/Ethnic_groups_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina"): [Bosniaks](/wiki/Bosniaks "Bosniaks"), who form more than a half of the population, followed by [Serbs](/wiki/Serbs_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina") at one-third and [Croats](/wiki/Croats_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina") at one-sixth; minorities include [Jews](/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "History of the Jews in Bosnia and Herzegovina"), [Roma](/wiki/Romani_people_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Romani people in Bosnia and Herzegovina"), [Albanians, Montenegrins, Ukrainians and Turks](/wiki/National_minorities_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "National minorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina"), who are among 17 recognized "national minorities". Bosnia and Herzegovina has a [bicameral](/wiki/Bicameralism "Bicameralism") legislature and a [presidency](/wiki/Presidency_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina") made up of one member from each of the three major ethnic groups ([directorial system](/wiki/Directorial_system "Directorial system")). The central government's power is minimal, as the country is largely decentralised; it comprises two autonomous entities—the [Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina") and [Republika Srpska](/wiki/Republika_Srpska "Republika Srpska")—and a third unit, the [Brčko District](/wiki/Br%C4%8Dko_District "Brčko District"), governed by its own local government.

Bosnia and Herzegovina is a [developing country](/wiki/Developing_country "Developing country") and [an upper-middle income economy](/wiki/Economy_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Economy of Bosnia and Herzegovina"), dominated by industry and agriculture, followed by tourism and [services](/wiki/Tertiary_sector_of_the_economy "Tertiary sector of the economy"); tourism has increased significantly in recent years.[[18]](#cite_note-21)[[19]](#cite_note-22) The country has a [social security](/wiki/Welfare_spending "Welfare spending") and universal healthcare system, while [primary and secondary education](/wiki/Education_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Education in Bosnia and Herzegovina") is free. It is a member of the [United Nations](/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"), [Council of Europe](/wiki/Council_of_Europe "Council of Europe"), [OSCE](/wiki/Organization_for_Security_and_Co-operation_in_Europe "Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe"), [CEFTA](/wiki/Central_European_Free_Trade_Agreement "Central European Free Trade Agreement"), and is also a founding member of the [SEECP](/wiki/South-East_European_Cooperation_Process "South-East European Cooperation Process"). Bosnia and Herzegovina has been an [EU candidate country](/wiki/Accession_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_to_the_European_Union "Accession of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the European Union") since 2022, and a [NATO](/wiki/NATO "NATO") membership candidate since 2010.[[20]](#cite_note-23)

Etymology
---------

The first preserved widely acknowledged mention of a form of the name "[Bosnia](/wiki/Bosnia_(region) "Bosnia (region)")" is in *[De Administrando Imperio](/wiki/De_Administrando_Imperio "De Administrando Imperio")*, a politico-geographical handbook written by the [Byzantine emperor](/wiki/List_of_Byzantine_emperors "List of Byzantine emperors") [Constantine VII](/wiki/Constantine_VII "Constantine VII") in the mid-10th century (between 948 and 952) describing the "small land" (χωρίον) in [Greek](/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language") of "Bosona" (Βοσώνα).[[21]](#cite_note-Moravcsik-153-24)

The name of the land is believed to derive from the name of the river [Bosna](/wiki/Bosna_(river) "Bosna (river)") that courses through the Bosnian heartland. According to [philologist](/wiki/Philology "Philology") Anton Mayer, the name *Bosna* could derive from [Illyrian](/wiki/Illyrian_language "Illyrian language") \*"Bass-an-as", which in turn could derive from the Proto-Indo-European root *[bʰegʷ-](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Reconstruction:Proto-Indo-European/b%CA%B0eg%CA%B7- "wikt:Reconstruction:Proto-Indo-European/bʰegʷ-")*, meaning "the running water".[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25)

The name *Herzegovina* means "herzog's [land]", and "herzog" derives from the German word for "duke".[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25) It originates from the title of a 15th-century Bosnian magnate, [Stjepan Vukčić Kosača](/wiki/Stjepan_Vuk%C4%8Di%C4%87_Kosa%C4%8Da "Stjepan Vukčić Kosača"), who was "Herceg [Herzog] of Hum and the Coast" (1448).[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFine1994578-26) Hum (formerly called [Zachlumia](/wiki/Zachlumia "Zachlumia")) was an early medieval principality that had been conquered by the Bosnian Banate in the first half of the 14th century. When the Ottomans took over administration of the region, they called it the [Sanjak of Herzegovina](/wiki/Sanjak_of_Herzegovina "Sanjak of Herzegovina") (*Hersek*). It was included within the [Bosnia Eyalet](/wiki/Bosnia_Eyalet "Bosnia Eyalet") until the formation of the short-lived [Herzegovina Eyalet](/wiki/Herzegovina_Eyalet "Herzegovina Eyalet") in the 1830s, which reemerged in the 1850s, after which the administrative region became commonly known as *Bosnia and Herzegovina*.[[24]](#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica-27)

On initial [proclamation of independence in 1992](/wiki/1992_Bosnian_independence_referendum "1992 Bosnian independence referendum"), the country's official name was the [Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Republic_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina"), but following the 1995 [Dayton Agreement](/wiki/Dayton_Agreement "Dayton Agreement") and the new [constitution](/wiki/Constitution_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina") that accompanied it, the official name was changed to Bosnia and Herzegovina.[*[dubious](/wiki/Wikipedia:Accuracy_dispute#Disputed_statement "Wikipedia:Accuracy dispute") – [discuss](/wiki/Talk:Bosnia_and_Herzegovina#Dubious "Talk:Bosnia and Herzegovina")*][*[why?](/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*][[25]](#cite_note-28)

History
-------

Main articles: [History of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/History_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "History of Bosnia and Herzegovina") and [Early history of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Early_history_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Early history of Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/NHM_-_Bandin_Fahrzeug_mit_V%C3%B6geln.jpg/250px-NHM_-_Bandin_Fahrzeug_mit_V%C3%B6geln.jpg)](/wiki/File:NHM_-_Bandin_Fahrzeug_mit_V%C3%B6geln.jpg)

Iron Age cult carriage from Banjani, near [Sokolac](/wiki/Sokolac,_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Sokolac, Bosnia and Herzegovina")

### Early history

Bosnia has been inhabited since at least the [Paleolithic era](/wiki/Paleolithic "Paleolithic"). Notably, the [Badanj Cave](/wiki/Badanj_Cave "Badanj Cave") near [Stolac](/wiki/Stolac "Stolac") features one of the oldest known cave engravings, depicting an animal figure believed to be a horse, dating back to approximately 13,000 to 12,000 BC.[[26]](#cite_note-29)[[27]](#cite_note-30)[[28]](#cite_note-31) During the [Neolithic period](/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic"), significant cultures such as the [Butmir](/wiki/Butmir "Butmir") and [Kakanj](/wiki/Kakanj "Kakanj") emerged along the [Bosna River](/wiki/Bosna_(river) "Bosna (river)"). The Butmir culture, flourishing around 5100 to 4500 BC, is renowned for its distinctive ceramics and anthropomorphic figurines. Excavations near [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo") have uncovered intricately decorated pottery and realistic human figurines from this culture.[[29]](#cite_note-32)

From the 8th century BCE, Illyrian tribes evolved into kingdoms. The most notable Illyrian kingdoms and dynasties were those of [Bardylis of the Dardani](/wiki/Bardylis "Bardylis") and of [Agron of the Ardiaei](/wiki/Agron_of_Illyria "Agron of Illyria") who created the last and best-known Illyrian kingdom. Agron ruled over the Ardiaei and had extended his rule to other tribes as well. From the 7th century BCE, bronze was replaced by iron, after which only jewelry and art objects were still made out of bronze.[[30]](#cite_note-geography-33) Illyrian tribes, under the influence of [Hallstatt cultures](/wiki/Hallstatt_culture "Hallstatt culture") to the north, formed regional centers that were slightly different. Parts of Central Bosnia were inhabited by the [Daesitiates](/wiki/Daesitiates "Daesitiates") tribe.[[30]](#cite_note-geography-33) The Iron Age [Glasinac-Mati culture](/wiki/Glasinac-Mati_culture "Glasinac-Mati culture") is associated with the [Autariatae](/wiki/Autariatae "Autariatae") tribe.[[30]](#cite_note-geography-33)

A very important role in their life was the cult of the dead, which is seen in their careful burials and burial ceremonies, as well as the richness of their burial sites.[[30]](#cite_note-geography-33) In the 4th century BCE, the first invasion of [Celts](/wiki/Celts "Celts") was recorded. They brought the technique of the [pottery wheel](/wiki/Potter%27s_wheel "Potter's wheel"), new types of fibulas and different bronze and iron belts. They only passed through en route to Greece.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Mogorjelo_Villa_Rustica.jpg/250px-Mogorjelo_Villa_Rustica.jpg)](/wiki/File:Mogorjelo_Villa_Rustica.jpg)

[Mogorjelo](/wiki/Mogorjelo "Mogorjelo"), an ancient Roman suburban Villa Rustica from the 4th century, near [Čapljina](/wiki/%C4%8Capljina "Čapljina")

In the [Neretva Delta](/wiki/Neretva_Delta "Neretva Delta") in the south, there were important [Hellenistic](/wiki/Hellenistic_period "Hellenistic period") influences of the Illyrian [Daors](/wiki/Daorson "Daorson") tribe.[[31]](#cite_note-34) Their capital was *Daorson* in Ošanići near [Stolac](/wiki/Stolac "Stolac").[[32]](#cite_note-35) Daorson, in the 4th century BCE, was surrounded by [megalithic](/wiki/Megalith "Megalith"), 5 m high stonewalls (as large as those of [Mycenae](/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae") in Greece), composed of large trapezoid stone blocks. Daors made unique bronze coins and sculptures.

Conflict between the Illyrians and [Romans](/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome") started in 229 BCE, but Rome did not complete its annexation of the region until AD 9. It was precisely in modern-day Bosnia and Herzegovina that Rome fought one of the most difficult battles in its history since the [Punic Wars](/wiki/Punic_Wars "Punic Wars"), as described by the Roman historian [Suetonius](/wiki/Suetonius "Suetonius").[[33]](#cite_note-36) This was the Roman campaign against [Illyricum](/wiki/Illyricum_(Roman_province) "Illyricum (Roman province)"), known as *[Bellum Batonianum](/wiki/Bellum_Batonianum "Bellum Batonianum")*.[[34]](#cite_note-37) The conflict arose after an attempt to recruit Illyrians, and a revolt spanned for four years (6–9 AD), after which they were subdued.[[35]](#cite_note-38)[*[page needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")*] In the Roman period, Latin-speaking settlers from the entire [Roman Empire](/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") settled among the Illyrians, and Roman soldiers were encouraged to retire in the region.[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm20023-39)

Following the split of the Empire between 337 and 395 AD, Dalmatia and Pannonia became parts of the [Western Roman Empire](/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire "Western Roman Empire"). The region was conquered by the [Ostrogoths](/wiki/Ostrogoths "Ostrogoths") in 455 AD. It subsequently changed hands between the [Alans](/wiki/Alans "Alans") and the [Huns](/wiki/Huns "Huns"). By the 6th century, Emperor [Justinian I](/wiki/Justinian_I "Justinian I") had reconquered the area for the [Byzantine Empire](/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire"). Slavs overwhelmed the Balkans in the 6th and 7th centuries. Illyrian cultural traits were adopted by the South Slavs, as evidenced in certain customs and traditions, and placenames.[[37]](#cite_note-40)

### Middle Ages

Main article: [Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Middle Ages](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_in_the_Middle_Ages "Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Middle Ages")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Hvalov_zbornik1.jpg/250px-Hvalov_zbornik1.jpg)](/wiki/File:Hvalov_zbornik1.jpg)

[Hval's Codex](/wiki/Hval%27s_Codex "Hval's Codex"), illustrated Slavic manuscript from medieval Bosnia

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Queen_Catherine_of_Bosnia.jpg/250px-Queen_Catherine_of_Bosnia.jpg)](/wiki/File:Queen_Catherine_of_Bosnia.jpg)

[Ledger stone](/wiki/Ledger_stone "Ledger stone") to [Queen Catherine of Bosnia](/wiki/Queen_Catherine_of_Bosnia "Queen Catherine of Bosnia"), the last queen of the [House of Kosača](/wiki/House_of_Kosa%C4%8Da "House of Kosača").

The [Early Slavs](/wiki/Early_Slavs "Early Slavs") raided the Western Balkans, including Bosnia, in the 6th and early 7th century (amid the [Migration Period](/wiki/Migration_Period "Migration Period")), and were composed of small tribal units drawn from a single Slavic confederation known to the Byzantines as the *[Sclaveni](/wiki/Sclaveni "Sclaveni")* (whilst the related *[Antes](/wiki/Antes_people "Antes people")*, roughly speaking, colonized the eastern portions of the Balkans).[[38]](#cite_note-Columbia_University_Press-41)[[39]](#cite_note-42)
Tribes recorded by the ethnonyms of "Serb" and "Croat" are described as a second, later, migration of different people during the second quarter of the 7th century who could not have been particularly numerous;[[38]](#cite_note-Columbia_University_Press-41)[[40]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFine199153,_56-43)[[41]](#cite_note-Heather-44) these early "Serb" and "Croat" tribes, whose exact identity is subject to scholarly debate,[[41]](#cite_note-Heather-44) came to predominate over the Slavs in the neighbouring regions. According to Noel Malcolm, the tribal Croats "settled in an area roughly corresponding to modern Croatia, and probably also including most of Bosnia proper, apart from the eastern strip of the Drina valley" while the tribal Serbs settled an area "corresponding to modern south-western Serbia (later known as [Raška](/wiki/Ra%C5%A1ka_(region) "Raška (region)")), and gradually extended their rule into the territories of [Duklja](/wiki/Duklja "Duklja") and [Hum](/wiki/Zachlumia "Zachlumia")".[[42]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm20028-45) [John Van Antwerp Fine Jr.](/wiki/John_Van_Antwerp_Fine_Jr. "John Van Antwerp Fine Jr."), on the other hand, describes the settling of the tribal Croats to involve Croatia, Dalmatia and Western Bosnia, with the rest of Bosnia seemingly being a territory between early Serb and Croat rule.[[43]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFine199153(I)-46)

Bosnia is also believed to be first mentioned *as a land (horion Bosona)* in Byzantine Emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus' *De Administrando Imperio* in the mid 10th century, at the end of a chapter entitled *Of the Serbs and the country in which they now dwell*.[[44]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBasic2009123-47) This has been scholarly interpreted in several ways and used especially by the Serb national ideologists to prove Bosnia as originally a "Serb" land.[[44]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBasic2009123-47) Other scholars have asserted the inclusion of Bosnia in the chapter to merely be the result of Serbian Grand Duke [Časlav](/wiki/%C4%8Caslav_of_Serbia "Časlav of Serbia")'s temporary rule over Bosnia at the time, while also pointing out Porphyrogenitus does not say anywhere explicitly that Bosnia is a "Serb land".[[45]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBasic2009123–28-48) In fact, the very translation of the critical sentence where the word *Bosona* (Bosnia) appears is subject to varying interpretation.[[44]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBasic2009123-47) In time, Bosnia formed a unit under its own [ruler](/wiki/Kulin_Ban "Kulin Ban"), who called himself Bosnian.[[46]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFine199153-49) Bosnia, along with other territories, became part of [Duklja](/wiki/Duklja "Duklja") in the 11th century, although it retained its own nobility and institutions.[[47]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFine1991223-50)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Medieval_Bosnian_State_Expansion-en.svg/250px-Medieval_Bosnian_State_Expansion-en.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Medieval_Bosnian_State_Expansion-en.svg)

Bosnia in the Middle Ages spanning the [Banate of Bosnia](/wiki/Banate_of_Bosnia "Banate of Bosnia") and the succeeding [Kingdom of Bosnia](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Bosnia "Kingdom of Bosnia")

In the [High Middle Ages](/wiki/High_Middle_Ages "High Middle Ages"), political circumstance led to the area being contested between the [Kingdom of Hungary](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary "Kingdom of Hungary") and the Byzantine Empire. Following another shift of power between the two in the early 12th century, Bosnia found itself outside the control of both and emerged as the [Banate of Bosnia](/wiki/Banate_of_Bosnia "Banate of Bosnia") (under the rule of local *[bans](/wiki/Ban_(title) "Ban (title)")*).[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25)[[48]](#cite_note-51) The first Bosnian ban known by name was [Ban Borić](/wiki/Ban_Bori%C4%87 "Ban Borić").[[49]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFine1991288-52) The second was [Ban Kulin](/wiki/Ban_Kulin "Ban Kulin"), whose rule marked the start of a controversy involving the [Bosnian Church](/wiki/Bosnian_Church "Bosnian Church") – considered heretical by the [Roman Catholic Church](/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church "Roman Catholic Church"). In response to Hungarian attempts to use church politics regarding the issue as a way to reclaim sovereignty over Bosnia, Kulin held a council of local church leaders to renounce the heresy and embraced Catholicism in 1203. Despite this, Hungarian ambitions remained unchanged long after Kulin's death in 1204, waning only after an unsuccessful invasion in 1254. During this time, the population was called *Dobri [Bošnjani](/wiki/Bo%C5%A1njani "Bošnjani")* ("Good Bosnians").[[50]](#cite_note-53)[[51]](#cite_note-54) The names Serb and Croat, though occasionally appearing in peripheral areas, were not used in Bosnia proper.[[52]](#cite_note-lrb.co.uk-55)

Bosnian history from then until the early 14th century was marked by a power struggle between the [Šubić](/wiki/%C5%A0ubi%C4%87_family "Šubić family") and [Kotromanić](/wiki/Kotromani%C4%87_dynasty "Kotromanić dynasty") families. This conflict came to an end in 1322, when [Stephen II Kotromanić](/wiki/Stephen_II,_Ban_of_Bosnia "Stephen II, Ban of Bosnia") became *Ban*. By the time of his death in 1353, he was successful in annexing territories to the north and west, as well as Zahumlje and parts of Dalmatia. He was succeeded by his ambitious nephew [Tvrtko](/wiki/Tvrtko_I_of_Bosnia "Tvrtko I of Bosnia") who, following a prolonged struggle with nobility and inter-family strife, gained full control of the country in 1367. By the year 1377, Bosnia was elevated into a kingdom with the coronation of Tvrtko as the first [Bosnian King](/wiki/List_of_rulers_of_Bosnia "List of rulers of Bosnia") in Mile near [Visoko](/wiki/Visoko_during_the_Middle_Ages "Visoko during the Middle Ages") in the Bosnian heartland.[[53]](#cite_note-Mile-56)[[54]](#cite_note-An-57)[[55]](#cite_note-58)

Following his death in 1391, however, Bosnia fell into a long period of decline. The [Ottoman Empire](/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") had started its [conquest of Europe](/wiki/Ottoman_wars_in_Europe "Ottoman wars in Europe") and posed a major threat to the [Balkans](/wiki/Balkans "Balkans") throughout the first half of the 15th century. Finally, after decades of political and social instability, the Kingdom of Bosnia ceased to exist in 1463 after its conquest by the Ottoman Empire.[[56]](#cite_note-59)

There was a general awareness in medieval Bosnia, at least amongst the nobles, that they shared a joint state with Serbia and that they belonged to the same ethnic group. That awareness diminished over time, due to differences in political and social development, but it was kept in Herzegovina and parts of Bosnia which were a part of Serbian state.[[57]](#cite_note-60)

### Ottoman Empire

Main articles: [Ottoman conquest of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Ottoman_conquest_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Ottoman conquest of Bosnia and Herzegovina") and [Ottoman Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Ottoman_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Ottoman Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Bosnia_Eyalet%2C_Central_europe_1683.png/250px-Bosnia_Eyalet%2C_Central_europe_1683.png)](/wiki/File:Bosnia_Eyalet,_Central_europe_1683.png)

The [Bosnia Eyalet](/wiki/Bosnia_Eyalet "Bosnia Eyalet") in 1683

The [Ottoman conquest of Bosnia](/wiki/Ottoman_conquest_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Ottoman conquest of Bosnia and Herzegovina") marked a new era in the country's history and introduced drastic changes in the political and cultural landscape. The Ottomans incorporated Bosnia as an integral province of the Ottoman Empire with its historical name and territorial integrity.[[58]](#cite_note-61) Within Bosnia, the Ottomans introduced a number of key changes in the territory's socio-political administration; including a new landholding system, a reorganization of administrative units, and a complex system of social differentiation by class and religious affiliation.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25)

Following Ottoman occupation, there was a steady flow of people out of Bosnia and a large number of abandoned villages in Bosnia are mentioned in the Ottoman registers,[[59]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) while those who stayed eventually became [Muslims](/wiki/Muslims "Muslims"). Many Catholics in Bosnia fled to neighboring Catholic lands in the early Ottoman occupation.[[60]](#cite_note-63) The evidence indicates that the early Muslim conversions in Ottoman Bosnia in the 15th–16th century were among the locals who stayed rather than mass Muslim settlements from outside Bosnia.[[59]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) In Herzegovina, many [Orthodox](/wiki/Eastern_Orthodoxy "Eastern Orthodoxy") people had also embraced Islam.[[59]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) By the late 16th and early 17th century, Muslims are considered to have become an absolute majority in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Albanian Catholic priest [Pjetër Mazreku](/wiki/Pjet%C3%ABr_Mazreku "Pjetër Mazreku") reported in 1624 that there were 450,000 Muslims, 150,000 Catholics and 75,000 Eastern Orthodox in Bosnia and Herzegovina.[[59]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-62)

There was a lack of [Orthodox Church](/wiki/Serbian_Orthodox_Church "Serbian Orthodox Church") activity in Bosnia proper in the pre-Ottoman period.[[61]](#cite_note-64) An Orthodox Christian population in Bosnia was introduced as a direct result of Ottoman policy.[[62]](#cite_note-Bosnia:_A_Short_History_p._55-65) From the 15th century and onwards, Orthodox Christians (Orthodox [Vlachs](/wiki/Vlachs "Vlachs") and non-Vlach Orthodox Serbs) from Serbia and other regions settled in Bosnia and Herzegovina.[[63]](#cite_note-66) Favored by the Ottomans over the Catholics, many Orthodox churches were allowed to be built in Bosnia by the Ottomans.[[64]](#cite_note-67)[[62]](#cite_note-Bosnia:_A_Short_History_p._55-65) Quite a few Vlachs also became Islamized in Bosnia, and some (mainly in Croatia) became Catholics.[[65]](#cite_note-68)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina-02166_-_Po%C4%8Ditelj_%2810476710854%29.jpg/250px-Bosnia_and_Herzegovina-02166_-_Po%C4%8Ditelj_%2810476710854%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Bosnia_and_Herzegovina-02166_-_Po%C4%8Ditelj_(10476710854).jpg)

[Počitelj Citadel](/wiki/Po%C4%8Ditelj_Citadel "Počitelj Citadel") in [Čapljina](/wiki/%C4%8Capljina "Čapljina"), built by [King Tvrtko I of Bosnia](/wiki/King_Tvrtko_I_of_Bosnia "King Tvrtko I of Bosnia") in 1383.

The four centuries of Ottoman rule also had a drastic impact on Bosnia's population make-up, which changed several times as a result of the empire's conquests, frequent wars with European powers, forced and economic migrations, and epidemics. A native Slavic-speaking Muslim community emerged and eventually became the largest of the ethno-religious groups due to a lack of strong Christian church organizations and continuous rivalry between the Orthodox and Catholic churches, while the indigenous [Bosnian Church](/wiki/Bosnian_Church "Bosnian Church") disappeared altogether (ostensibly by conversion of its members to Islam). The Ottomans referred to them as *kristianlar* while the Orthodox and Catholics were called *gebir* or *kafir*, meaning "unbeliever".[[66]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVelikonja200329–30-69) The Bosnian [Franciscans](/wiki/Franciscans "Franciscans") (and the Catholic population as a whole) were protected by official imperial decrees and in accordance and the full extent of Ottoman laws; however, in effect, these often merely affected arbitrary rule and behavior of powerful local elite.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25)

As the Ottoman Empire continued its rule in the Balkans ([Rumelia](/wiki/Rumelia "Rumelia")), Bosnia was somewhat relieved of the pressures of being a frontier province and experienced a period of general welfare. A number of cities, such as [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo") and [Mostar](/wiki/Mostar "Mostar"), were established and grew into regional centers of trade and urban culture and were then visited by Ottoman traveler [Evliya Çelebi](/wiki/Evliya_%C3%87elebi "Evliya Çelebi") in 1648. Within these cities, various Ottoman Sultans financed the construction of many works of [Bosnian architecture](/wiki/Architecture_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Architecture of Bosnia and Herzegovina") such as the country's first library in Sarajevo, [madrassas](/wiki/Madrasa "Madrasa"), a school of [Sufi philosophy](/wiki/Sufi_philosophy "Sufi philosophy"), and a clock tower (*Sahat Kula*), bridges such as the [Stari Most](/wiki/Stari_Most "Stari Most"), the [Emperor's Mosque](/wiki/Emperor%27s_Mosque "Emperor's Mosque") and the [Gazi Husrev-beg Mosque](/wiki/Gazi_Husrev-beg_Mosque "Gazi Husrev-beg Mosque").[[67]](#cite_note-Syed_Akhtar_Usmani_2011_p._473-70)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Stari_Most_2006.JPG/250px-Stari_Most_2006.JPG)](/wiki/File:Stari_Most_2006.JPG)

The [Mostar Bridge](/wiki/Stari_Most "Stari Most") was commissioned by [Suleiman the Magnificent](/wiki/Suleiman_the_Magnificent "Suleiman the Magnificent") in 1557

Furthermore, several Bosnian Muslims played influential roles in the Ottoman Empire's cultural and [political history](/wiki/Political_history "Political history") during this time.[[68]](#cite_note-Riedlmayer-71) Bosnian recruits formed a large component of the Ottoman ranks in the battles of [Mohács](/wiki/Battle_of_Moh%C3%A1cs "Battle of Mohács") and [Krbava field](/wiki/Battle_of_Krbava_Field "Battle of Krbava Field"), while numerous other Bosnians rose through the ranks of the Ottoman military to occupy the highest positions of power in the Empire, including admirals such as [Matrakçı Nasuh](/wiki/Matrak%C3%A7%C4%B1_Nasuh "Matrakçı Nasuh"); generals such as [Isa-Beg Ishaković](/wiki/Isa_Bey_Ishakovi%C4%87 "Isa Bey Ishaković"), [Gazi Husrev-beg](/wiki/Gazi_Husrev_Bey "Gazi Husrev Bey"), [Telli Hasan Pasha](/wiki/Telli_Hasan_Pasha "Telli Hasan Pasha") and [Sarı Süleyman Pasha](/wiki/Sar%C4%B1_S%C3%BCleyman_Pasha "Sarı Süleyman Pasha"); administrators such as [Ferhad Pasha Sokolović](/wiki/Ferhad_Pasha_Sokolovi%C4%87 "Ferhad Pasha Sokolović") and [Osman Gradaščević](/wiki/Osman_Grada%C5%A1%C4%8Devi%C4%87 "Osman Gradaščević"); and Grand [Viziers](/wiki/Vizier "Vizier") such as the influential [Sokollu Mehmed Pasha](/wiki/Sokollu_Mehmed_Pasha "Sokollu Mehmed Pasha") and [Damat Ibrahim Pasha](/wiki/Damat_Ibrahim_Pasha "Damat Ibrahim Pasha"). Some Bosnians emerged as [Sufi](/wiki/Sufism "Sufism") mystics, scholars such as [Muhamed Hevaji Uskufi Bosnevi](/wiki/Muhamed_Hevaji_Uskufi_Bosnevi "Muhamed Hevaji Uskufi Bosnevi"), [Ali Džabić](/wiki/Ali_D%C5%BEabi%C4%87 "Ali Džabić"); and poets in the [Turkish](/wiki/Turkish_language "Turkish language"), [Albanian](/wiki/Albanian_language "Albanian language"), [Arabic](/wiki/Arabic "Arabic"), and [Persian languages](/wiki/Persian_language "Persian language").[[69]](#cite_note-Imamović,_Mustafa_1996-72)

However, by the late 17th century the Empire's military misfortunes caught up with the country, and the end of the [Great Turkish War](/wiki/Great_Turkish_War "Great Turkish War") with the [treaty of Karlowitz](/wiki/Treaty_of_Karlowitz "Treaty of Karlowitz") in 1699 again made Bosnia the Empire's westernmost province. The 18th century was marked by further military failures, numerous revolts within Bosnia, and several outbreaks of plague.[[70]](#cite_note-73)
The Porte's efforts at modernizing the Ottoman state were met with distrust growing to hostility in Bosnia, where local aristocrats stood to lose much through the proposed [Tanzimat](/wiki/Tanzimat "Tanzimat") reforms. This, combined with frustrations over territorial, political concessions in the north-east, and the plight of [Slavic](/wiki/Slavs "Slavs") [Muslim](/wiki/Muslims "Muslims") refugees arriving from the [Sanjak of Smederevo](/wiki/Sanjak_of_Smederevo "Sanjak of Smederevo") into [Bosnia Eyalet](/wiki/Bosnia_Eyalet "Bosnia Eyalet"), culminated in a partially unsuccessful revolt by [Husein Gradaščević](/wiki/Husein_Grada%C5%A1%C4%8Devi%C4%87 "Husein Gradaščević"), who endorsed a Bosnia Eyalet autonomous from the authoritarian rule of the Ottoman Sultan [Mahmud II](/wiki/Mahmud_II "Mahmud II"), who persecuted, executed and abolished the [Janissaries](/wiki/Janissary "Janissary") and reduced the role of autonomous [Pashas](/wiki/Pasha "Pasha") in Rumelia. Mahmud II sent his [Grand vizier](/wiki/Grand_vizier "Grand vizier") to subdue Bosnia Eyalet and succeeded only with the reluctant assistance of [Ali Pasha Rizvanbegović](/wiki/Ali_Pasha_Rizvanbegovi%C4%87 "Ali Pasha Rizvanbegović").[[69]](#cite_note-Imamović,_Mustafa_1996-72) Related rebellions were extinguished by 1850, but the situation continued to deteriorate.

New nationalist movements appeared in Bosnia by the middle of the 19th century. Shortly after Serbia's breakaway from the Ottoman Empire in the early 19th century, Serbian and Croatian nationalism rose up in Bosnia, and such nationalists made irredentist claims to Bosnia's territory. This trend continued to grow in the rest of the 19th and 20th centuries.[[71]](#cite_note-74)

Agrarian unrest eventually sparked the [Herzegovinian rebellion](/wiki/Herzegovina_uprising_(1875%E2%80%931877) "Herzegovina uprising (1875–1877)"), a widespread peasant uprising, in 1875. The conflict rapidly spread and came to involve several Balkan states and Great Powers, a situation that led to the [Congress of Berlin](/wiki/Congress_of_Berlin "Congress of Berlin") and the [Treaty of Berlin](/wiki/Treaty_of_Berlin_(1878) "Treaty of Berlin (1878)") in 1878.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25)

### Austria-Hungary

Main articles: [Austro-Hungarian campaign in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1878](/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_campaign_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_in_1878 "Austro-Hungarian campaign in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1878") and [Austro-Hungarian rule in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_rule_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Austro-Hungarian rule in Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Sarajevo_1878..jpg/250px-Sarajevo_1878..jpg)](/wiki/File:Sarajevo_1878..jpg)

Austro-Hungarian troops [enter Sarajevo](/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_campaign_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_in_1878 "Austro-Hungarian campaign in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1878"), 1878

At the Congress of [Berlin](/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") in 1878, the [Austro-Hungarian](/wiki/Austria-Hungary "Austria-Hungary") Foreign Minister [Gyula Andrássy](/wiki/Gyula_Andr%C3%A1ssy "Gyula Andrássy") obtained the occupation and administration of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he also obtained the right to station garrisons in the [Sanjak of Novi Pazar](/wiki/Sanjak_of_Novi_Pazar "Sanjak of Novi Pazar"), which would remain under [Ottoman](/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") administration until 1908, when the Austro-Hungarian troops withdrew from the Sanjak.

Although Austro-Hungarian officials quickly came to an agreement with the Bosnians, tensions remained and a mass emigration of Bosnians occurred.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25) However, a state of relative stability was reached soon enough and Austro-Hungarian authorities were able to embark on a number of social and administrative reforms they intended would make Bosnia and Herzegovina into a "model" colony.

[Habsburg rule](/wiki/Habsburg_Monarchy "Habsburg Monarchy") had several key concerns in Bosnia. It tried to dissipate the South Slav nationalism by disputing the earlier Serb and Croat claims to Bosnia and encouraging identification of Bosnian or [Bosniak](/wiki/Bosniaks "Bosniaks") identity.[[72]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHajdarpasic2015161–165-75) Habsburg rule also tried to provide for modernisation by codifying laws, introducing new political institutions, establishing and expanding industries.[[73]](#cite_note-76)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Friedrich_Alois_Sch%C3%B6nn_-_An_der_lateinischen_Br%C3%BCcke_in_Sarajewo_-_171_-_%C3%96sterreichische_Galerie_Belvedere.jpg/250px-Friedrich_Alois_Sch%C3%B6nn_-_An_der_lateinischen_Br%C3%BCcke_in_Sarajewo_-_171_-_%C3%96sterreichische_Galerie_Belvedere.jpg)](/wiki/File:Friedrich_Alois_Sch%C3%B6nn_-_An_der_lateinischen_Br%C3%BCcke_in_Sarajewo_-_171_-_%C3%96sterreichische_Galerie_Belvedere.jpg)

People of Sarajevo in 1883

Austria–Hungary began to plan the annexation of Bosnia, but due to international disputes the issue was not resolved until the [annexation crisis](/wiki/Bosnian_Crisis "Bosnian Crisis") of 1908.[[74]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlbertini200594-77) Several external matters affected the status of Bosnia and its relationship with Austria–Hungary. [A bloody coup](/wiki/May_Coup_(Serbia) "May Coup (Serbia)") occurred in Serbia in 1903, which brought a radical anti-Austrian government into power in [Belgrade](/wiki/Belgrade "Belgrade").[[75]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlbertini2005140-78) Then in 1908, the revolt in the Ottoman Empire raised concerns that the [Istanbul](/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul") government might seek the outright return of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These factors caused the Austro-Hungarian government to seek a permanent resolution of the Bosnian question sooner, rather than later.

Taking advantage of the turmoil in the Ottoman Empire, Austro-Hungarian diplomacy tried to obtain provisional Russian approval for changes over the status of Bosnia and Herzegovina and published the annexation proclamation on 6 October 1908.[[76]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlbertini2005227-79) Despite international objections to the Austro-Hungarian annexation, Russians and their client state, Serbia, were compelled to accept the Austro-Hungarian annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in March 1909.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In 1910, Habsburg Emperor [Franz Joseph](/wiki/Franz_Joseph_I_of_Austria "Franz Joseph I of Austria") proclaimed the first constitution in Bosnia, which led to relaxation of earlier laws, elections and formation of the [Bosnian parliament](/wiki/Diet_of_Bosnia "Diet of Bosnia") and growth of new political life.[[77]](#cite_note-80)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/DC-1914-27-d-Sarajevo-cropped.jpg/250px-DC-1914-27-d-Sarajevo-cropped.jpg)](/wiki/File:DC-1914-27-d-Sarajevo-cropped.jpg)

The [assassination](/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand "Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand") of [Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria](/wiki/Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand_of_Austria "Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria") and [Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg](/wiki/Sophie,_Duchess_of_Hohenberg "Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg") by [Gavrilo Princip](/wiki/Gavrilo_Princip "Gavrilo Princip") in Sarajevo, 28 June 1914

On 28 June 1914, [Gavrilo Princip](/wiki/Gavrilo_Princip "Gavrilo Princip"), a [Bosnian Serb](/wiki/Serbs_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina") member of the revolutionary movement [Young Bosnia](/wiki/Young_Bosnia "Young Bosnia"), [assassinated](/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand "Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand") the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, [Archduke Franz Ferdinand](/wiki/Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand_of_Austria "Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria"), in Sarajevo—an event that was the spark that set off [World War I](/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). At the end of the war, the Bosnian Muslims had lost more men per capita than any other ethnic group in the Habsburg Empire whilst serving in the [Bosnian-Herzegovinian Infantry](/wiki/Bosnian-Herzegovinian_Infantry "Bosnian-Herzegovinian Infantry") of the [Austro-Hungarian Army](/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_Army "Austro-Hungarian Army").[[78]](#cite_note-Schachinger-81) Nonetheless, Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole managed to escape the conflict relatively unscathed.[[68]](#cite_note-Riedlmayer-71)

The Austro-Hungarian authorities established an auxiliary militia known as the [Schutzkorps](/wiki/Schutzkorps "Schutzkorps") with a moot role in the empire's policy of [anti-Serb](/wiki/Anti-Serb_sentiment "Anti-Serb sentiment") repression.[[79]](#cite_note-Banac1988-82) Schutzkorps, predominantly recruited among the Bosnian Muslim population, were tasked with hunting down rebel Serbs (the *[Chetniks](/wiki/Chetniks "Chetniks")* and *[Komitadji](/wiki/Komitadji "Komitadji")*)[[80]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVelikonja2003141-83) and became known for their persecution of [Serbs](/wiki/Serbs "Serbs") particularly in Serb populated areas of eastern Bosnia, where they partly retaliated against Serbian Chetniks who in fall 1914 had carried out attacks against the Muslim population in the area.[[81]](#cite_note-84)[[82]](#cite_note-85) The proceedings of the Austro-Hungarian authorities led to around 5,500 citizens of Serb ethnicity in Bosnia and Herzegovina being arrested, and between 700 and 2,200 died in prison while 460 were executed.[[80]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVelikonja2003141-83) Around 5,200 Serb families were forcibly expelled from Bosnia and Herzegovina.[[80]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVelikonja2003141-83)

### Kingdom of Yugoslavia

Main article: [History of Bosnia and Herzegovina § Kingdom of Yugoslavia (1918–41)](/wiki/History_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina#Kingdom_of_Yugoslavia_(1918–41) "History of Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/%C4%8Cuvajte_Jugoslaviju.jpg/250px-%C4%8Cuvajte_Jugoslaviju.jpg)](/wiki/File:%C4%8Cuvajte_Jugoslaviju.jpg)

"Keep/Protect Yugoslavia" (Čuvajte Jugoslaviju), a variant of the alleged last words of [King Alexander I](/wiki/Alexander_I_of_Yugoslavia "Alexander I of Yugoslavia"), in an illustration of Yugoslav peoples dancing the [kolo](/wiki/Kolo_(dance) "Kolo (dance)")

Following World War I, Bosnia and Herzegovina joined the South Slav [Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Yugoslavia "Kingdom of Yugoslavia") (soon renamed Yugoslavia). Political life in Bosnia and Herzegovina at this time was marked by two major trends: social and economic unrest over [property redistribution](/wiki/Distribution_(economics) "Distribution (economics)") and the formation of several political parties that frequently changed coalitions and alliances with parties in other Yugoslav regions.[[68]](#cite_note-Riedlmayer-71)

The dominant ideological conflict of the Yugoslav state, between Croatian regionalism and Serbian centralization, was approached differently by Bosnia and Herzegovina's major [ethnic groups](/wiki/Ethnic_group "Ethnic group") and was dependent on the overall political atmosphere.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25) The political reforms brought about in the newly established Yugoslav kingdom saw few benefits for the Bosnian Muslims; according to the 1910 final census of land ownership and population according to religious affiliation conducted in Austria-Hungary, Muslims owned 91.1%, Orthodox Serbs owned 6.0%, Croat Catholics owned 2.6% and others, 0.3% of the property. Following the reforms, Bosnian Muslims were dispossessed of a total of 1,175,305 hectares of agricultural and forest land.[[83]](#cite_note-86) Although the initial split of the country into 33 [oblasts](/wiki/Oblast "Oblast") erased the presence of traditional geographic entities from the map, the efforts of Bosnian politicians, such as [Mehmed Spaho](/wiki/Mehmed_Spaho "Mehmed Spaho"), ensured the six oblasts carved up from Bosnia and Herzegovina corresponded to the six sanjaks from Ottoman times and, thus, matched the country's traditional boundary as a whole.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25)

The establishment of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1929, however, brought the redrawing of administrative regions into [banates](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Yugoslavia#Subdivisions "Kingdom of Yugoslavia") or *[banovinas](/wiki/Banovina_(region) "Banovina (region)")* that purposely avoided all historical and ethnic lines, removing any trace of a Bosnian entity.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25) Serbo-Croat tensions over the structuring of the Yugoslav state continued, with the concept of a separate Bosnian division receiving little or no consideration.

The [Cvetković-Maček Agreement](/wiki/Cvetkovi%C4%87%E2%80%93Ma%C4%8Dek_Agreement "Cvetković–Maček Agreement") that created the [Croatian banate](/wiki/Banovina_of_Croatia "Banovina of Croatia") in 1939 encouraged what was essentially a [partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Partition_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina") between Croatia and Serbia.[[69]](#cite_note-Imamović,_Mustafa_1996-72) However the rising threat of [Adolf Hitler](/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler")'s [Nazi Germany](/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") forced Yugoslav politicians to shift their attention. Following a period that saw attempts at appeasement, the signing of the [Tripartite Treaty](/wiki/Tripartite_Pact "Tripartite Pact"), and a [coup d'état](/wiki/Yugoslav_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat "Yugoslav coup d'état"), Yugoslavia was finally invaded by Germany on 6 April 1941.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25)

### World War II (1941–45)

Main article: [History of Bosnia and Herzegovina (1941–1945)](/wiki/History_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_(1941%E2%80%931945) "History of Bosnia and Herzegovina (1941–1945)")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Neretva_most.jpg/250px-Neretva_most.jpg)](/wiki/File:Neretva_most.jpg)

The railway bridge over the [Neretva](/wiki/Neretva "Neretva") River in [Jablanica](/wiki/Jablanica,_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Jablanica, Bosnia and Herzegovina"), twice destroyed during the 1943 [Operation Weiss](/wiki/Operation_Weiss "Operation Weiss") offensive

Once the Kingdom of Yugoslavia was conquered by German forces in [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), all of Bosnia and Herzegovina was ceded to the Nazi puppet regime, the [Independent State of Croatia](/wiki/Independent_State_of_Croatia "Independent State of Croatia") (NDH) led by the [Ustaše](/wiki/Usta%C5%A1e "Ustaše"). The NDH leaders embarked on a [campaign of extermination](/wiki/Genocide_of_Serbs_in_the_Independent_State_of_Croatia "Genocide of Serbs in the Independent State of Croatia") of Serbs, Jews, [Romani](/wiki/Romani_people "Romani people") as well as dissident Croats, and, later, [Josip Broz Tito](/wiki/Josip_Broz_Tito "Josip Broz Tito")'s [Partisans](/wiki/Yugoslav_Partisans "Yugoslav Partisans") by setting up a number of [death camps](/wiki/Jasenovac_concentration_camp "Jasenovac concentration camp").[[84]](#cite_note-87) The regime systematically and brutally massacred Serbs in villages in the countryside, using a variety of tools.[[85]](#cite_note-88) The scale of the violence meant that approximately every sixth Serb living in Bosnia and Herzegovina was the victim of a massacre and virtually every Serb had a family member that was killed in the war, mostly by the Ustaše. The experience had a profound impact in the collective memory of Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.[[86]](#cite_note-89) An estimated 209,000 Serbs or 16.9% of its Bosnia population were killed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war.[[87]](#cite_note-90)

The Ustaše recognized both Catholicism and Islam as the national religions, but held the position [Eastern Orthodox Church](/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church "Eastern Orthodox Church"), as a symbol of Serb identity, was their greatest foe.[[88]](#cite_note-Ramet,_p._118-91) Although Croats were by far the largest ethnic group to constitute the Ustaše, the Vice President of the NDH and leader of the Yugoslav Muslim Organization [Džafer Kulenović](/wiki/D%C5%BEafer_Kulenovi%C4%87 "Džafer Kulenović") was a Muslim, and Muslims in total constituted nearly 12% of the Ustaše military and civil service authority.[[89]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVelikonja2003179-92)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Vje%C4%8Dna_vatra_in_2019.jpg/250px-Vje%C4%8Dna_vatra_in_2019.jpg)](/wiki/File:Vje%C4%8Dna_vatra_in_2019.jpg)

[Eternal flame](/wiki/Eternal_flame_(Sarajevo) "Eternal flame (Sarajevo)") memorial to military and civilian [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") victims in Sarajevo

Many Serbs themselves took up arms and joined the Chetniks, a Serb nationalist movement with the aim of establishing an ethnically homogeneous '[Greater Serbian](/wiki/Greater_Serbia "Greater Serbia")' state[[90]](#cite_note-93) within the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. The Chetniks, in turn, pursued a [genocidal campaign](/wiki/Chetnik_war_crimes_in_World_War_II "Chetnik war crimes in World War II") against ethnic Muslims and Croats, as well as persecuting a large number of [communist](/wiki/Communism "Communism") Serbs and other Communist sympathizers, with the Muslim populations of Bosnia, Herzegovina and [Sandžak](/wiki/Sand%C5%BEak "Sandžak") being a primary target.[[91]](#cite_note-94) Once captured, Muslim villagers were systematically massacred by the Chetniks.[[92]](#cite_note-95) Of the 75,000 Muslims who died in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war,[[93]](#cite_note-Cohen-96) approximately 30,000 (mostly civilians) were killed by the Chetniks.[[94]](#cite_note-Geiger-97) Massacres against Croats were smaller in scale but similar in action.[[95]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomasevich1975259-98) Between 64,000 and 79,000 Bosnian Croats were killed between April 1941 to May 1945.[[93]](#cite_note-Cohen-96) Of these, about 18,000 were killed by the Chetniks.[[94]](#cite_note-Geiger-97)

A percentage of Muslims served in Nazi [*Waffen-SS*](/wiki/13th_Waffen_Mountain_Division_of_the_SS_Handschar_(1st_Croatian) "13th Waffen Mountain Division of the SS Handschar (1st Croatian)") units.[[96]](#cite_note-99) These units were responsible for massacres of Serbs in northwest and eastern Bosnia, most notably in [Vlasenica](/wiki/Vlasenica "Vlasenica").[[97]](#cite_note-100) On 12 October 1941, a group of 108 prominent Sarajevan Muslims signed the [Resolution of Sarajevo Muslims](/wiki/Resolution_of_Sarajevo_Muslims "Resolution of Sarajevo Muslims") by which they condemned the persecution of Serbs organized by the Ustaše, made distinction between Muslims who participated in such persecutions and the Muslim population as a whole, presented information about the persecutions of Muslims by Serbs, and requested security for all citizens of the country, regardless of their identity.[[98]](#cite_note-101)

Starting in 1941, Yugoslav communists under the leadership of Josip Broz Tito organized their own multi-ethnic resistance group, the Partisans, who fought against both [Axis](/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers") and Chetnik forces. On 29 November 1943, the [Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Anti-Fascist_Council_for_the_National_Liberation_of_Yugoslavia "Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia") (AVNOJ) with Tito at its helm held a founding conference in [Jajce](/wiki/Jajce "Jajce") where Bosnia and Herzegovina was reestablished as a republic within the Yugoslav federation in its Habsburg borders.[[99]](#cite_note-102) During the entire course of [World War II in Yugoslavia](/wiki/World_War_II_in_Yugoslavia "World War II in Yugoslavia"), 64.1% of all Bosnian Partisans were Serbs, 23% were Muslims and 8.8% Croats.[[100]](#cite_note-anubih.ba-Hoare-103)

Military success eventually prompted the [Allies](/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") to support the Partisans, resulting in the successful [Maclean Mission](/wiki/Maclean_Mission "Maclean Mission"), but Tito declined their offer to help and relied on his own forces instead. All the major military offensives by the antifascist movement of Yugoslavia against Nazis and their local supporters were conducted in Bosnia and Herzegovina and its peoples bore the brunt of the fighting. More than 300,000 people died in Bosnia and Herzegovina in World War II, or more than 10% of the population.[[101]](#cite_note-104) At the end of the war, the establishment of the [Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia"), with the [constitution of 1946](/wiki/1946_Yugoslav_Constitution "1946 Yugoslav Constitution"), officially made Bosnia and Herzegovina one of six constituent republics in the new state.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25)

### Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (1945–1992)

Main article: [Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Socialist_Republic_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Flag_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_%281946%E2%80%931992%29.svg/250px-Flag_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_%281946%E2%80%931992%29.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Flag_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_(1946%E2%80%931992).svg)

Bosnia and Herzegovina's flag while part of the [Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia")

Due to its central geographic position within the Yugoslav federation, post-war Bosnia was selected as a base for the development of the military defense industry. This contributed to a large concentration of arms and military personnel in Bosnia; a significant factor in [the war that followed the break-up of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War") in the 1990s.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25) However, Bosnia's existence within Yugoslavia, for the large part, was relatively peaceful and very prosperous, with high employment, a strong industrial and export oriented economy, a good education system and social and medical security for every citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Several international corporations operated in Bosnia—[Volkswagen](/wiki/Volkswagen "Volkswagen") as part of TAS (car factory in Sarajevo, from 1972), [Coca-Cola](/wiki/Coca-Cola "Coca-Cola") (from 1975), SKF Sweden (from 1967), [Marlboro](/wiki/Marlboro_(cigarette) "Marlboro (cigarette)") (a tobacco factory in Sarajevo), and [Holiday Inn](/wiki/Holiday_Inn "Holiday Inn") hotels. Sarajevo was the site of the [1984 Winter Olympics](/wiki/1984_Winter_Olympics "1984 Winter Olympics").

During the 1950s and 1960s, Bosnia was a political backwater of Yugoslavia. In the 1970s, a strong Bosnian political elite arose, fueled in part by Tito's leadership in the [Non-Aligned Movement](/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement "Non-Aligned Movement") and Bosnians serving in Yugoslavia's diplomatic corps. While working within the Socialist system, politicians such as [Džemal Bijedić](/wiki/D%C5%BEemal_Bijedi%C4%87 "Džemal Bijedić"), [Branko Mikulić](/wiki/Branko_Mikuli%C4%87 "Branko Mikulić") and [Hamdija Pozderac](/wiki/Hamdija_Pozderac "Hamdija Pozderac") reinforced and protected the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina.[[102]](#cite_note-Stojic-105) Their efforts proved key during the turbulent period following Tito's death in 1980, and are today considered some of the early steps towards [Bosnian independence](/wiki/Independence_Day_(Bosnia_and_Herzegovina) "Independence Day (Bosnia and Herzegovina)"). However, the republic did not escape the increasingly nationalistic climate of the time. With the fall of communism and the start of the [breakup of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Breakup_of_Yugoslavia "Breakup of Yugoslavia"), doctrine of tolerance began to lose its potency, creating an opportunity for nationalist elements in the society to spread their influence.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

### Bosnian War (1992–1995)

Main article: [Bosnian War](/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War")

See also: [Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Republic_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Breakup_of_Yugoslavia.gif/500px-Breakup_of_Yugoslavia.gif)](/wiki/File:Breakup_of_Yugoslavia.gif)

Dissolution of [Yugoslavia](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia")

On 18 November 1990, [multi-party parliamentary elections](/wiki/1990_Bosnian_general_election "1990 Bosnian general election") were held throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. A second round followed on 25 November, resulting in a [national assembly](/wiki/Parliamentary_Assembly_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina") where communist power was replaced by a coalition of three ethnically based parties.[[103]](#cite_note-phron1-106) Following [Slovenia](/wiki/Slovenia "Slovenia") and [Croatia](/wiki/Croatia "Croatia")'s declarations of independence from Yugoslavia, a significant split developed among the residents of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the issue of whether to remain within Yugoslavia (overwhelmingly favored by Serbs) or seek independence (overwhelmingly favored by [Muslims](/wiki/Muslims_(ethnic_group) "Muslims (ethnic group)") and Croats).[[104]](#cite_note-The_Princeton_Encyclopedia_of_Self-Determination_1995-107)

The Serb members of parliament, consisting mainly of the [Serb Democratic Party](/wiki/Serb_Democratic_Party_(Bosnia_and_Herzegovina) "Serb Democratic Party (Bosnia and Herzegovina)") members, abandoned the central parliament in Sarajevo, and formed the [Assembly of the Serb People of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/National_Assembly_(Republika_Srpska) "National Assembly (Republika Srpska)") on 24 October 1991, which marked the end of the three-ethnic coalition that governed after the elections in 1990. This Assembly established the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina on 9 January 1992. It was renamed [Republika Srpska](/wiki/Republika_Srpska_(1992%E2%80%931995) "Republika Srpska (1992–1995)") in August 1992. On 18 November 1991, the party branch in Bosnia and Herzegovina of the ruling party in the Republic of Croatia, the [Croatian Democratic Union](/wiki/Croatian_Democratic_Union "Croatian Democratic Union") (HDZ), proclaimed the existence of the [Croatian Community of Herzeg-Bosnia](/wiki/Croatian_Republic_of_Herzeg-Bosnia "Croatian Republic of Herzeg-Bosnia") in a separate part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the [Croatian Defence Council](/wiki/Croatian_Defence_Council "Croatian Defence Council") (HVO) as its military branch.[[105]](#cite_note-ICTY:_Prlić_et_al._(IT-04-74)-108) It went unrecognized by the [Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Council_of_Ministers_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina"), which declared it illegal.[[106]](#cite_note-109)[[107]](#cite_note-110)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Norsk_Sisu_fra_NORLOGB.jpg/250px-Norsk_Sisu_fra_NORLOGB.jpg)](/wiki/File:Norsk_Sisu_fra_NORLOGB.jpg)

[UN](/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") troops in front of the [Executive Council Building](/wiki/Greece%E2%80%93Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_Friendship_Building "Greece–Bosnia and Herzegovina Friendship Building"), burned after being struck by tank fire during the [siege of Sarajevo](/wiki/Siege_of_Sarajevo "Siege of Sarajevo"), 1995

A declaration of the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina on 15 October 1991 was followed by a [referendum for independence](/wiki/1992_Bosnian_independence_referendum "1992 Bosnian independence referendum") on 29 February and 1 March 1992, which was boycotted by the great majority of Serbs. The turnout in the independence referendum was 63.4 per cent and 99.7 per cent of voters voted for independence.[[108]](#cite_note-111) Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence on 3 March 1992 and received international recognition the following month on 6 April 1992.[[109]](#cite_note-112) The [Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Republic_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina") was admitted as a member state of the [United Nations](/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") on 22 May 1992.[[110]](#cite_note-113) Serbian leader [Slobodan Milošević](/wiki/Slobodan_Milo%C5%A1evi%C4%87 "Slobodan Milošević") and Croatian leader [Franjo Tuđman](/wiki/Franjo_Tu%C4%91man "Franjo Tuđman") are believed to have agreed on a [partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Partition_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina") in March 1991, with the aim of establishing [Greater Serbia](/wiki/Greater_Serbia "Greater Serbia") and [Greater Croatia](/wiki/Greater_Croatia "Greater Croatia").[[111]](#cite_note-114)

Following Bosnia and Herzegovina's declaration of independence, Bosnian Serb militias mobilized in different parts of the country. Government forces were poorly equipped and unprepared for the war.[[112]](#cite_note-ICTY:_Naletilić_and_Martinović_verdict_—_A._Historical_background-115) International recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina increased diplomatic pressure for the [Yugoslav People's Army](/wiki/Yugoslav_People%27s_Army "Yugoslav People's Army") (JNA) to withdraw from the republic's territory, which they officially did in June 1992. The Bosnian Serb members of the JNA simply changed insignia, formed the [Army of Republika Srpska](/wiki/Army_of_Republika_Srpska "Army of Republika Srpska") (VRS), and continued fighting. Armed and equipped from JNA stockpiles in Bosnia, supported by volunteers and various paramilitary forces from Serbia, and receiving extensive humanitarian, logistical and financial support from the [Federal Republic of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Serbia_and_Montenegro "Serbia and Montenegro"), [Republika Srpska](/wiki/Republika_Srpska "Republika Srpska")'s offensives in 1992 managed to place much of the country under its control.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25) The Bosnian Serb advance was accompanied by the [ethnic cleansing](/wiki/Ethnic_cleansing "Ethnic cleansing") of Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats from VRS-controlled areas. Dozens of concentration camps were established in which inmates were subjected to violence and abuse, including rape.[[113]](#cite_note-ICTY:_Kunarac,_Kovač_and_Vuković_judgement_—_Foča-116) The ethnic cleansing culminated in the [Srebrenica massacre](/wiki/Srebrenica_massacre "Srebrenica massacre") of more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys in July 1995, which was ruled to have been a [genocide](/wiki/Genocide "Genocide") by the [International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia](/wiki/International_Criminal_Tribunal_for_the_former_Yugoslavia "International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia") (ICTY).[[114]](#cite_note-117) Bosniak and Bosnian Croat forces also committed war crimes against civilians from different ethnic groups, though on a smaller scale.[[115]](#cite_note-118)[[116]](#cite_note-119)[[117]](#cite_note-haverford-120)[[118]](#cite_note-un-121) Most of the Bosniak and Croat atrocities were committed during the [Croat–Bosniak War](/wiki/Croat%E2%80%93Bosniak_War "Croat–Bosniak War"), a sub-conflict of the Bosnian War that pitted the [Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Army_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina") (ARBiH) against the HVO. The Bosniak-Croat conflict ended in March 1994, with the signing of the [Washington Agreement](/wiki/Washington_Agreement_(1994) "Washington Agreement (1994)"), leading to the creation of a joint Bosniak-Croat [Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina"), which amalgamated HVO-held territory with that held by the [Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Army_of_the_Republic_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina") (ARBiH).[[119]](#cite_note-Lumen_Learning_–_Simple_Book_Production_2017-122)

### Recent history

Main article: [2014 unrest in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/2014_unrest_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "2014 unrest in Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Bosnian_social_protests_Tuzla.jpg/250px-Bosnian_social_protests_Tuzla.jpg)](/wiki/File:Bosnian_social_protests_Tuzla.jpg)

[Tuzla](/wiki/Tuzla "Tuzla") government building burning after [anti-government clashes](/wiki/2014_unrest_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "2014 unrest in Bosnia and Herzegovina") on 7 February 2014

On 4 February 2014, the [protests](/wiki/2014_unrest_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "2014 unrest in Bosnia and Herzegovina") against the [Government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Government_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina"), one of the country's two entities, dubbed the Bosnian Spring, the name being taken from the [Arab Spring](/wiki/Arab_Spring "Arab Spring"), began in the northern town of [Tuzla](/wiki/Tuzla "Tuzla"). Workers from several factories that had been privatised and gone bankrupt assembled to demand action over jobs, unpaid salaries and pensions.[[120]](#cite_note-123) Soon protests spread to the rest of the Federation, with violent clashes reported in close to 20 towns, the biggest of which were [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo"), [Zenica](/wiki/Zenica "Zenica"), [Mostar](/wiki/Mostar "Mostar"), [Bihać](/wiki/Biha%C4%87 "Bihać"), [Brčko](/wiki/Br%C4%8Dko "Brčko") and Tuzla.[[121]](#cite_note-124) The Bosnian news media reported that hundreds of people had been injured during the protests, including dozens of police officers, with bursts of violence in Sarajevo, in the northern city of Tuzla, in Mostar in the south, and in Zenica in central Bosnia. The same level of unrest or activism did not occur in Republika Srpska, but hundreds of people also gathered in support of protests in the city of [Banja Luka](/wiki/Banja_Luka "Banja Luka") against its separate government.[[122]](#cite_note-125)[[123]](#cite_note-126)[[124]](#cite_note-127)

The protests marked the largest outbreak of public anger over high unemployment and two decades of political inertia in the country since the end of the Bosnian War in 1995.[[125]](#cite_note-128) According to a report made by [Christian Schmidt](/wiki/Christian_Schmidt "Christian Schmidt") of the [Office of High Representative](/wiki/High_Representative_for_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina") in late 2021, Bosnia and Herzegovina has been experiencing intensified political and ethnic tensions, which could potentially break the country apart and slide it back into war once again.[[126]](#cite_note-129)[[127]](#cite_note-130) The [European Union](/wiki/European_Union "European Union") fears this will lead to further [Balkanization](/wiki/Balkanization "Balkanization") in the region.[[128]](#cite_note-131)

On 15 December 2022, Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised by the European Union as a candidate country for [accession](/wiki/Accession_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_to_the_European_Union "Accession of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the European Union") following the decision of the [European Council](/wiki/European_Council "European Council").[[129]](#cite_note-sarajevotimes-132)

Bosnia and Herzegovina is in the western [Balkans](/wiki/Balkans "Balkans"), bordering [Croatia](/wiki/Croatia "Croatia") (932 km or 579 mi) to the north and west, [Serbia](/wiki/Serbia "Serbia") (302 km or 188 mi) to the east, and [Montenegro](/wiki/Montenegro "Montenegro") (225 km or 140 mi) to the southeast. It has a coastline about 20 kilometres (12 miles) long surrounding the town of [Neum](/wiki/Neum "Neum").[[130]](#cite_note-coastline-133)[[131]](#cite_note-134) It lies between latitudes [42°](/wiki/42nd_parallel_north "42nd parallel north") and [46° N](/wiki/46th_parallel_north "46th parallel north"), and longitudes [15°](/wiki/15th_meridian_east "15th meridian east") and [20° E](/wiki/20th_meridian_east "20th meridian east").

The country's name comes from the two alleged regions [Bosnia](/wiki/Bosnia_(region) "Bosnia (region)") and [Herzegovina](/wiki/Herzegovina "Herzegovina"), whose border was never defined. Historically, Bosnia's official name never included any of its many regions until the Austro-Hungarian occupation.

The country is mostly mountainous, encompassing the central [Dinaric Alps](/wiki/Dinaric_Alps "Dinaric Alps"). The northeastern parts reach into the [Pannonian Basin](/wiki/Pannonian_Basin "Pannonian Basin"), while in the south it borders the [Adriatic](/wiki/Adriatic_Sea "Adriatic Sea"). The Dinaric Alps generally run in a southeast–northwest direction, and get higher towards the south. The highest point of the country is the peak of [Maglić](/wiki/Magli%C4%87_(mountain) "Maglić (mountain)") at 2,386 metres (7,828.1 feet), on the Montenegrin border. Other major mountains include [Volujak](/wiki/Volujak_(mountain) "Volujak (mountain)"), [Zelengora](/wiki/Zelengora "Zelengora"), [Lelija](/wiki/Lelija "Lelija"), [Lebršnik](/wiki/Lebr%C5%A1nik "Lebršnik"), [Orjen](/wiki/Orjen "Orjen"), [Kozara](/wiki/Kozara "Kozara"), [Grmeč](/wiki/Grme%C4%8D "Grmeč"), [Čvrsnica](/wiki/%C4%8Cvrsnica "Čvrsnica"), [Prenj](/wiki/Prenj "Prenj"), [Vran](/wiki/Vran "Vran"), [Vranica](/wiki/Vranica "Vranica"), [Velež](/wiki/Vele%C5%BE_(Bosnia_and_Herzegovina) "Velež (Bosnia and Herzegovina)"), [Vlašić](/wiki/Vla%C5%A1i%C4%87_(Bosnian_mountain) "Vlašić (Bosnian mountain)"), [Cincar](/wiki/Cincar "Cincar"), [Romanija](/wiki/Romanija "Romanija"), [Jahorina](/wiki/Jahorina "Jahorina"), [Bjelašnica](/wiki/Bjela%C5%A1nica "Bjelašnica"), [Treskavica](/wiki/Treskavica "Treskavica") and [Trebević](/wiki/Trebevi%C4%87 "Trebević"). The geological composition of the Dinaric chain of mountains in Bosnia consists primarily of [limestone](/wiki/Limestone "Limestone") (including [Mesozoic](/wiki/Mesozoic "Mesozoic") limestone), with deposits of [iron](/wiki/Iron "Iron"), [coal](/wiki/Coal "Coal"), [zinc](/wiki/Zinc "Zinc"), [manganese](/wiki/Manganese "Manganese"), [bauxite](/wiki/Bauxite "Bauxite"), [lead](/wiki/Lead "Lead"), and [salt](/wiki/Salt "Salt") present in some areas, especially in central and northern Bosnia.[[132]](#cite_note-135)

Overall, nearly 50% of Bosnia and Herzegovina is forested. Most forest areas are in the centre, east and west parts of Bosnia. Herzegovina has a drier Mediterranean climate, with dominant [karst](/wiki/Karst "Karst") topography. Northern Bosnia ([Posavina](/wiki/Posavina "Posavina")) contains very fertile agricultural land along the [Sava](/wiki/Sava "Sava") river and the corresponding area is heavily farmed. This farmland is a part of the Pannonian Plain stretching into neighboring Croatia and Serbia. The country has only 20 kilometres (12 miles) of coastline,[[130]](#cite_note-coastline-133)[[133]](#cite_note-Neum_coastline-136) around the town of Neum in the [Herzegovina-Neretva Canton](/wiki/Herzegovina-Neretva_Canton "Herzegovina-Neretva Canton"). Although the city is surrounded by Croatian peninsulas, by international law, Bosnia and Herzegovina has a [right of passage](/wiki/Right_of_passage "Right of passage") to the outer sea.

[Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo") is the capital[[1]](#cite_note-Constitution-1) and largest city.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECIA2019-9) Other major cities include [Banja Luka](/wiki/Banja_Luka "Banja Luka") and [Prijedor](/wiki/Prijedor "Prijedor") in the northwest region known as [Bosanska Krajina](/wiki/Bosanska_Krajina "Bosanska Krajina"), [Tuzla](/wiki/Tuzla "Tuzla"), [Bijeljina](/wiki/Bijeljina "Bijeljina"), [Doboj](/wiki/Doboj "Doboj") and [Brčko](/wiki/Br%C4%8Dko "Brčko") in the northeast, [Zenica](/wiki/Zenica "Zenica") in the central part of the country, and [Mostar](/wiki/Mostar "Mostar"), the largest city in the southern region of [Herzegovina](/wiki/Herzegovina "Herzegovina").

There are seven major rivers in Bosnia and Herzegovina:[[134]](#cite_note-fao-137)

* The [Sava](/wiki/Sava "Sava") is the largest river of the country, and forms its northern [natural border](/wiki/Natural_border "Natural border") with Croatia. It drains 76%[[134]](#cite_note-fao-137) of the country's territory into the [Danube](/wiki/Danube "Danube") and then the [Black Sea](/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea"). Bosnia and Herzegovina is a member of the [International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River](/wiki/International_Commission_for_the_Protection_of_the_Danube_River "International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River") (ICPDR).
* The [Una](/wiki/Una_(Sava) "Una (Sava)"), [Sana](/wiki/Sana_(river) "Sana (river)") and [Vrbas](/wiki/Vrbas_(river) "Vrbas (river)") are right tributaries of the Sava. They are in the northwestern region of [Bosanska Krajina](/wiki/Bosanska_Krajina "Bosanska Krajina").
* The [Bosna](/wiki/Bosna_(river) "Bosna (river)") river gave its name to the country, and is the longest river fully contained within it. It stretches through central Bosnia, from its source near [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo") to Sava in the north.
* The [Drina](/wiki/Drina "Drina") flows through the eastern part of Bosnia, and for the most part it forms a natural border with Serbia.
* The [Neretva](/wiki/Neretva "Neretva") is the major river of Herzegovina and the only major river that flows south, into the Adriatic Sea.

### Biodiversity

Main article: [Environment of Bosnia and Herzegovina § Biodiversity](/wiki/Environment_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina#Biodiversity "Environment of Bosnia and Herzegovina")

[Phytogeographically](/wiki/Phytogeography "Phytogeography"), Bosnia and Herzegovina belongs to the [Boreal Kingdom](/wiki/Boreal_Kingdom "Boreal Kingdom") and is shared between the Illyrian province of the [Circumboreal Region](/wiki/Circumboreal_Region "Circumboreal Region") and Adriatic province of the [Mediterranean Region](/wiki/Mediterranean_Basin "Mediterranean Basin"). According to the [World Wide Fund for Nature](/wiki/World_Wide_Fund_for_Nature "World Wide Fund for Nature") (WWF), the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina can be subdivided into four [ecoregions](/wiki/Ecoregion "Ecoregion"): [Balkan mixed forests](/wiki/Balkan_mixed_forests "Balkan mixed forests"), [Dinaric Mountains mixed forests](/wiki/Dinaric_Mountains_mixed_forests "Dinaric Mountains mixed forests"), [Pannonian mixed forests](/wiki/Pannonian_mixed_forests "Pannonian mixed forests") and [Illyrian deciduous forests](/wiki/Illyrian_deciduous_forests "Illyrian deciduous forests").[[135]](#cite_note-DinersteinOlson2017-138) The country had a 2018 [Forest Landscape Integrity Index](/wiki/Forest_Landscape_Integrity_Index "Forest Landscape Integrity Index") mean score of 5.99/10, ranking it 89th globally out of 172 countries.[[136]](#cite_note-FLII-Supplementary-139) In Bosnia and Herzegovina [forest cover](/wiki/Forest_cover "Forest cover") is around 43% of the total land area, equivalent to 2,187,910 hectares (ha) of forest in 2020, down from 2,210,000 hectares (ha) in 1990. For the year 2015, 74% of the forest area was reported to be under [public ownership](/wiki/State_ownership "State ownership") and 26% [private ownership](/wiki/Private_property "Private property").[[137]](#cite_note-140)[[138]](#cite_note-141)

### Government

Main article: [Political divisions of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Political_divisions_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Political divisions of Bosnia and Herzegovina")
