Following a period that saw attempts at appeasement, the signing of the [Tripartite Treaty](/wiki/Tripartite_Pact \"Tripartite Pact\"), and a [coup d\\'état](/wiki/Yugoslav_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat \"Yugoslav coup d\\'état\"), Yugoslavia was finally invaded by Germany on 6 April 1941.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25)\\n\\n### World War II (1941–45)\\n\\nMain article: [History of Bosnia and Herzegovina (1941–1945)](/wiki/History_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_(1941%E2%80%931945) \"History of Bosnia and Herzegovina (1941–1945)\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Neretva_most.jpg/250px-Neretva_most.jpg)](/wiki/File:Neretva_most.jpg)\\n\\nThe railway bridge over the [Neretva](/wiki/Neretva \"Neretva\") River in [Jablanica](/wiki/Jablanica,_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Jablanica, Bosnia and Herzegovina\"), twice destroyed during the 1943 [Operation Weiss](/wiki/Operation_Weiss \"Operation Weiss\") offensive\\n\\nOnce the Kingdom of Yugoslavia was conquered by German forces in [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II \"World War II\"), all of Bosnia and Herzegovina was ceded to the Nazi puppet regime, the [Independent State of Croatia](/wiki/Independent_State_of_Croatia \"Independent State of Croatia\") (NDH) led by the [Ustaše](/wiki/Usta%C5%A1e \"Ustaše\"). The NDH leaders embarked on a [campaign of extermination](/wiki/Genocide_of_Serbs_in_the_Independent_State_of_Croatia \"Genocide of Serbs in the Independent State of Croatia\") of Serbs, Jews, [Romani](/wiki/Romani_people \"Romani people\") as well as dissident Croats, and, later, [Josip Broz Tito](/wiki/Josip_Broz_Tito \"Josip Broz Tito\")\\'s [Partisans](/wiki/Yugoslav_Partisans \"Yugoslav Partisans\") by setting up a number of [death camps](/wiki/Jasenovac_concentration_camp \"Jasenovac concentration camp\").[[84]](#cite_note-87) The regime systematically and brutally massacred Serbs in villages in the countryside, using a variety of tools.[[85]](#cite_note-88) The scale of the violence meant that approximately every sixth Serb living in Bosnia and Herzegovina was the victim of a massacre and virtually every Serb had a family member that was killed in the war, mostly by the Ustaše. The experience had a profound impact in the collective memory of Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.[[86]](#cite_note-89) An estimated 209,000 Serbs or 16.9% of its Bosnia population were killed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war.[[87]](#cite_note-90)\\n\\nThe Ustaše recognized both Catholicism and Islam as the national religions, but held the position [Eastern Orthodox Church](/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church \"Eastern Orthodox Church\"), as a symbol of Serb identity, was their greatest foe.[[88]](#cite_note-Ramet,_p._118-91) Although Croats were by far the largest ethnic group to constitute the Ustaše, the Vice President of the NDH and leader of the Yugoslav Muslim Organization [Džafer Kulenović](/wiki/D%C5%BEafer_Kulenovi%C4%87 \"Džafer Kulenović\") was a Muslim, and Muslims in total constituted nearly 12% of the Ustaše military and civil service authority.[[89]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVelikonja2003179-92)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Vje%C4%8Dna_vatra_in_2019.jpg/250px-Vje%C4%8Dna_vatra_in_2019.jpg)](/wiki/File:Vje%C4%8Dna_vatra_in_2019.jpg)\\n\\n[Eternal flame](/wiki/Eternal_flame_(Sarajevo) \"Eternal flame (Sarajevo)\") memorial to military and civilian [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II \"World War II\") victims in Sarajevo\\n\\nMany Serbs themselves took up arms and joined the Chetniks, a Serb nationalist movement with the aim of establishing an ethnically homogeneous \\'[Greater Serbian](/wiki/Greater_Serbia \"Greater Serbia\")\\' state[[90]](#cite_note-93) within the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. The Chetniks, in turn, pursued a [genocidal campaign](/wiki/Chetnik_war_crimes_in_World_War_II \"Chetnik war crimes in World War II\") against ethnic Muslims and Croats, as well as persecuting a large number of [communist](/wiki/Communism \"Communism\") Serbs and other Communist sympathizers, with the Muslim populations of Bosnia, Herzegovina and [Sandžak](/wiki/Sand%C5%BEak \"Sandžak\") being a primary target.[[91]](#cite_note-94) Once captured, Muslim villagers were systematically massacred by the Chetniks.[[92]](#cite_note-95) Of the 75,000 Muslims who died in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war,[[93]](#cite_note-Cohen-96) approximately 30,000 (mostly civilians) were killed by the Chetniks.[[94]](#cite_note-Geiger-97) Massacres against Croats were smaller in scale but similar in action.[[95]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomasevich1975259-98) Between 64,000 and 79,000 Bosnian Croats were killed between April 1941 to May 1945.[[93]](#cite_note-Cohen-96) Of these, about 18,000 were killed by the Chetniks.[[94]](#cite_note-Geiger-97)\\n\\nA percentage of Muslims served in Nazi [*Waffen-SS*](/wiki/13th_Waffen_Mountain_Division_of_the_SS_Handschar_(1st_Croatian) \"13th Waffen Mountain Division of the SS Handschar (1st Croatian)\") units.[[96]](#cite_note-99) These units were responsible for massacres of Serbs in northwest and eastern Bosnia, most notably in [Vlasenica](/wiki/Vlasenica \"Vlasenica\").[[97]](#cite_note-100) On 12 October 1941, a group of 108 prominent Sarajevan Muslims signed the [Resolution of Sarajevo Muslims](/wiki/Resolution_of_Sarajevo_Muslims \"Resolution of Sarajevo Muslims\") by which they condemned the persecution of Serbs organized by the Ustaše, made distinction between Muslims who participated in such persecutions and the Muslim population as a whole, presented information about the persecutions of Muslims by Serbs, and requested security for all citizens of the country, regardless of their identity.[[98]](#cite_note-101)\\n\\nStarting in 1941, Yugoslav communists under the leadership of Josip Broz Tito organized their own multi-ethnic resistance group, the Partisans, who fought against both [Axis](/wiki/Axis_powers \"Axis powers\") and Chetnik forces. On 29 November 1943, the [Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Anti-Fascist_Council_for_the_National_Liberation_of_Yugoslavia \"Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia\") (AVNOJ) with Tito at its helm held a founding conference in [Jajce](/wiki/Jajce \"Jajce\") where Bosnia and Herzegovina was reestablished as a republic within the Yugoslav federation in its Habsburg borders.[[99]](#cite_note-102) During the entire course of [World War II in Yugoslavia](/wiki/World_War_II_in_Yugoslavia \"World War II in Yugoslavia\"), 64.1% of all Bosnian Partisans were Serbs, 23% were Muslims and 8.8% Croats.[[100]](#cite_note-anubih.ba-Hoare-103)\\n\\nMilitary success eventually prompted the [Allies](/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II \"Allies of World War II\") to support the Partisans, resulting in the successful [Maclean Mission](/wiki/Maclean_Mission \"Maclean Mission\"), but Tito declined their offer to help and relied on his own forces instead. All the major military offensives by the antifascist movement of Yugoslavia against Nazis and their local supporters were conducted in Bosnia and Herzegovina and its peoples bore the brunt of the fighting. More than 300,000 people died in Bosnia and Herzegovina in World War II, or more than 10% of the population.[[101]](#cite_note-104) At the end of the war, the establishment of the [Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia \"Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia\"), with the [constitution of 1946](/wiki/1946_Yugoslav_Constitution \"1946 Yugoslav Constitution\"), officially made Bosnia and Herzegovina one of six constituent republics in the new state.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25)\\n\\n### Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (1945–1992)\\n\\nMain article: [Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Socialist_Republic_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Flag_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_%281946%E2%80%931992%29.svg/250px-Flag_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_%281946%E2%80%931992%29.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Flag_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_(1946%E2%80%931992).svg)\\n\\nBosnia and Herzegovina\\'s flag while part of the [Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia \"Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia\")\\n\\nDue to its central geographic position within the Yugoslav federation, post-war Bosnia was selected as a base for the development of the military defense industry. This contributed to a large concentration of arms and military personnel in Bosnia; a significant factor in [the war that followed the break-up of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Bosnian_War \"Bosnian War\") in the 1990s.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25) However, Bosnia\\'s existence within Yugoslavia, for the large part, was relatively peaceful and very prosperous, with high employment, a strong industrial and export oriented economy, a good education system and social and medical security for every citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Several international corporations operated in Bosnia—[Volkswagen](/wiki/Volkswagen \"Volkswagen\") as part of TAS (car factory in Sarajevo, from 1972), [Coca-Cola](/wiki/Coca-Cola \"Coca-Cola\") (from 1975), SKF Sweden (from 1967), [Marlboro](/wiki/Marlboro_(cigarette) \"Marlboro (cigarette)\") (a tobacco factory in Sarajevo), and [Holiday Inn](/wiki/Holiday_Inn \"Holiday Inn\") hotels. Sarajevo was the site of the [1984 Winter Olympics](/wiki/1984_Winter_Olympics \"1984 Winter Olympics\").\\n\\nDuring the 1950s and 1960s, Bosnia was a political backwater of Yugoslavia. In the 1970s, a strong Bosnian political elite arose, fueled in part by Tito\\'s leadership in the [Non-Aligned Movement](/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement \"Non-Aligned Movement\") and Bosnians serving in Yugoslavia\\'s diplomatic corps. While working within the Socialist system, politicians such as [Džemal Bijedić](/wiki/D%C5%BEemal_Bijedi%C4%87 \"Džemal Bijedić\"), [Branko Mikulić](/wiki/Branko_Mikuli%C4%87 \"Branko Mikulić\") and [Hamdija Pozderac](/wiki/Hamdija_Pozderac \"Hamdija Pozderac\") reinforced and protected the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina.[[102]](#cite_note-Stojic-105) Their efforts proved key during the turbulent period following Tito\\'s death in 1980, and are today considered some of the early steps towards [Bosnian independence](/wiki/Independence_Day_(Bosnia_and_Herzegovina) \"Independence Day (Bosnia and Herzegovina)\"). However, the republic did not escape the increasingly nationalistic climate of the time. With the fall of communism and the start of the [breakup of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Breakup_of_Yugoslavia \"Breakup of Yugoslavia\"), doctrine of tolerance began to lose its potency, creating an opportunity for nationalist elements in the society to spread their influence.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\n### Bosnian War (1992–1995)\\n\\nMain article: [Bosnian War](/wiki/Bosnian_War \"Bosnian War\")\\n\\nSee also: [Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Republic_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Breakup_of_Yugoslavia.gif/500px-Breakup_of_Yugoslavia.gif)](/wiki/File:Breakup_of_Yugoslavia.gif)\\n\\nDissolution of [Yugoslavia](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia \"Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia\")\\n\\nOn 18 November 1990, [multi-party parliamentary elections](/wiki/1990_Bosnian_general_election \"1990 Bosnian general election\") were held throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. A second round followed on 25 November, resulting in a [national assembly](/wiki/Parliamentary_Assembly_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") where communist power was replaced by a coalition of three ethnically based parties.[[103]](#cite_note-phron1-106) Following [Slovenia](/wiki/Slovenia \"Slovenia\") and [Croatia](/wiki/Croatia \"Croatia\")\\'s declarations of independence from Yugoslavia, a significant split developed among the residents of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the issue of whether to remain within Yugoslavia (overwhelmingly favored by Serbs) or seek independence (overwhelmingly favored by [Muslims](/wiki/Muslims_(ethnic_group) \"Muslims (ethnic group)\") and Croats).[[104]](#cite_note-The_Princeton_Encyclopedia_of_Self-Determination_1995-107)\\n\\nThe Serb members of parliament, consisting mainly of the [Serb Democratic Party](/wiki/Serb_Democratic_Party_(Bosnia_and_Herzegovina) \"Serb Democratic Party (Bosnia and Herzegovina)\") members, abandoned the central parliament in Sarajevo, and formed the [Assembly of the Serb People of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/National_Assembly_(Republika_Srpska) \"National Assembly (Republika Srpska)\") on 24 October 1991, which marked the end of the three-ethnic coalition that governed after the elections in 1990. This Assembly established the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina on 9 January 1992. It was renamed [Republika Srpska](/wiki/Republika_Srpska_(1992%E2%80%931995) \"Republika Srpska (1992–1995)\") in August 1992. On 18 November 1991, the party branch in Bosnia and Herzegovina of the ruling party in the Republic of Croatia, the [Croatian Democratic Union](/wiki/Croatian_Democratic_Union \"Croatian Democratic Union\") (HDZ), proclaimed the existence of the [Croatian Community of Herzeg-Bosnia](/wiki/Croatian_Republic_of_Herzeg-Bosnia \"Croatian Republic of Herzeg-Bosnia\") in a separate part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the [Croatian Defence Council](/wiki/Croatian_Defence_Council \"Croatian Defence Council\") (HVO) as its military branch.[[105]](#cite_note-ICTY:_Prlić_et_al._(IT-04-74)-108) It went unrecognized by the [Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Council_of_Ministers_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"), which declared it illegal.[[106]](#cite_note-109)[[107]](#cite_note-110)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Norsk_Sisu_fra_NORLOGB.jpg/250px-Norsk_Sisu_fra_NORLOGB.jpg)](/wiki/File:Norsk_Sisu_fra_NORLOGB.jpg)\\n\\n[UN](/wiki/United_Nations \"United Nations\") troops in front of the [Executive Council Building](/wiki/Greece%E2%80%93Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_Friendship_Building \"Greece–Bosnia and Herzegovina Friendship Building\"), burned after being struck by tank fire during the [siege of Sarajevo](/wiki/Siege_of_Sarajevo \"Siege of Sarajevo\"), 1995\\n\\nA declaration of the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina on 15 October 1991 was followed by a [referendum for independence](/wiki/1992_Bosnian_independence_referendum \"1992 Bosnian independence referendum\") on 29 February and 1 March 1992, which was boycotted by the great majority of Serbs. The turnout in the independence referendum was 63.4 per cent and 99.7 per cent of voters voted for independence.[[108]](#cite_note-111) Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence on 3 March 1992 and received international recognition the following month on 6 April 1992.[[109]](#cite_note-112) The [Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Republic_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") was admitted as a member state of the [United Nations](/wiki/United_Nations \"United Nations\") on 22 May 1992.[[110]](#cite_note-113) Serbian leader [Slobodan Milošević](/wiki/Slobodan_Milo%C5%A1evi%C4%87 \"Slobodan Milošević\") and Croatian leader [Franjo Tuđman](/wiki/Franjo_Tu%C4%91man \"Franjo Tuđman\") are believed to have agreed on a [partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Partition_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") in March 1991, with the aim of establishing [Greater Serbia](/wiki/Greater_Serbia \"Greater Serbia\") and [Greater Croatia](/wiki/Greater_Croatia \"Greater Croatia\").[[111]](#cite_note-114)\\n\\nFollowing Bosnia and Herzegovina\\'s declaration of independence, Bosnian Serb militias mobilized in different parts of the country. Government forces were poorly equipped and unprepared for the war.[[112]](#cite_note-ICTY:_Naletilić_and_Martinović_verdict_—_A._Historical_background-115) International recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina increased diplomatic pressure for the [Yugoslav People\\'s Army](/wiki/Yugoslav_People%27s_Army \"Yugoslav People\\'s Army\") (JNA) to withdraw from the republic\\'s territory, which they officially did in June 1992. The Bosnian Serb members of the JNA simply changed insignia, formed the [Army of Republika Srpska](/wiki/Army_of_Republika_Srpska \"Army of Republika Srpska\") (VRS), and continued fighting. Armed and equipped from JNA stockpiles in Bosnia, supported by volunteers and various paramilitary forces from Serbia, and receiving extensive humanitarian, logistical and financial support from the [Federal Republic of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Serbia_and_Montenegro \"Serbia and Montenegro\"), [Republika Srpska](/wiki/Republika_Srpska \"Republika Srpska\")\\'s offensives in 1992 managed to place much of the country under its control.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalcolm2002-25) The Bosnian Serb advance was accompanied by the [ethnic cleansing](/wiki/Ethnic_cleansing \"Ethnic cleansing\") of Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats from VRS-controlled areas. Dozens of concentration camps were established in which inmates were subjected to violence and abuse, including rape.[[113]](#cite_note-ICTY:_Kunarac,_Kovač_and_Vuković_judgement_—_Foča-116) The ethnic cleansing culminated in the [Srebrenica massacre](/wiki/Srebrenica_massacre \"Srebrenica massacre\") of more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys in July 1995, which was ruled to have been a [genocide](/wiki/Genocide \"Genocide\") by the [International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia](/wiki/International_Criminal_Tribunal_for_the_former_Yugoslavia \"International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia\") (ICTY).[[114]](#cite_note-117) Bosniak and Bosnian Croat forces also committed war crimes against civilians from different ethnic groups, though on a smaller scale.[[115]](#cite_note-118)[[116]](#cite_note-119)[[117]](#cite_note-haverford-120)[[118]](#cite_note-un-121) Most of the Bosniak and Croat atrocities were committed during the [Croat–Bosniak War](/wiki/Croat%E2%80%93Bosniak_War \"Croat–Bosniak War\"), a sub-conflict of the Bosnian War that pitted the [Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Army_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") (ARBiH) against the HVO. The Bosniak-Croat conflict ended in March 1994, with the signing of the [Washington Agreement](/wiki/Washington_Agreement_(1994) \"Washington Agreement (1994)\"), leading to the creation of a joint Bosniak-Croat [Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"), which amalgamated HVO-held territory with that held by the [Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Army_of_the_Republic_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") (ARBiH).[[119]](#cite_note-Lumen_Learning_–_Simple_Book_Production_2017-122)\\n\\n### Recent history\\n\\nMain article: [2014 unrest in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/2014_unrest_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"2014 unrest in Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Bosnian_social_protests_Tuzla.jpg/250px-Bosnian_social_protests_Tuzla.jpg)](/wiki/File:Bosnian_social_protests_Tuzla.jpg)\\n\\n[Tuzla](/wiki/Tuzla \"Tuzla\") government building burning after [anti-government clashes](/wiki/2014_unrest_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"2014 unrest in Bosnia and Herzegovina\") on 7 February 2014\\n\\nOn 4 February 2014, the [protests](/wiki/2014_unrest_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"2014 unrest in Bosnia and Herzegovina\") against the [Government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Government_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"), one of the country\\'s two entities, dubbed the Bosnian Spring, the name being taken from the [Arab Spring](/wiki/Arab_Spring \"Arab Spring\"), began in the northern town of [Tuzla](/wiki/Tuzla \"Tuzla\"). Workers from several factories that had been privatised and gone bankrupt assembled to demand action over jobs, unpaid salaries and pensions.[[120]](#cite_note-123) Soon protests spread to the rest of the Federation, with violent clashes reported in close to 20 towns, the biggest of which were [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\"), [Zenica](/wiki/Zenica \"Zenica\"), [Mostar](/wiki/Mostar \"Mostar\"), [Bihać](/wiki/Biha%C4%87 \"Bihać\"), [Brčko](/wiki/Br%C4%8Dko \"Brčko\") and Tuzla.[[121]](#cite_note-124) The Bosnian news media reported that hundreds of people had been injured during the protests, including dozens of police officers, with bursts of violence in Sarajevo, in the northern city of Tuzla, in Mostar in the south, and in Zenica in central Bosnia. The same level of unrest or activism did not occur in Republika Srpska, but hundreds of people also gathered in support of protests in the city of [Banja Luka](/wiki/Banja_Luka \"Banja Luka\") against its separate government.[[122]](#cite_note-125)[[123]](#cite_note-126)[[124]](#cite_note-127)\\n\\nThe protests marked the largest outbreak of public anger over high unemployment and two decades of political inertia in the country since the end of the Bosnian War in 1995.[[125]](#cite_note-128) According to a report made by [Christian Schmidt](/wiki/Christian_Schmidt \"Christian Schmidt\") of the [Office of High Representative](/wiki/High_Representative_for_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina\") in late 2021, Bosnia and Herzegovina has been experiencing intensified political and ethnic tensions, which could potentially break the country apart and slide it back into war once again.[[126]](#cite_note-129)[[127]](#cite_note-130) The [European Union](/wiki/European_Union \"European Union\") fears this will lead to further [Balkanization](/wiki/Balkanization \"Balkanization\") in the region.[[128]](#cite_note-131)\\n\\nOn 15 December 2022, Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised by the European Union as a candidate country for [accession](/wiki/Accession_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_to_the_European_Union \"Accession of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the European Union\") following the decision of the [European Council](/wiki/European_Council \"European Council\").[[129]](#cite_note-sarajevotimes-132)\\n\\nGeography\\n---------\\n\\nMain article: [Geography of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Geography_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Geography of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\nSee also: [List of mountains](/wiki/List_of_mountains_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"List of mountains in Bosnia and Herzegovina\"), [lakes](/wiki/List_of_lakes_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"List of lakes of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"), and [rivers of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/List_of_rivers_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"List of rivers of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/NP001_nacionalni_park_sutjeska_perucica.jpg/250px-NP001_nacionalni_park_sutjeska_perucica.jpg)](/wiki/File:NP001_nacionalni_park_sutjeska_perucica.jpg)\\n\\n[Sutjeska National Park](/wiki/Sutjeska_National_Park \"Sutjeska National Park\") contains [Maglić](/wiki/Magli%C4%87_(mountain) \"Maglić (mountain)\"), the highest mountain in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as [Perućica](/wiki/Peru%C4%87ica \"Perućica\"), one of the last remaining [primeval forests](/wiki/Old-growth_forest \"Old-growth forest\") in Europe\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/NP002_-_14.jpg/250px-NP002_-_14.jpg)](/wiki/File:NP002_-_14.jpg)\\n\\n[Kozara Mountain](/wiki/Kozara \"Kozara\"), [Kozara National Park](/wiki/Kozara_National_Park \"Kozara National Park\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/%C5%A0trba%C4%8Dki_buk_1.jpg/250px-%C5%A0trba%C4%8Dki_buk_1.jpg)](/wiki/File:%C5%A0trba%C4%8Dki_buk_1.jpg)\\n\\n[Štrbački buk](/wiki/%C5%A0trba%C4%8Dki_buk \"Štrbački buk\") waterfall on the [Una](/wiki/Una_(Sava) \"Una (Sava)\") River, [Una National Park](/wiki/Una_National_Park \"Una National Park\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Drina_Canyon.JPG/250px-Drina_Canyon.JPG)](/wiki/File:Drina_Canyon.JPG)\\n\\n[Drina](/wiki/Drina \"Drina\") river canyon, [Drina National Park](/wiki/Drina_National_Park \"Drina National Park\")\\n\\nBosnia and Herzegovina is in the western [Balkans](/wiki/Balkans \"Balkans\"), bordering [Croatia](/wiki/Croatia \"Croatia\") (932\\xa0km or 579\\xa0mi) to the north and west, [Serbia](/wiki/Serbia \"Serbia\") (302\\xa0km or 188\\xa0mi) to the east, and [Montenegro](/wiki/Montenegro \"Montenegro\") (225\\xa0km or 140\\xa0mi) to the southeast. It has a coastline about 20 kilometres (12 miles) long surrounding the town of [Neum](/wiki/Neum \"Neum\").[[130]](#cite_note-coastline-133)[[131]](#cite_note-134) It lies between latitudes [42°](/wiki/42nd_parallel_north \"42nd parallel north\") and [46° N](/wiki/46th_parallel_north \"46th parallel north\"), and longitudes [15°](/wiki/15th_meridian_east \"15th meridian east\") and [20° E](/wiki/20th_meridian_east \"20th meridian east\").\\n\\nThe country\\'s name comes from the two alleged regions [Bosnia](/wiki/Bosnia_(region) \"Bosnia (region)\") and [Herzegovina](/wiki/Herzegovina \"Herzegovina\"), whose border was never defined. Historically, Bosnia\\'s official name never included any of its many regions until the Austro-Hungarian occupation.\\n\\nThe country is mostly mountainous, encompassing the central [Dinaric Alps](/wiki/Dinaric_Alps \"Dinaric Alps\"). The northeastern parts reach into the [Pannonian Basin](/wiki/Pannonian_Basin \"Pannonian Basin\"), while in the south it borders the [Adriatic](/wiki/Adriatic_Sea \"Adriatic Sea\"). The Dinaric Alps generally run in a southeast–northwest direction, and get higher towards the south. The highest point of the country is the peak of [Maglić](/wiki/Magli%C4%87_(mountain) \"Maglić (mountain)\") at 2,386 metres (7,828.1 feet), on the Montenegrin border. Other major mountains include [Volujak](/wiki/Volujak_(mountain) \"Volujak (mountain)\"), [Zelengora](/wiki/Zelengora \"Zelengora\"), [Lelija](/wiki/Lelija \"Lelija\"), [Lebršnik](/wiki/Lebr%C5%A1nik \"Lebršnik\"), [Orjen](/wiki/Orjen \"Orjen\"), [Kozara](/wiki/Kozara \"Kozara\"), [Grmeč](/wiki/Grme%C4%8D \"Grmeč\"), [Čvrsnica](/wiki/%C4%8Cvrsnica \"Čvrsnica\"), [Prenj](/wiki/Prenj \"Prenj\"), [Vran](/wiki/Vran \"Vran\"), [Vranica](/wiki/Vranica \"Vranica\"), [Velež](/wiki/Vele%C5%BE_(Bosnia_and_Herzegovina) \"Velež (Bosnia and Herzegovina)\"), [Vlašić](/wiki/Vla%C5%A1i%C4%87_(Bosnian_mountain) \"Vlašić (Bosnian mountain)\"), [Cincar](/wiki/Cincar \"Cincar\"), [Romanija](/wiki/Romanija \"Romanija\"), [Jahorina](/wiki/Jahorina \"Jahorina\"), [Bjelašnica](/wiki/Bjela%C5%A1nica \"Bjelašnica\"), [Treskavica](/wiki/Treskavica \"Treskavica\") and [Trebević](/wiki/Trebevi%C4%87 \"Trebević\"). The geological composition of the Dinaric chain of mountains in Bosnia consists primarily of [limestone](/wiki/Limestone \"Limestone\") (including [Mesozoic](/wiki/Mesozoic \"Mesozoic\") limestone), with deposits of [iron](/wiki/Iron \"Iron\"), [coal](/wiki/Coal \"Coal\"), [zinc](/wiki/Zinc \"Zinc\"), [manganese](/wiki/Manganese \"Manganese\"), [bauxite](/wiki/Bauxite \"Bauxite\"), [lead](/wiki/Lead \"Lead\"), and [salt](/wiki/Salt \"Salt\") present in some areas, especially in central and northern Bosnia.[[132]](#cite_note-135)\\n\\nOverall, nearly 50% of Bosnia and Herzegovina is forested. Most forest areas are in the centre, east and west parts of Bosnia. Herzegovina has a drier Mediterranean climate, with dominant [karst](/wiki/Karst \"Karst\") topography. Northern Bosnia ([Posavina](/wiki/Posavina \"Posavina\")) contains very fertile agricultural land along the [Sava](/wiki/Sava \"Sava\") river and the corresponding area is heavily farmed. This farmland is a part of the Pannonian Plain stretching into neighboring Croatia and Serbia. The country has only 20 kilometres (12 miles) of coastline,[[130]](#cite_note-coastline-133)[[133]](#cite_note-Neum_coastline-136) around the town of Neum in the [Herzegovina-Neretva Canton](/wiki/Herzegovina-Neretva_Canton \"Herzegovina-Neretva Canton\"). Although the city is surrounded by Croatian peninsulas, by international law, Bosnia and Herzegovina has a [right of passage](/wiki/Right_of_passage \"Right of passage\") to the outer sea.\\n\\n[Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\") is the capital[[1]](#cite_note-Constitution-1) and largest city.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECIA2019-9) Other major cities include [Banja Luka](/wiki/Banja_Luka \"Banja Luka\") and [Prijedor](/wiki/Prijedor \"Prijedor\") in the northwest region known as [Bosanska Krajina](/wiki/Bosanska_Krajina \"Bosanska Krajina\"), [Tuzla](/wiki/Tuzla \"Tuzla\"), [Bijeljina](/wiki/Bijeljina \"Bijeljina\"), [Doboj](/wiki/Doboj \"Doboj\") and [Brčko](/wiki/Br%C4%8Dko \"Brčko\") in the northeast, [Zenica](/wiki/Zenica \"Zenica\") in the central part of the country, and [Mostar](/wiki/Mostar \"Mostar\"), the largest city in the southern region of [Herzegovina](/wiki/Herzegovina \"Herzegovina\").\\n\\nThere are seven major rivers in Bosnia and Herzegovina:[[134]](#cite_note-fao-137)\\n\\n* The [Sava](/wiki/Sava \"Sava\") is the largest river of the country, and forms its northern [natural border](/wiki/Natural_border \"Natural border\") with Croatia. It drains 76%[[134]](#cite_note-fao-137) of the country\\'s territory into the [Danube](/wiki/Danube \"Danube\") and then the [Black Sea](/wiki/Black_Sea \"Black Sea\"). Bosnia and Herzegovina is a member of the [International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River](/wiki/International_Commission_for_the_Protection_of_the_Danube_River \"International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River\") (ICPDR).\\n* The [Una](/wiki/Una_(Sava) \"Una (Sava)\"), [Sana](/wiki/Sana_(river) \"Sana (river)\") and [Vrbas](/wiki/Vrbas_(river) \"Vrbas (river)\") are right tributaries of the Sava. They are in the northwestern region of [Bosanska Krajina](/wiki/Bosanska_Krajina \"Bosanska Krajina\").\\n* The [Bosna](/wiki/Bosna_(river) \"Bosna (river)\") river gave its name to the country, and is the longest river fully contained within it. It stretches through central Bosnia, from its source near [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\") to Sava in the north.\\n* The [Drina](/wiki/Drina \"Drina\") flows through the eastern part of Bosnia, and for the most part it forms a natural border with Serbia.\\n* The [Neretva](/wiki/Neretva \"Neretva\") is the major river of Herzegovina and the only major river that flows south, into the Adriatic Sea.\\n\\n### Biodiversity\\n\\nMain article: [Environment of Bosnia and Herzegovina §\\xa0Biodiversity](/wiki/Environment_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina#Biodiversity \"Environment of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[Phytogeographically](/wiki/Phytogeography \"Phytogeography\"), Bosnia and Herzegovina belongs to the [Boreal Kingdom](/wiki/Boreal_Kingdom \"Boreal Kingdom\") and is shared between the Illyrian province of the [Circumboreal Region](/wiki/Circumboreal_Region \"Circumboreal Region\") and Adriatic province of the [Mediterranean Region](/wiki/Mediterranean_Basin \"Mediterranean Basin\"). According to the [World Wide Fund for Nature](/wiki/World_Wide_Fund_for_Nature \"World Wide Fund for Nature\") (WWF), the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina can be subdivided into four [ecoregions](/wiki/Ecoregion \"Ecoregion\"): [Balkan mixed forests](/wiki/Balkan_mixed_forests \"Balkan mixed forests\"), [Dinaric Mountains mixed forests](/wiki/Dinaric_Mountains_mixed_forests \"Dinaric Mountains mixed forests\"), [Pannonian mixed forests](/wiki/Pannonian_mixed_forests \"Pannonian mixed forests\") and [Illyrian deciduous forests](/wiki/Illyrian_deciduous_forests \"Illyrian deciduous forests\").[[135]](#cite_note-DinersteinOlson2017-138) The country had a 2018 [Forest Landscape Integrity Index](/wiki/Forest_Landscape_Integrity_Index \"Forest Landscape Integrity Index\") mean score of 5.99/10, ranking it 89th globally out of 172 countries.[[136]](#cite_note-FLII-Supplementary-139) In Bosnia and Herzegovina [forest cover](/wiki/Forest_cover \"Forest cover\") is around 43% of the total land area, equivalent to 2,187,910 hectares (ha) of forest in 2020, down from 2,210,000 hectares (ha) in 1990. For the year 2015, 74% of the forest area was reported to be under [public ownership](/wiki/State_ownership \"State ownership\") and 26% [private ownership](/wiki/Private_property \"Private property\").[[137]](#cite_note-140)[[138]](#cite_note-141)\\n\\nPolitics\\n--------\\n\\nMain article: [Politics of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Politics_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Politics of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n### Government\\n\\nMain article: [Political divisions of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Political_divisions_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Political divisions of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/%C5%BDeljko_Kom%C5%A1i%C4%87_%282025-12-17%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-%C5%BDeljko_Kom%C5%A1i%C4%87_%282025-12-17%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:%C5%BDeljko_Kom%C5%A1i%C4%87_(2025-12-17)_(cropped).jpg)\\n\\n[Željko Komšić](/wiki/%C5%BDeljko_Kom%C5%A1i%C4%87 \"Željko Komšić\")  \\n[Chairman of the Presidency](/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Presidency_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Borjana_Kri%C5%A1to_%282025-06-11%29.jpg/250px-Borjana_Kri%C5%A1to_%282025-06-11%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Borjana_Kri%C5%A1to_(2025-06-11).jpg)\\n\\n[Borjana Krišto](/wiki/Borjana_Kri%C5%A1to \"Borjana Krišto\")  \\n[Chairwoman of the Council of Ministers](/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Council_of_Ministers_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Chairman of the Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\nAs a result of the [Dayton Agreement](/wiki/Dayton_Agreement \"Dayton Agreement\"), the civilian peace implementation is supervised by the [High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/High_Representative_for_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina\") selected by the [Peace Implementation Council](/wiki/Peace_Implementation_Council \"Peace Implementation Council\") (PIC). The High Representative is the highest political authority in the country. The High Representative has many governmental and legislative powers, including the dismissal of elected and non-elected officials. Due to the vast powers of the High Representative over [Bosnian politics](/wiki/Politics_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Politics of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") and essential [veto](/wiki/Veto \"Veto\") powers, the position has also been compared to that of a [viceroy](/wiki/Viceroy \"Viceroy\").[[139]](#cite_note-142)[[140]](#cite_note-143)[[141]](#cite_note-144)[[142]](#cite_note-145)\\n\\nPolitics take place in a framework of a [parliamentary](/wiki/Parliamentary_system \"Parliamentary system\") [representative democracy](/wiki/Representative_democracy \"Representative democracy\"), whereby [executive power](/wiki/Executive_(government) \"Executive (government)\") is exercised by the [Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Council_of_Ministers_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"). [Legislative power](/wiki/Legislature \"Legislature\") is vested in both the Council of Ministers and the [Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Parliamentary_Assembly_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"). Members of the Parliamentary Assembly are chosen according to a [proportional representation](/wiki/Proportional_representation \"Proportional representation\") (PR) system.[[143]](#cite_note-146)[[144]](#cite_note-147)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Map_Bih_entities.png/250px-Map_Bih_entities.png)](/wiki/File:Map_Bih_entities.png)\\n\\nBosnia and Herzegovina consists of the [Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") (FBiH), [Republika Srpska](/wiki/Republika_Srpska \"Republika Srpska\") (RS) and [Brčko District](/wiki/Br%C4%8Dko_District \"Brčko District\") (BD)\\n\\nBosnia and Herzegovina is a [liberal democracy](/wiki/Liberal_democracy \"Liberal democracy\").[*[clarification needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify \"Wikipedia:Please clarify\")*] It has several levels of political structuring, according to the [Dayton Agreement](/wiki/Dayton_Agreement \"Dayton Agreement\"). The most important of these levels is the division of the country into two entities: the [Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") and [Republika Srpska](/wiki/Republika_Srpska \"Republika Srpska\"). The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina covers 51% of Bosnia and Herzegovina\\'s total area, while Republika Srpska covers 49%. The entities, based largely on the territories held by the two warring sides at the time, were formally established by the Dayton Agreement in 1995 because of the tremendous changes in Bosnia and Herzegovina\\'s ethnic structure. At the national level, there exists only a finite set of exclusive or joint competencies, whereas the majority of authority rests within the entities.[[145]](#cite_note-148) [Sumantra Bose](/wiki/Sumantra_Bose \"Sumantra Bose\") describes Bosnia and Herzegovina as a consociational [confederation](/wiki/Confederation \"Confederation\").[[146]](#cite_note-149)\\n\\nThe [Brčko District](/wiki/Br%C4%8Dko_District \"Brčko District\") in the north of the country was created in 2000, out of land from both entities. It officially belongs to both, but is governed by neither, and functions under a decentralized system of local government. For election purposes, Brčko District voters can choose to participate in either the Federation or Republika Srpska elections. The Brčko District has been praised for maintaining a multiethnic population and a level of prosperity significantly above the national average.[[147]](#cite_note-OHR-150)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/8a/Parliament_%286042784223%29.jpg/250px-Parliament_%286042784223%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Parliament_(6042784223).jpg)\\n\\nBosnia and Herzegovina\\'s [government building](/wiki/Greece%E2%80%93Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_Friendship_Building \"Greece–Bosnia and Herzegovina Friendship Building\") in [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Hipotekarna_banka_palata_predsjednika.JPG/250px-Hipotekarna_banka_palata_predsjednika.JPG)](/wiki/File:Hipotekarna_banka_palata_predsjednika.JPG)\\n\\n[Palace of the Republic](/wiki/Palace_of_the_Republic,_Banja_Luka \"Palace of the Republic, Banja Luka\") in [Banja Luka](/wiki/Banja_Luka \"Banja Luka\")\\n\\nThe third level of Bosnia and Herzegovina\\'s political subdivision is manifested in [cantons](/wiki/Cantons_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Cantons of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"). They are unique to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina entity, which consists of ten of them. Each has a cantonal government, which is under the law of the Federation as a whole. Some cantons are ethnically mixed and have special laws to ensure the equality of all constituent people.[[148]](#cite_note-Mansfield_2003_pp._2052–2093-151)\\n\\nThe fourth level of political division in Bosnia and Herzegovina are the [municipalities](/wiki/Municipalities_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"). The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is divided into 79 municipalities, and Republika Srpska into 64. Municipalities also have their own local government, and are typically based on the most significant city or place in their territory. As such, many municipalities have a long tradition and history with their present boundaries. Some others, however, were only created following the recent war after traditional municipalities were split by the [Inter-Entity Boundary Line](/wiki/Inter-Entity_Boundary_Line \"Inter-Entity Boundary Line\"). Each canton in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina consists of several municipalities, which are divided into local communities.[[149]](#cite_note-CoR-152)\\n\\nBesides entities, cantons, and municipalities, Bosnia and Herzegovina also has four \"official\" cities. These are: [Banja Luka](/wiki/Banja_Luka \"Banja Luka\"), [Mostar](/wiki/Mostar \"Mostar\"), [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\") and [East Sarajevo](/wiki/Isto%C4%8Dno_Sarajevo \"Istočno Sarajevo\"). The territory and government of the cities of Banja Luka and Mostar corresponds to the municipalities of the same name, while the cities of Sarajevo and East Sarajevo officially consist of several municipalities. Cities have their own city government whose power is in between that of the municipalities and cantons (or the entity, in the case of Republika Srpska).\\n\\nMore recently, several central institutions have been established (such as a [defense ministry](/wiki/Defence_minister \"Defence minister\"), security ministry, state court, [indirect taxation](/wiki/Indirect_tax \"Indirect tax\") service and so on) in the process of transferring part of the jurisdiction from the entities to the state. The representation of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina is by elites who represent the country\\'s three major groups, with each having a guaranteed share of power.\\n\\nThe [Chair](/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Presidency_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") of the [Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Presidency_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") rotates among three members ([Bosniak](/wiki/Bosniaks \"Bosniaks\"), [Serb](/wiki/Serbs \"Serbs\"), [Croat](/wiki/Croats \"Croats\")), each elected as the chair for an eight-month term within their four-year term as a member. The three members of the Presidency are elected directly by the people, with Federation voters voting for the Bosniak and the Croat and the Republika Srpska voters voting for the Serb.\\n\\nThe [Chair of the Council of Ministers](/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Council_of_Ministers_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Chairman of the Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") is nominated by the Presidency and approved by the parliamentary [House of Representatives](/wiki/House_of_Representatives_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"House of Representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"). The Chair of the Council of Ministers is then responsible for appointing a Foreign Minister, Minister of Foreign Trade and others as appropriate.\\n\\nThe Parliamentary Assembly is the lawmaking body in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It consists of two houses: the [House of Peoples](/wiki/House_of_Peoples_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"House of Peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") and the House of Representatives. The House of Peoples has 15 delegates chosen by parliaments of the entities, two-thirds of which come from the Federation (5 Bosniaks and 5 Croats) and one-third from the Republika Srpska (5 Serbs). The House of Representatives is composed of 42 Members elected by the people under a form of proportional representation, two-thirds elected from the Federation and one-third elected from Republika Srpska.[[150]](#cite_note-Heath-Brown_2017_p._221-153)\\n\\nThe [Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") is the supreme, final arbiter of legal matters. It is composed of nine members: four members are selected by the [Federal House of Representatives](/wiki/House_of_Representatives_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"House of Representatives of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"), two by the [National Assembly of Republika Srpska](/wiki/National_Assembly_(Republika_Srpska) \"National Assembly (Republika Srpska)\") and three by the President of the [European Court of Human Rights](/wiki/European_Court_of_Human_Rights \"European Court of Human Rights\") after consultation with the Presidency, who cannot be Bosnian citizens.[[151]](#cite_note-154)\\n\\nHowever, the highest political authority in the country is the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, the chief [executive officer](/wiki/Executive_officer \"Executive officer\") for the international civilian presence in the country and is selected by the [European Union](/wiki/European_Union \"European Union\"). Since 1995, the High Representative has been able to bypass the elected parliamentary assembly, and since 1997 has been able to remove elected officials. The methods selected by the High Representative have been criticized as undemocratic.[[152]](#cite_note-155) International supervision [is to end when the country is deemed politically and democratically stable and self-sustaining](/wiki/High_Representative_for_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina#Conditions_for_closure_of_the_Office_of_the_High_Representative \"High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina\").\\n\\n### Foreign relations\\n\\nMain article: [Foreign relations of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Foreign_relations_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Foreign relations of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\nSee also: [Accession of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the European Union](/wiki/Accession_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_to_the_European_Union \"Accession of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the European Union\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Secretary_Clinton_Meets_With_President_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_Zeljko_Komsic_%286507403825%29.jpg/250px-Secretary_Clinton_Meets_With_President_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_Zeljko_Komsic_%286507403825%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Secretary_Clinton_Meets_With_President_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_Zeljko_Komsic_(6507403825).jpg)\\n\\n[Željko Komšić](/wiki/%C5%BDeljko_Kom%C5%A1i%C4%87 \"Željko Komšić\"), Croat member of the [Bosnian Presidency](/wiki/Presidency_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"), and [Hillary Clinton](/wiki/Hillary_Clinton \"Hillary Clinton\"), U.S. Secretary of State, 13 December 2011\\n\\n[European Union integration](/wiki/Accession_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_to_the_European_Union \"Accession of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the European Union\") is one of the main political objectives of Bosnia and Herzegovina; it initiated the [Stabilisation and Association Process](/wiki/Stabilisation_and_Association_Process \"Stabilisation and Association Process\") in 2007. Countries participating in the SAP have been offered the possibility to become, once they fulfill the necessary conditions, Member States of the EU.[[153]](#cite_note-156) Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate country for EU accession since December 2022.[[129]](#cite_note-sarajevotimes-132) Accession talks are set to begin following the impeding of more reforms.[[154]](#cite_note-157)\\n\\nThe implementation of the [Dayton Agreement](/wiki/Dayton_Agreement \"Dayton Agreement\") in 1995 has focused the efforts of policymakers in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the international community, on regional stabilization in the countries-successors of the [former Yugoslavia](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia \"Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia\").[[155]](#cite_note-Usa_2012_p._269-158)\\n\\nWithin Bosnia and Herzegovina, relations with its neighbors of [Croatia](/wiki/Croatia \"Croatia\"), [Serbia](/wiki/Serbia \"Serbia\") and [Montenegro](/wiki/Montenegro \"Montenegro\") have been fairly stable since the signing of the Dayton Agreement. On 23 April 2010, Bosnia and Herzegovina received the [Membership Action Plan](/wiki/Enlargement_of_NATO#Membership_Action_Plan \"Enlargement of NATO\") from [NATO](/wiki/NATO \"NATO\"), which is the last step before full membership in the alliance. Full membership was initially expected in 2014 or 2015, depending on the progress of reforms.[[156]](#cite_note-159) In December 2018, NATO approved a Bosnian Membership Action Plan.[[157]](#cite_note-160)\\n\\nBosnia and Herzegovina is the 61st most peaceful country in the world, according to the 2024 [Global Peace Index](/wiki/Global_Peace_Index \"Global Peace Index\").[[158]](#cite_note-161)\\n\\n### Military\\n\\nMain article: [Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Armed Forces of Bosnia and [TH-1H Huey](/wiki/Bell_UH-1_Iroquois \"Bell UH-1 Iroquois\") [main transport aircraft](/wiki/Military_transport_aircraft \"Military transport aircraft\") |\\n\\nThe [Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") (OSBiH) were unified into a single entity in 2005, with the merger of the [Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Army_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") and the [Army of Republika Srpska](/wiki/Army_of_Republika_Srpska \"Army of Republika Srpska\"), which had defended their respective regions.[[159]](#cite_note-Lobjakas_2005-162) The [Ministry of Defence](/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_(Bosnia_and_Herzegovina) \"Ministry of Defence (Bosnia and Herzegovina)\") was formed in 2004.[[160]](#cite_note-NATO_2004-163)\\n\\nThe Bosnian military consists of the [Bosnian Ground Forces](/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") and [Air Force and Air Defense](/wiki/Air_Force_and_Anti-Aircraft_Defence_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Air Force and Anti-Aircraft Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina\").[[161]](#cite_note-European_Western_Balkans_2017-164) The Ground Forces number 7,200 active and 5,000 reserve personnel.[[162]](#cite_note-mod.gov.ba_2016-165) They are armed with a mix of American, Yugoslav, Soviet, and European-made weaponry, vehicles, and military equipment. The Air Force and Air Defense Forces have 1,500 personnel and about 62 aircraft. The Air Defense Forces operate [MANPADS](/wiki/Man-portable_air-defense_system \"Man-portable air-defense system\") hand-held missiles, [surface-to-air missile](/wiki/Surface-to-air_missile \"Surface-to-air missile\") (SAM) batteries, anti-aircraft cannons, and radar. The Army has recently adopted remodeled [MARPAT](/wiki/MARPAT \"MARPAT\") uniforms, used by Bosnian soldiers serving with the [International Security Assistance Force](/wiki/International_Security_Assistance_Force \"International Security Assistance Force\") (ISAF) in [Afghanistan](/wiki/Afghanistan \"Afghanistan\"). A domestic production program is now underway to ensure that army units are equipped with the correct ammunition.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nBeginning in 2007, the Ministry of Defence undertook the army\\'s first ever international assistance mission, enlisting the military to serve with ISAF peace missions to Afghanistan, [Iraq](/wiki/Iraq \"Iraq\") and the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo \"Democratic Republic of the Congo\") in 2007. Five officers, acting as officers/advisors, served in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. 45 soldiers, mostly acting as base security and medical assistants, served in Afghanistan. 85 Bosnian soldiers served as base security in Iraq, occasionally conducting infantry patrols there as well. All three deployed groups have been commended by their respective international forces as well as the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The international assistance operations are still ongoing.[[163]](#cite_note-NATO_2015-166)\\n\\nThe Air Force and Anti-Aircraft Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed when elements of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the [Republika Srpska Air Force](/wiki/Republika_Srpska_Air_Force \"Republika Srpska Air Force\") were merged in 2006. The Air Force has seen improvements in the last few years with added funds for aircraft repairs and improved cooperation with the [Ground Forces](/wiki/Army \"Army\") as well as to the citizens of the country. The Ministry of Defence is pursuing the acquisition of new aircraft including helicopters and perhaps even fighter jets.[[164]](#cite_note-167)\\n\\nEconomy\\n-------\\n\\nMain article: [Economy of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Economy_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Economy of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\nSee also: [List of companies of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/List_of_companies_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"List of companies of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/GDP_per_capita_development_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina.svg/250px-GDP_per_capita_development_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina.svg.png)](/wiki/File:GDP_per_capita_development_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina.svg)\\n\\nEstimated development of real GDP per capita of Bosnia and Herzegovina, since 1952\\n\\nDuring the [Bosnian War](/wiki/Bosnian_War \"Bosnian War\"), the economy suffered €200\\xa0billion in material damages, roughly €356.80\\xa0billion in 2025 (inflation adjusted).[[165]](#cite_note-168)[[166]](#cite_note-169) Bosnia and Herzegovina faces the dual-problem of rebuilding a war-torn country and introducing transitional liberal market reforms to its formerly mixed economy. One legacy of the previous era is a strong industry; under former republic president [Džemal Bijedić](/wiki/D%C5%BEemal_Bijedi%C4%87 \"Džemal Bijedić\") and [Yugoslav](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia \"Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia\") President [Josip Broz Tito](/wiki/Josip_Broz_Tito \"Josip Broz Tito\"), metal industries were promoted in the republic, resulting in the development of a large share of Yugoslavia\\'s plants; [SR Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Socialist_Republic_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") had a very strong industrial export oriented economy in the 1970s and 1980s, with large scale exports worth millions of [US$](/wiki/USD \"USD\").\\n\\nFor most of Bosnia\\'s history, agriculture has been conducted on privately owned farms; Fresh food has traditionally been exported from the republic.[[167]](#cite_note-170)\\n\\nThe war in the 1990s, caused a dramatic change in the Bosnian economy.[[168]](#cite_note-171) GDP fell by 60% and the destruction of physical infrastructure devastated the economy.[[169]](#cite_note-172) With much of the production capacity unrestored, the Bosnian economy still faces considerable difficulties. Figures show GDP and per capita income increased 10% from 2003 to 2004; this and Bosnia\\'s shrinking [national debt](/wiki/Government_debt \"Government debt\") being negative trends, and high unemployment 38.7% and a large [trade deficit](/wiki/Balance_of_trade \"Balance of trade\") remain cause for concern.\\n\\nThe national currency is the (Euro-pegged) [convertible mark](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_convertible_mark \"Bosnia and Herzegovina convertible mark\") (KM), controlled by the [currency board](/wiki/Currency_board \"Currency board\"). Annual inflation is the lowest relative to other countries in the region at 1.9% in 2004.[[170]](#cite_note-173) The international debt was $5.1\\xa0billion (as of 31 December 2014). [Real GDP](/wiki/Gross_domestic_product \"Gross domestic product\") growth rate was 5% for 2004 according to the [Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Central_Bank_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") and Statistical Office of Bosnia and Herzegovina.\\n\\nBosnia and Herzegovina has displayed positive progress in the previous years, which decisively moved its place from the lowest income equality rank of [income equality rankings](/wiki/List_of_countries_by_income_equality \"List of countries by income equality\") fourteen out of 193 nations.[[171]](#cite_note-174)\\n\\nAccording to [Eurostat](/wiki/Eurostat \"Eurostat\") data, Bosnia and Herzegovina\\'s PPS GDP per capita stood at 29 per cent of the EU average in 2010.[[172]](#cite_note-175)\\n\\nThe [International Monetary Fund](/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund \"International Monetary Fund\") (IMF) announced a loan to Bosnia worth US$500\\xa0million to be delivered by [Stand-By Arrangement](/wiki/IMF_Stand-By_Arrangement \"IMF Stand-By Arrangement\"). This was scheduled to be approved in September 2012.[[173]](#cite_note-176)\\n\\nThe [United States Embassy](/wiki/Embassy_of_the_United_States,_Sarajevo \"Embassy of the United States, Sarajevo\") in [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\") produces the Country Commercial Guide – an annual report that delivers a comprehensive look at Bosnia and Herzegovina\\'s commercial and economic environment, using economic, political, and market analysis.\\n\\nBy some estimates, [grey economy](/wiki/Informal_economy \"Informal economy\") is 25.5% of GDP.[[174]](#cite_note-177)\\n\\nIn 2017, exports grew by 17% when compared to the previous year, totaling €5.65\\xa0billion.[[175]](#cite_note-178) The total volume of [foreign trade](/wiki/International_trade \"International trade\") in 2017 amounted to €14.97\\xa0billion and increased by 14% compared to the previous year. Imports of goods increased by 12% and amounted to €9.32\\xa0billion. The [coverage of imports by exports](/wiki/Balance_of_trade \"Balance of trade\") increased by 3% compared to the previous year and now it is 61 percent. In 2017, Bosnia and Herzegovina mostly exported [car seats](/wiki/Car_seat \"Car seat\"), [electricity](/wiki/Electricity \"Electricity\"), [processed wood](/wiki/Wood_processing \"Wood processing\"), [aluminium](/wiki/Aluminium \"Aluminium\") and [furniture](/wiki/Furniture \"Furniture\"). In the same year, it mostly imported [crude oil](/wiki/Petroleum \"Petroleum\"), [automobiles](/wiki/Car \"Car\"), [motor oil](/wiki/Motor_oil \"Motor oil\"), [coal](/wiki/Coal \"Coal\") and [briquettes](/wiki/Briquette \"Briquette\").[[176]](#cite_note-179)\\n\\nThe unemployment rate in 2017 was 20.5%, but [The Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies](/wiki/The_Vienna_Institute_for_International_Economic_Studies \"The Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies\") is predicting falling unemployment rate for the next few years. In 2018, the unemployment should be 19.4% and it should further fall to 18.8% in 2019. In 2020, the unemployment rate should go down to 18.3%.[[177]](#cite_note-180)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/a8/Avaz_Twist_Tower_in_Sarajevo_2014.jpg/250px-Avaz_Twist_Tower_in_Sarajevo_2014.jpg)](/wiki/File:Avaz_Twist_Tower_in_Sarajevo_2014.jpg)\\n\\nThe [Avaz Twist Tower](/wiki/Avaz_Twist_Tower \"Avaz Twist Tower\") in [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\"), the tallest building in Bosnia and Herzegovina\\n\\nOn 31 December 2017, the [Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Council_of_Ministers_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") issued the report on public debt of Bosnia and Herzegovina, stating the public debt was reduced by €389.97\\xa0million, or by more than 6% when compared to 31 December 2016. Also, 71.2% of the tourists came from foreign countries.[[205]](#cite_note-208)\\n\\nIn 2006, when ranking the best cities in the world, [Lonely Planet](/wiki/Lonely_Planet \"Lonely Planet\") placed [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\"), the [national capital](/wiki/Capital_city \"Capital city\")[[1]](#cite_note-Constitution-1) and host of the [1984 Winter Olympics](/wiki/1984_Winter_Olympics \"1984 Winter Olympics\"), as #43 on the list.[[206]](#cite_note-209) Tourism in Sarajevo is chiefly focused on historical, religious, and cultural aspects. In 2010, Lonely Planet\\'s \"Best in Travel\" nominated it as one of the top ten cities to visit that year.[[207]](#cite_note-210) Sarajevo also won travel blog Foxnomad\\'s \"Best City to Visit\" competition in 2012, beating more than one hundred other cities around the entire world.[[208]](#cite_note-211)\\n\\n[Međugorje](/wiki/Medjugorje \"Medjugorje\") has become one of the most popular pilgrimage sites for [Catholics](/wiki/Catholics \"Catholics\") from around the world and has turned into Europe\\'s third most important religious place, where each year more than 1\\xa0million people visit.[[209]](#cite_note-212) It has been estimated that 30\\xa0million pilgrims have come to Međugorje since the reputed apparitions began in 1981.[[210]](#cite_note-reuters-213) Since 2019, pilgrimages to Međugorje have been officially authorized and organized by the [Vatican](/wiki/Holy_See \"Holy See\").[[211]](#cite_note-Vatican_News_2019-214)\\n\\nBosnia has also become an increasingly popular skiing and [Ecotourism](/wiki/Ecotourism \"Ecotourism\") destination. The mountains that hosted the winter olympic games of [Bjelašnica](/wiki/Bjela%C5%A1nica \"Bjelašnica\"), [Jahorina](/wiki/Jahorina \"Jahorina\") and [Igman](/wiki/Igman \"Igman\") are the most visited skiing mountains in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina remains one of the last undiscovered natural regions of the southern area of the [Alps](/wiki/Alps \"Alps\"), with vast tracts of wild and untouched nature attracting adventurers and nature lovers. *[National Geographic](/wiki/National_Geographic \"National Geographic\")* named Bosnia and Herzegovina as the best mountain biking adventure destination for 2012.[[212]](#cite_note-test-215) The central [Bosnian Dinaric Alps](/wiki/Dinaric_Alps \"Dinaric Alps\") are favored by hikers and mountaineers, as they contain both [Mediterranean](/wiki/Mediterranean_climate \"Mediterranean climate\") and [Alpine](/wiki/Alpine_climate \"Alpine climate\") climates. [Whitewater rafting](/wiki/Rafting \"Rafting\") has become somewhat of a [national pastime](/wiki/National_sport \"National sport\") in Bosnia and Herzegovina.[[213]](#cite_note-Zuvela_2007-216) The primary rivers used for whitewater rafting in the country include the [Vrbas](/wiki/Vrbas_(river) \"Vrbas (river)\"), [Tara](/wiki/Tara_(Drina) \"Tara (Drina)\"), [Drina](/wiki/Drina \"Drina\"), [Neretva](/wiki/Neretva \"Neretva\") and [Una](/wiki/Una_(Sava) \"Una (Sava)\").[[214]](#cite_note-All_about_buses_2018-217) Meanwhile, the most prominent rivers are the Vrbas and Tara, as they both hosted [The 2009 World Rafting Championship](/wiki/International_Rafting_Federation \"International Rafting Federation\").[[215]](#cite_note-IRF_admin_2010-218)[[216]](#cite_note-Sito-Sucic_2009-219) The reason the Tara river is immensely popular for whitewater rafting is because it contains the deepest [river canyon](/wiki/Canyon \"Canyon\") in Europe, the [Tara River Canyon](/wiki/Tara_River_Canyon \"Tara River Canyon\").[[217]](#cite_note-Tara_Sport_2019-220)[[218]](#cite_note-The_Telegraph_2016-221)\\n\\nMost recently, the *[Huffington Post](/wiki/HuffPost \"HuffPost\")* named Bosnia and Herzegovina the \"9th Greatest Adventure in the World for 2013\", adding that the country boasts \"the cleanest water and air in Europe; the greatest untouched forests; and the most wildlife. The best way to experience is the three rivers trip, which purls through the best the Balkans have to offer.\"[[219]](#cite_note-222)\\n\\n### Transport\\n\\nMain article: [Transport in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Transport_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Transport in Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Sarajevo_Airport_1_2024.jpg/250px-Sarajevo_Airport_1_2024.jpg)](/wiki/File:Sarajevo_Airport_1_2024.jpg)\\n\\n[Sarajevo International Airport](/wiki/Sarajevo_International_Airport \"Sarajevo International Airport\")\\n\\n[Sarajevo International Airport](/wiki/Sarajevo_International_Airport \"Sarajevo International Airport\"), also known as Butmir Airport, is the main [international airport](/wiki/International_airport \"International airport\") in Bosnia and Herzegovina, located 3.3\\xa0[NM](/wiki/Nautical_mile \"Nautical mile\") (6.1\\xa0km; 3.8\\xa0mi) southwest of the [Sarajevo main railway station](/wiki/Sarajevo_main_railway_station \"Sarajevo main railway station\")[[220]](#cite_note-AIP-223) in the city of [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\") in the suburb of [Butmir](/wiki/Butmir \"Butmir\").\\n\\nRailway operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina are successors of the [Yugoslav Railways](/wiki/Yugoslav_Railways \"Yugoslav Railways\") within the country boundaries following independence from the [former Yugoslavia](/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia \"Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia\") in 1992. Today, they are operated by the [Railways of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Railways_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Railways of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") (ŽFBiH) in the [Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") and by [Republika Srpska Railways](/wiki/Republika_Srpska_Railways \"Republika Srpska Railways\") (ŽRS) in [Republika Srpska](/wiki/Republika_Srpska \"Republika Srpska\").\\n\\n### Telecommunications\\n\\nMain article: [Telecommunications in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Telecommunications_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Telecommunications in Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\nThe Bosnian communications market was fully [liberalised](/wiki/Economic_liberalization \"Economic liberalization\") in January 2006. The three [landline](/wiki/Landline \"Landline\") telephone operators predominantly provide services in their operating areas but have nationwide licenses for domestic and international calls. Mobile data services are also available, including high-speed [EDGE](/wiki/Enhanced_Data_rates_for_GSM_Evolution \"Enhanced Data rates for GSM Evolution\"), [3G](/wiki/3G \"3G\") and [4G](/wiki/4G \"4G\") services.[[221]](#cite_note-224)\\n\\n*[Oslobođenje](/wiki/Oslobo%C4%91enje \"Oslobođenje\")* (Liberation), founded in 1943, is one of the country\\'s longest running continuously circulating newspapers. There are many national publications, including the *[Dnevni avaz](/wiki/Dnevni_avaz \"Dnevni avaz\")* (Daily Voice), founded in 1995, and *Jutarnje Novine* (Morning News), to name but a few in circulation in Sarajevo.[[222]](#cite_note-225) Other local periodicals include the Croatian *[Hrvatska riječ](/wiki/Hrvatska_rije%C4%8D \"Hrvatska riječ\")* newspaper and Bosnian *[Start](/w/index.php?title=Start_(Bosnian_magazine)&action=edit&redlink=1 \"Start (Bosnian magazine) (page does not exist)\")* magazine, as well as *Slobodna Bosna* (*Free Bosnia*) and *BH Dani* (*BH Days*) weekly newspapers. *[Novi Plamen](/wiki/Novi_Plamen \"Novi Plamen\")*, a monthly magazine, was the most left-wing publication. International news station [Al Jazeera](/wiki/Al_Jazeera_Media_Network \"Al Jazeera Media Network\") maintains a [sister channel](/wiki/Sister_channel \"Sister channel\") catering to the [Balkan](/wiki/Balkans \"Balkans\") region, [Al Jazeera Balkans](/wiki/Al_Jazeera_Balkans \"Al Jazeera Balkans\"), broadcasting out of and based in Sarajevo.[[223]](#cite_note-226) Since 2014, the [N1 platform](/wiki/N1_(TV_channel) \"N1 (TV channel)\") has broadcast as an affiliate of [CNN International](/wiki/CNN_International \"CNN International\"), with offices in Sarajevo, [Zagreb](/wiki/Zagreb \"Zagreb\") and [Belgrade](/wiki/Belgrade \"Belgrade\").[[224]](#cite_note-227)\\n\\nAs of 2021, Bosnia and Herzegovina ranked second highest in [press freedom](/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press \"Freedom of the press\") in the region, after [Croatia](/wiki/Croatia \"Croatia\"), and is placed 58th internationally.[[225]](#cite_note-228)\\n\\nAs of December\\xa02021[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bosnia_and_Herzegovina&action=edit), there are 3,374,094 internet users in the country, or 95.55% of the entire population.[[226]](#cite_note-229)\\n\\nDemographics\\n------------\\n\\nMain articles: [Demographics of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Demographics_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Demographics of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") and [Bosnians](/wiki/Bosnians \"Bosnians\")\\n\\nSee also: [Demographic history of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Demographic_history_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Demographic history of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\nAccording to the [1991 census](/wiki/1991_population_census_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"1991 population census in Bosnia and Herzegovina\"), Bosnia and Herzegovina had a population of 4,369,319, while the 1996 World Bank Group census showed a decrease to 3,764,425.[[227]](#cite_note-230) Large population migrations during the [Yugoslav Wars](/wiki/Yugoslav_Wars \"Yugoslav Wars\") in the 1990s have caused demographic shifts in the country. Between 1991 and 2013, political disagreements made it impossible to organize a census. A census had been planned for 2011,[[228]](#cite_note-231) and then for 2012,[[229]](#cite_note-232) but was delayed until October 2013. The [2013 census](/wiki/2013_population_census_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"2013 population census in Bosnia and Herzegovina\") found a total population of 3,531,159 people,[[5]](#cite_note-Popis2013-5) a drop of approximately 20% since 1991.[[230]](#cite_note-233) The 2013 census figures include non-permanent Bosnian residents and for this reason are contested by Republika Srpska officials and Serb politicians (see Ethnic groups below).[[231]](#cite_note-WithoutSerbAgreement-234)\\n\\nAccording to [United Nations Population Fund](/wiki/United_Nations_Population_Fund \"United Nations Population Fund\"), between 2013 and 2020, Bosnia and Herzegovina was losing 25,000 people yearly. The demographic expert Stevo Palašić concluded that between 1991 and 2023, Bosnia and Herzegovina lost 1.4 million people or one-third of its population. [Tim Judah](/wiki/Tim_Judah \"Tim Judah\") considers the 2022 state agency estimate of 3.4 million inhabitants \"extremely optimistic\" and wrongly based on the 2013 census. Pašalić, who based his calculation on the official data, estimates the number to 2.9 million. Other demographic experts from Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Miodrag Pantović and Nermin Oruč, estimate that the total population in Bosnia and Herzegovina is slightly below 1.5 million.[[11]](#cite_note-Vecernji-12)\\n\\n### Urban areas\\n\\nMain article: [List of cities in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"List of cities in Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\") is home to 419,957 inhabitants in its urban area which comprises the [City of Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo#Municipalities_and_city_government \"Sarajevo\") as well as the municipalities of [Ilidža](/wiki/Ilid%C5%BEa \"Ilidža\"), [Vogošća](/wiki/Vogo%C5%A1%C4%87a \"Vogošća\"), [Istočna Ilidža](/wiki/Isto%C4%8Dna_Ilid%C5%BEa \"Istočna Ilidža\"), [Istočno Novo Sarajevo](/wiki/Isto%C4%8Dno_Novo_Sarajevo \"Istočno Novo Sarajevo\") and [Istočni Stari Grad](/wiki/Isto%C4%8Dni_Stari_Grad \"Istočni Stari Grad\").[[232]](#cite_note-235) \"Kiseljak\"), [Kreševo](/wiki/Kre%C5%A1evo \"Kreševo\") and [Visoko](/wiki/Visoko \"Visoko\").[[233]](#cite_note-236)\\n\\n### Ethnic groups\\n\\nMain article: [Ethnic groups in Bosnia and [Bosniaks](/wiki/Bosniaks \"Bosniaks\") (50.1%)\\n2. [Serbs](/wiki/Serbs_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") (30.8%)\\n3.
