No answer (0.20%)\\n\\nBosnia and Herzegovina is home to three ethnic \"[constituent peoples](/wiki/Ethnic_groups_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\", namely [Bosniaks](/wiki/Bosniaks \"Bosniaks\"), [Serbs](/wiki/Serbs \"Serbs\") and [Croats](/wiki/Croats \"Croats\"), plus a number of smaller groups including [Jews](/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"History of the Jews in Bosnia and Herzegovina\") and [Roma](/wiki/Romani_people_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Romani people in Bosnia and Herzegovina\").[[234]](#cite_note-237) According to data from the 2013 census published by the [Agency for Statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Statistical_system_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina#The_Agency_for_Statistics_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_(BHAS) \"Statistical system of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"), Bosniaks constitute 50.1% of the population, Serbs 30.8%, Croats 15.5% and others 2.7%, with the remaining respondents not declaring their ethnicity or not answering.[[5]](#cite_note-Popis2013-5) The census results are contested by the [Republika Srpska](/wiki/Republika_Srpska \"Republika Srpska\") statistical office and by [Bosnian Serb](/wiki/Serbs_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") politicians.[[235]](#cite_note-238) The dispute over the census concerns the inclusion of non-permanent Bosnian residents in the figures, which Republika Srpska officials oppose.[[231]](#cite_note-WithoutSerbAgreement-234) The [European Union](/wiki/European_Union \"European Union\")\\'s statistics office, [Eurostat](/wiki/Eurostat \"Eurostat\"), concluded in May 2016 that the census methodology used by the Bosnian statistical agency is in line with international recommendations.[[236]](#cite_note-239)\\n\\n### Languages\\n\\nBosnia\\'s constitution does not specify any official languages.[[237]](#cite_note-240)[[238]](#cite_note-241)[[4]](#cite_note-Footitt-4) However, academics Hilary Footitt and Michael Kelly note the [Dayton Agreement](/wiki/Dayton_Agreement \"Dayton Agreement\") states it[*[clarification needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify \"Wikipedia:Please clarify\")*] is \"done in [Bosnian](/wiki/Bosnian_language \"Bosnian language\"), [Croatian](/wiki/Croatian_language \"Croatian language\"), English and [Serbian](/wiki/Serbian_language \"Serbian language\")\", and they describe this as the \"de facto recognition of three official languages\" at the state level. The equal status of Bosnian, Serbian and Croatian was verified by the [Constitutional Court](/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") in 2000.[[4]](#cite_note-Footitt-4) It ruled the provisions of the [Federation](/wiki/Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") and Republika Srpska constitutions on language were incompatible with the state constitution, since they only recognised Bosnian and Croatian (in the case of the Federation) and Serbian (in the case of Republika Srpska) as official languages at the entity level. As a result, the wording of the entity constitutions was changed and all three languages were made official in both entities.[[4]](#cite_note-Footitt-4) The three [standard languages](/wiki/Standard_language \"Standard language\") are fully [mutually intelligible](/wiki/Mutual_intelligibility \"Mutual intelligibility\") and are known collectively under the appellation of [Serbo-Croatian](/wiki/Serbo-Croatian \"Serbo-Croatian\"), despite this term not being formally recognized in the country. Use of one of the three languages has become a marker of ethnic identity.[[239]](#cite_note-242) Michael Kelly and Catherine Baker argue: \"The three official languages of today\\'s Bosnian state...represent the symbolic assertion of national identity over the pragmatism of mutual intelligibility\".[[240]](#cite_note-243)\\n\\nAccording to the 1992 [European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages](/wiki/European_Charter_for_Regional_or_Minority_Languages \"European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages\") (ECRML), Bosnia and Herzegovina recognizes the following minority languages: [Albanian](/wiki/Albanian_language \"Albanian language\"), [Montenegrin](/wiki/Montenegrin_language \"Montenegrin language\"), [Czech](/wiki/Czech_language \"Czech language\"), [Italian](/wiki/Italian_language \"Italian language\"), [Hungarian](/wiki/Hungarian_language \"Hungarian language\"), [Macedonian](/wiki/Macedonian_language \"Macedonian language\"), [German](/wiki/German_language \"German language\"), [Polish](/wiki/Polish_language \"Polish language\"), [Romani](/wiki/Romani_language \"Romani language\"), [Romanian](/wiki/Romanian_language \"Romanian language\"), [Rusyn](/wiki/Rusyn_language \"Rusyn language\"), [Slovak](/wiki/Slovak_language \"Slovak language\"), [Slovene](/wiki/Slovene_language \"Slovene language\"), [Turkish](/wiki/Turkish_language \"Turkish language\"), [Ukrainian](/wiki/Ukrainian_language \"Ukrainian language\") and Jewish ([Yiddish](/wiki/Yiddish \"Yiddish\") and [Ladino](/wiki/Judaeo-Spanish \"Judaeo-Spanish\")).[[241]](#cite_note-charter-ratifications-244)\\n\\nThe German minority in Bosnia and Herzegovina are mostly remnants of [Danube Swabians](/wiki/Danube_Swabians \"Danube Swabians\"), who settled in the area after the [Habsburg monarchy](/wiki/Austrian_Empire \"Austrian Empire\") claimed the Balkans from the [Ottoman Empire](/wiki/Ottoman_Empire \"Ottoman Empire\"). Due to [expulsions](/wiki/Flight_and_expulsion_of_Germans_(1944%E2%80%931950) \"Flight and expulsion of Germans (1944–1950)\") and [(forced) assimilation](/wiki/Persecution_of_Germans \"Persecution of Germans\") after the two [World wars](/wiki/World_war \"World war\"), the number of ethnic Germans in Bosnia and Herzegovina was drastically diminished.[[242]](#cite_note-245)\\n\\nIn the 2013 census, 52.86% of the population consider their mother tongue Bosnian, 30.76% Serbian, 14.6% Croatian and 1.57% another language, with 0.21% not giving an answer.[[5]](#cite_note-Popis2013-5)\\n\\n### Religion\\n\\nMain article: [Religion in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Religion_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Religion in Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\nReligion in Bosnia and Herzegovina (2013 census)[[5]](#cite_note-Popis2013-5)\\n\\n|  |  |  |  |  |\\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\\n| Religion | |  | Percent | |\\n| [Muslim](/wiki/Muslims \"Muslims\") | |  | 50.7% | |\\n| [Orthodox Christian](/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church \"Eastern Orthodox Church\") | |  | 30.7% | |\\n| [Catholic Christian](/wiki/Catholic_Church \"Catholic Church\") | |  | 15.2% | |\\n| Other | |  | 1.2% | |\\n| [Atheist](/wiki/Atheism \"Atheism\") | |  | 0.7% | |\\n| [Agnostic](/wiki/Agnosticism \"Agnosticism\") | |  | 0.3% | |\\n| Not declared | |  | 0.9% | |\\n| No answer | |  | 0.2% | |\\n\\nBosnia and Herzegovina is a religiously diverse country. According to the 2013 census, [Muslims](/wiki/Muslims \"Muslims\") constituted 50.7% of the population, while [Orthodox Christians](/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church \"Eastern Orthodox Church\") made up 30.7%, [Catholic Christians](/wiki/Catholic_Church \"Catholic Church\") 15.2%, 1.2% other and 1.1% [atheist](/wiki/Atheism \"Atheism\") or [agnostic](/wiki/Agnosticism \"Agnosticism\"), with the remainder not declaring or not answering the question.[[5]](#cite_note-Popis2013-5) A 2012 survey found 54% of Bosnia\\'s Muslims were [non-denominational](/wiki/Non-denominational_Muslim \"Non-denominational Muslim\"), while 38% followed [Sunnism](/wiki/Sunni_Islam \"Sunni Islam\").[[243]](#cite_note-246)\\n\\n### Education\\n\\nMain article: [Education in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Education_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Education in Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Sarajevo_University_building.JPG/250px-Sarajevo_University_building.JPG)](/wiki/File:Sarajevo_University_building.JPG)\\n\\nThe [University of Sarajevo](/wiki/University_of_Sarajevo \"University of Sarajevo\")\\'s [Faculty of Law](/wiki/Faculty_of_Law,_University_of_Sarajevo \"Faculty of Law, University of Sarajevo\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Mostar_gimnasium.jpg/250px-Mostar_gimnasium.jpg)](/wiki/File:Mostar_gimnasium.jpg)\\n\\n[Gimnazija Mostar](/wiki/Gimnazija_Mostar \"Gimnazija Mostar\") in [Mostar](/wiki/Mostar \"Mostar\")\\n\\nPrimary schooling lasts for nine years. Secondary education is provided by general and technical secondary schools (typically [Gymnasiums](/wiki/Gymnasium_(school) \"Gymnasium (school)\")) where studies typically last for four years. All forms of secondary schooling include an element of [vocational training](/wiki/Vocational_education \"Vocational education\"). Pupils graduating from general secondary schools obtain the *[Matura](/wiki/Matura \"Matura\")* and can enroll in any tertiary educational institution or academy by passing a qualification examination prescribed by the governing body or institution. Students graduating technical subjects obtain a [Diploma](/wiki/Diploma \"Diploma\").[[244]](#cite_note-247)\\n\\nThe first bespoke higher-education institution was a school of [Sufi](/wiki/Sufism \"Sufism\") philosophy established by [Gazi Husrev-beg](/wiki/Gazi_Husrev_Bey \"Gazi Husrev Bey\") in 1531. Numerous other religious schools then followed. In 1887, under the [Austro-Hungarian Empire](/wiki/Austria-Hungary \"Austria-Hungary\"), a [Sharia](/wiki/Sharia \"Sharia\") law school began a five-year program.[[245]](#cite_note-248)\\n\\nIn the 1940s, the [University of Sarajevo](/wiki/University_of_Sarajevo \"University of Sarajevo\") became the city\\'s first secular higher education institute. In the 1950s, post-baccalaurate graduate degrees became available.[[246]](#cite_note-249) Severely damaged during the [war](/wiki/Bosnian_War \"Bosnian War\"), it was recently rebuilt in partnership with more than 40 other universities. There are various other institutions of higher education, including: [University Džemal Bijedić of Mostar](/wiki/University_D%C5%BEemal_Bijedi%C4%87_of_Mostar \"University Džemal Bijedić of Mostar\"), GHI score of less than 5.[[247]](#cite_note-250)\\n\\nCulture\\n-------\\n\\nMain article: [Culture of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Culture_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Culture of Bosnia and Hall](/wiki/Vije%C4%87nica \"Vijećnica\")\\n\\n### Architecture\\n\\nMain article: [Architecture of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Architecture_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Architecture of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\nThe [architecture of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Architecture_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Architecture of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") is largely influenced by four major periods where political and social changes influenced the creation of distinct cultural and architectural habits of the population. Each period made its influence felt and contributed to a greater diversity of cultures and architectural language in this region.\\n\\n### Media\\n\\nMain article: [Mass media in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Mass_media_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Mass media in Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/d6/Radio_and_Television_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_%28BHRT%29_building%2C_Sarajevo.jpg/250px-Radio_and_Television_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_%28BHRT%29_building%2C_Sarajevo.jpg)](/wiki/File:Radio_and_Television_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_(BHRT)_building,_Sarajevo.jpg)\\n\\n[BHRT](/wiki/Radio_and_Television_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Radio and Television of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") headquarters in Sarajevo\\n\\nSome television, magazines, and newspapers in Bosnia and Herzegovina are state-owned, and some are for-profit corporations funded by [advertising](/wiki/Advertising \"Advertising\"), [subscription](/wiki/Subscription_business_model \"Subscription business model\"), and other sales-related revenues. The [Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Constitution_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") guarantees [freedom of speech](/wiki/Freedom_of_speech \"Freedom of speech\").\\n\\nAs a [country in transition](/wiki/Transition_economy \"Transition economy\") with a post-war legacy and a [complex domestic political structure](/wiki/Politics_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Politics of Bosnia and Herzegovina\"), Bosnia and Herzegovina\\'s media system is under transformation. In the early post-war period (1995–2005), media development was guided mainly by international donors and cooperation agencies, who invested to help reconstruct, diversify, democratize and professionalize media outlets.[[248]](#cite_note-251)[[249]](#cite_note-EJC-252)\\n\\nPost-war developments included the establishment of an independent Communication Regulatory Agency, the adoption of a Press Code, the establishment of the Press Council, the decriminalization of libel and defamation, the introduction of a rather advanced Freedom of Access to Information Law, and the creation of a Public Service Broadcasting System from the formerly state-owned broadcaster.\\nYet, internationally backed positive developments have been often obstructed by domestic elites, and the professionalisation of media and journalists has proceeded only slowly. Andrić](/wiki/Ivo_Andri%C4%87 \"Ivo Andrić\") with his wife [Milica](/wiki/Milica_Babi%C4%87-Jovanovi%C4%87 \"Milica Babić-Jovanović\"), upon learning he had won the [Nobel Prize in Literature](/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature \"Nobel Prize in Literature\")\\n\\nBosnia and Herzegovina has a rich literature, including the [Nobel Prize](/wiki/Nobel_Prize \"Nobel Prize\") winner [Ivo Andrić](/wiki/Ivo_Andri%C4%87 \"Ivo Andrić\") and poets such as [Antun Branko Šimić](/wiki/Antun_Branko_%C5%A0imi%C4%87 \"Antun Branko Šimić\"), [Aleksa Šantić](/wiki/Aleksa_%C5%A0anti%C4%87 \"Aleksa Šantić\"), [Jovan Dučić](/wiki/Jovan_Du%C4%8Di%C4%87 \"Jovan Dučić\") and [Mak Dizdar](/wiki/Mak_Dizdar \"Mak Dizdar\"), writers such as [Zlatko Topčić](/wiki/Zlatko_Top%C4%8Di%C4%87 \"Zlatko Topčić\"), [Meša Selimović](/wiki/Me%C5%A1a_Selimovi%C4%87 \"Meša Selimović\"), [Semezdin Mehmedinović](/wiki/Semezdin_Mehmedinovi%C4%87 \"Semezdin Mehmedinović\"), [Miljenko Jergović](/wiki/Miljenko_Jergovi%C4%87 \"Miljenko Jergović\"), [Isak Samokovlija](/wiki/Isak_Samokovlija \"Isak Samokovlija\"), [Safvet-beg Bašagić](/wiki/Safvet-beg_Ba%C5%A1agi%C4%87 \"Safvet-beg Bašagić\"), [Abdulah Sidran](/wiki/Abdulah_Sidran \"Abdulah Sidran\"), [Petar Kočić](/wiki/Petar_Ko%C4%8Di%C4%87 \"Petar Kočić\"), [Aleksandar Hemon](/wiki/Aleksandar_Hemon \"Aleksandar Hemon\"), [Mehmed Begić](/wiki/Mehmed_Begi%C4%87 \"Mehmed Begić\") and [Nedžad Ibrišimović](/wiki/Ned%C5%BEad_Ibri%C5%A1imovi%C4%87 \"Nedžad Ibrišimović\").\\n\\nThe [National Theater](/wiki/Sarajevo_National_Theatre \"Sarajevo National Theatre\") was founded in 1919 in [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\") and its first director was dramatist [Branislav Nušić](/wiki/Branislav_Nu%C5%A1i%C4%87 \"Branislav Nušić\"). Magazines such as *[Novi Plamen](/wiki/Novi_Plamen \"Novi Plamen\")* or *Sarajevske sveske* are some of the more prominent publications covering cultural and literary themes.\\n\\nBy the late 1950s, Ivo Andrić\\'s works had been translated into a number of languages. In 1958, the [Association of Writers of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Association_of_Writers_of_Yugoslavia \"Association of Writers of Yugoslavia\") nominated Andrić as its first ever candidate for the [Nobel Prize in Literature](/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature \"Nobel Prize in Literature\")\\n\\n### Art\\n\\nMain article: [Bosnian and Herzegovinan art](/wiki/Bosnian_and_Herzegovinan_art \"Bosnian and Herzegovinan art\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Bosniangraves_bosniska_gravar_februari_2007_stecak_stecci5.jpg/250px-Bosniangraves_bosniska_gravar_februari_2007_stecak_stecci5.jpg)](/wiki/File:Bosniangraves_bosniska_gravar_februari_2007_stecak_stecci5.jpg)\\n\\n[Stećci](/wiki/Ste%C4%87ak \"Stećak\") from [Radimlja](/wiki/Ste%C4%87ak_necropolis_Radimlja \"Stećak necropolis Radimlja\"), near [Stolac](/wiki/Stolac \"Stolac\") (13th century)\\n\\nThe [art of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_art \"Bosnia and Herzegovina art\") was always evolving and ranged from the original medieval tombstones called [Stećci](/wiki/Ste%C4%87ak \"Stećak\") to paintings in [Kotromanić](/wiki/Kotromani%C4%87_dynasty \"Kotromanić dynasty\") court. Twenty stećak necropolis sites in Bosnia and Herzegovina were added on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2006.[[250]](#cite_note-253) However, only with the arrival of [Austro-Hungarians](/wiki/Austria-Hungary \"Austria-Hungary\") did the painting renaissance in Bosnia really begin to flourish. The first educated artists from European academies appeared with the beginning of the 20th century. Among those are: [Gabrijel Jurkić](/wiki/Gabrijel_Jurki%C4%87 \"Gabrijel Jurkić\"), [Petar Šain](/wiki/Petar_%C5%A0ain \"Petar Šain\"), [Roman Petrović](/wiki/Roman_Petrovi%C4%87 \"Roman Petrović\") and [Lazar Drljača](/wiki/Lazar_Drlja%C4%8Da \"Lazar Drljača\").\\nAfter [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II \"World War II\"), artists like [Mersad Berber](/wiki/Mersad_Berber \"Mersad Berber\") and [Safet Zec](/wiki/Safet_Zec \"Safet Zec\") rose in popularity. In 2007, [Ars Aevi](/wiki/Ars_Aevi \"Ars Aevi\"), a museum of contemporary art that includes works by renowned world artists, was founded in Sarajevo.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\n### Music\\n\\nMain article: [Music of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Music_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Music of Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\nSee also: [List of Bosnia and Herzegovina patriotic songs](/wiki/List_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_patriotic_songs \"List of Bosnia and Herzegovina patriotic songs\") and [Bosnian root music](/wiki/Bosnian_root_music \"Bosnian root music\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/43._TKB_-_Seljo_z_Sarajewa_%28Bo%C5%9Bnia_i_Hercegowina%29_10.JPG/250px-43._TKB_-_Seljo_z_Sarajewa_%28Bo%C5%9Bnia_i_Hercegowina%29_10.JPG)](/wiki/File:43._TKB_-_Seljo_z_Sarajewa_(Bo%C5%9Bnia_i_Hercegowina)_10.JPG)\\n\\n[Bosniaks](/wiki/Bosniaks \"Bosniaks\") dancing a traditional [kolo](/wiki/Kolo_(dance) \"Kolo (dance)\")\\n\\nTypical Bosnian songs are *[ganga](/wiki/Ganga_(music) \"Ganga (music)\"), rera*, and the traditional Slavic music for the folk dances such as *[kolo](/wiki/Kolo_(dance) \"Kolo (dance)\")*, while from the Ottoman era the most popular is [Sevdalinka](/wiki/Sevdalinka \"Sevdalinka\"). Pop and Rock music has a tradition here as well, with the more famous musicians including [Dino Zonić](/wiki/Dino_Zoni%C4%87 \"Dino Zonić\"), [Goran Bregović](/wiki/Goran_Bregovi%C4%87 \"Goran Bregović\"), [Davorin Popović](/wiki/Davorin_Popovi%C4%87 \"Davorin Popović\"), [Kemal Monteno](/wiki/Kemal_Monteno \"Kemal Monteno\"), [Zdravko Čolić](/wiki/Zdravko_%C4%8Coli%C4%87 \"Zdravko Čolić\"), [Elvir Laković Laka](/wiki/Elvir_Lakovi%C4%87_Laka \"Elvir Laković Laka\"), [Edo Maajka](/wiki/Edo_Maajka \"Edo Maajka\"), [Hari Varešanović](/wiki/Hari_Vare%C5%A1anovi%C4%87 \"Hari Varešanović\"), [Dino Merlin](/wiki/Dino_Merlin \"Dino Merlin\"), [Mladen Vojičić Tifa](/wiki/Mladen_Voji%C4%8Di%C4%87_Tifa \"Mladen Vojičić Tifa\"), [Željko Bebek](/wiki/%C5%BDeljko_Bebek \"Željko Bebek\"), etc. Other composers such as [Đorđe Novković](/wiki/%C4%90or%C4%91e_Novkovi%C4%87 \"Đorđe Novković\"), [Al\\' Dino](/wiki/Al%27_Dino \"Al\\' Dino\"), [Haris Džinović](/wiki/Haris_D%C5%BEinovi%C4%87 \"Haris Džinović\"), [Kornelije Kovač](/wiki/Kornelije_Kova%C4%8D \"Kornelije Kovač\"), and many [rock and pop bands](/wiki/Musical_ensemble#Rock_and_pop_bands \"Musical ensemble\"), for example, [Bijelo Dugme](/wiki/Bijelo_Dugme \"Bijelo Dugme\"), [Crvena jabuka](/wiki/Crvena_jabuka \"Crvena jabuka\"), [Divlje jagode](/wiki/Divlje_jagode \"Divlje jagode\"), [Indexi](/wiki/Indexi \"Indexi\"), [Plavi orkestar](/wiki/Plavi_orkestar \"Plavi orkestar\"), [Zabranjeno Pušenje](/wiki/Zabranjeno_Pu%C5%A1enje \"Zabranjeno Pušenje\"), [Ambasadori](/wiki/Ambasadori \"Ambasadori\"), [Dubioza kolektiv](/wiki/Dubioza_kolektiv \"Dubioza kolektiv\"), who were among the leading ones in the former Yugoslavia. Bosnia is home to the composer [Dušan Šestić](/wiki/Du%C5%A1an_%C5%A0esti%C4%87 \"Dušan Šestić\"), the creator of the [National Anthem of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/National_Anthem_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"National Anthem of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") and father of singer [Marija Šestić](/wiki/Marija_%C5%A0esti%C4%87 \"Marija Šestić\"), to the jazz musician, educator and Bosnian jazz ambassador [Sinan Alimanović](/wiki/Sinan_Alimanovi%C4%87 \"Sinan Alimanović\"), composer [Saša Lošić](/wiki/Sa%C5%A1a_Lo%C5%A1i%C4%87 \"Saša Lošić\") and pianist [Saša Toperić](/wiki/Sa%C5%A1a_Toperi%C4%87 \"Saša Toperić\"). In the villages, especially in [Herzegovina](/wiki/Herzegovina \"Herzegovina\"), Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats play the ancient [gusle](/wiki/Gusle \"Gusle\"). The gusle is used mainly to recite epic poems in a usually dramatic tone.\\n\\nProbably the most distinctive and identifiably \"Bosnian\" of music, Sevdalinka is a kind of emotional, melancholic folk song that often describes sad subjects such as love and loss, the death of a dear person or heartbreak.[[251]](#cite_note-254) Sevdalinkas were traditionally performed with a [saz](/wiki/Ba%C4%9Flama \"Bağlama\"), a Turkish string instrument, which was later replaced by the accordion.[[252]](#cite_note-255) However the more modern arrangement is typically a vocalist accompanied by the accordion along with snare drums, upright bass, guitars, clarinets and violins.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/Ensemble_%22Kolo%22%2C_%C4%90ur%C4%91evdan_customs_from_Podgrme%C4%8D.jpg/250px-Ensemble_%22Kolo%22%2C_%C4%90ur%C4%91evdan_customs_from_Podgrme%C4%8D.jpg)](/wiki/File:Ensemble_%22Kolo%22,_%C4%90ur%C4%91evdan_customs_from_Podgrme%C4%8D.jpg)\\n\\n[Serbs](/wiki/Serbs_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") from [Bosanska Krajina](/wiki/Bosanska_Krajina \"Bosanska Krajina\") in traditional clothing\\n\\nRural folk traditions in Bosnia and Herzegovina include the shouted, [polyphonic](/wiki/Polyphony \"Polyphony\") ganga and \"ravne pjesme\" (*flat song*) styles, as well as instruments like a droneless [bagpipe](/wiki/Bagpipes \"Bagpipes\"), wooden [flute](/wiki/Flute \"Flute\") and [šargija](/wiki/%C5%A0argija \"Šargija\"). The gusle, an instrument found throughout the [Balkans](/wiki/Balkans \"Balkans\"), is also used to accompany ancient [Slavic](/wiki/Slavs \"Slavs\") [epic](/wiki/Epic_poetry \"Epic poetry\") [poems](/wiki/Poetry \"Poetry\"). There are also Bosnian folk songs in the [Ladino](/wiki/Judaeo-Spanish \"Judaeo-Spanish\") language, derived from the area\\'s Jewish population.\\n\\n*Bosnian roots music* came from [Central Bosnia](/wiki/Central_Bosnia \"Central Bosnia\"), [Posavina](/wiki/Posavina \"Posavina\"), the [Drina](/wiki/Drina \"Drina\") valley and [Kalesija](/wiki/Kalesija \"Kalesija\"). It is usually performed by singers with two violinists and a šargija player. These bands first appeared around [World War I](/wiki/World_War_I \"World War I\") and became popular in the 1960s. This is the third oldest music after the Sevdalinka and [ilahija](/wiki/Nasheed \"Nasheed\"). Self-taught people, mostly in two or three members of the different choices of old instruments, mostly in the violin, sacking, saz, drums, flutes (*zurle*) or wooden flute, as others have already called, the original performers of Bosnian music that can not be written notes, transmitted by ear from generation to generation, family is usually hereditary. It is thought to be brought from Persia-Kalesi tribe that settled in the area of the present Sprečanski valleys and hence probably the name Kalesija. In this part of Bosnia, it is the most common. This kind of music was enjoyed by all three peoples in Bosnia, Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats, and it contributed a lot to reconcile people socializing, entertainment and other organizations through festivals. In Kalesija, it is maintained each year with the original Bosnian Festival music.\\n\\n### Cinema and theatre\\n\\nMain article: [List of Bosnia and Herzegovina films](/wiki/List_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_films \"List of Bosnia and Herzegovina films\")\\n\\nSarajevo is internationally renowned for its eclectic and diverse selection of festivals. The [Sarajevo Film Festival](/wiki/Sarajevo_Film_Festival \"Sarajevo Film Festival\") was established in 1995, during the [Bosnian War](/wiki/Bosnian_War \"Bosnian War\") and has become the premier and largest film festival in the Balkans and [Southeast Europe](/wiki/Southeast_Europe \"Southeast Europe\").\\n\\nBosnia has a rich cinematic and film heritage, dating back to the [Kingdom of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Yugoslavia \"Kingdom of Yugoslavia\"); many Bosnian filmmakers have achieved international prominence and some have won international awards ranging from the [Academy Awards](/wiki/Academy_Awards \"Academy Awards\") to multiple [Palme d\\'Ors](/wiki/Palme_d%27Or \"Palme d\\'Or\") and [Golden Bears](/wiki/Golden_Bear \"Golden Bear\"). Some notable Bosnian screenwriters, directors and producers are [Danis Tanović](/wiki/Danis_Tanovi%C4%87 \"Danis Tanović\") (known for the Academy Award and [Golden Globe Award](/wiki/Golden_Globe_Awards \"Golden Globe Awards\") winning 2001 film *[No Man\\'s Land](/wiki/No_Man%27s_Land_(2001_film) \"No Man\\'s Land (2001 film)\")* and [Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize](/wiki/Silver_Bear_Grand_Jury_Prize \"Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize\") winning 2016 film *[Death in Sarajevo](/wiki/Death_in_Sarajevo \"Death in Sarajevo\")*),[[253]](#cite_note-256) [Jasmila Žbanić](/wiki/Jasmila_%C5%BDbani%C4%87 \"Jasmila Žbanić\") (won Golden Bear, Academy Award and [BAFTA](/wiki/British_Academy_Film_Awards \"British Academy Film Awards\") nominated 2020 film *[Quo Vadis, Aida?](/wiki/Quo_Vadis,_Aida%3F \"Quo Vadis, Aida?\")*), [Emir Kusturica](/wiki/Emir_Kusturica \"Emir Kusturica\") (won two Palme d\\'Ors at [Cannes](/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival \"Cannes Film Festival\")), [Zlatko Topčić](/wiki/Zlatko_Top%C4%8Di%C4%87 \"Zlatko Topčić\"), [Ademir Kenović](/wiki/Ademir_Kenovi%C4%87 \"Ademir Kenović\"), [Ahmed Imamović](/wiki/Ahmed_Imamovi%C4%87 \"Ahmed Imamović\"), [Pjer Žalica](/wiki/Pjer_%C5%BDalica \"Pjer Žalica\"), [Aida Begić](/wiki/Aida_Begi%C4%87 \"Aida Begić\"), etc.\\n\\n### Cuisine\\n\\nMain article: [Bosnia and Herzegovina cuisine](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_cuisine \"Bosnia and Herzegovina cuisine\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Bosnian_meat_platter.JPG/250px-Bosnian_meat_platter.JPG)](/wiki/File:Bosnian_meat_platter.JPG)\\n\\nBosnian meat platter that contains, among other things, [ćevapi](/wiki/%C4%86evapi \"Ćevapi\"), which is considered the [national dish](/wiki/National_dish \"National dish\") of Bosnia and Herzegovina\\n\\nBosnian cuisine uses many spices, in moderate quantities. Most dishes are light, as they are boiled; the sauces are fully natural, consisting of little more than the natural juices of the vegetables in the dish. Typical ingredients include tomatoes, potatoes, onions, [garlic](/wiki/Garlic \"Garlic\"), [peppers](/wiki/Capsicum \"Capsicum\"), [cucumbers](/wiki/Cucumber \"Cucumber\"), carrots, [cabbage](/wiki/Cabbage \"Cabbage\"), [mushrooms](/wiki/Mushroom \"Mushroom\"), [spinach](/wiki/Spinach \"Spinach\"), [zucchini](/wiki/Zucchini \"Zucchini\"), [dried beans](/wiki/Bean \"Bean\"), fresh beans, [plums](/wiki/Plum \"Plum\"), milk, [paprika](/wiki/Paprika \"Paprika\") and cream called [pavlaka](/wiki/Smetana_(dairy_product) \"Smetana (dairy product)\"). Bosnian cuisine is balanced between [Western](/wiki/Western_culture \"Western culture\") and [Eastern](/wiki/Eastern_world \"Eastern world\") influences. As a result of the [Ottoman](/wiki/Turkish_cuisine \"Turkish cuisine\") administration for almost 500 years, Bosnian food is closely related to Turkish, [Greek](/wiki/Greek_cuisine \"Greek cuisine\") and other former Ottoman and [Mediterranean](/wiki/Mediterranean_cuisine \"Mediterranean cuisine\") cuisines. However, due to Austrian rule, there are many influences from [Central Europe](/wiki/Central_European_cuisine \"Central European cuisine\"). Typical meat dishes include primarily beef and [lamb](/wiki/Lamb_and_mutton \"Lamb and mutton\"). Some local specialties are [ćevapi](/wiki/%C4%86evapi \"Ćevapi\"), [burek](/wiki/B%C3%B6rek \"Börek\"), [dolma](/wiki/Dolma \"Dolma\"), [sarma](/wiki/Sarma_(food) \"Sarma (food)\"), [pilav](/wiki/Pilaf \"Pilaf\"), [goulash](/wiki/Goulash \"Goulash\"), [ajvar](/wiki/Ajvar \"Ajvar\") and a whole range of Eastern sweets. Ćevapi is a grilled dish of minced meat, a type of [kebab](/wiki/Kebab \"Kebab\"), popular in former Yugoslavia and considered a national dish in Bosnia and Herzegovina[[254]](#cite_note-257) and [Serbia](/wiki/Serbia \"Serbia\").[[255]](#cite_note-258)[[256]](#cite_note-259)[[257]](#cite_note-260)\\n\\nLocal wines come from [Herzegovina](/wiki/Herzegovina \"Herzegovina\") where the climate is suitable for growing grapes. Herzegovinian *loza* (similar to Italian [Grappa](/wiki/Grappa \"Grappa\") but less sweet) is very popular. Plum (*rakija*) or apple (*jabukovača*) alcohol beverages are produced in the north. In the south, distilleries used to produce vast quantities of [brandy](/wiki/Brandy \"Brandy\") and supply all of ex-Yugoslav alcohol factories (brandy is the base of most [alcoholic drinks](/wiki/Alcoholic_drink \"Alcoholic drink\")).\\n\\nCoffeehouses, where [Bosnian coffee](/wiki/Turkish_coffee \"Turkish coffee\") is served in [džezva](/wiki/Cezve \"Cezve\") with [rahat lokum](/wiki/Turkish_delight \"Turkish delight\") and [sugar cubes](/wiki/Cube_sugar \"Cube sugar\"), are common in [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\") and every city in the country. Coffee drinking is a favorite Bosnian pastime and part of the culture. Bosnia and Herzegovina is the ninth country in the entire world by per capita coffee consumption.[[258]](#cite_note-261)\\n\\n### Sports\\n\\nSee also: [Bosnia and Herzegovina at the Olympics](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_at_the_Olympics \"Bosnia and Herzegovina at the Olympics\") and [Football in Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Football_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"Football in Bosnia and Herzegovina\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Asim_Ferhatovi%C4%87_Hase_Stadium.jpg/250px-Asim_Ferhatovi%C4%87_Hase_Stadium.jpg)](/wiki/File:Asim_Ferhatovi%C4%87_Hase_Stadium.jpg)\\n\\nThe [Asim Ferhatović Hase Stadium](/wiki/Ko%C5%A1evo_City_Stadium \"Koševo City Stadium\") in [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\") hosted the opening ceremony of the [1984 Winter Olympics](/wiki/1984_Winter_Olympics \"1984 Winter Olympics\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Jahorina_mountain_2018.jpg/250px-Jahorina_mountain_2018.jpg)](/wiki/File:Jahorina_mountain_2018.jpg)\\n\\nThe [Jahorina Ski Resort](/wiki/Jahorina_Ski_Resort \"Jahorina Ski Resort\"), a 1984 Winter Olympics venue, is the biggest and most popular ski resort in Bosnia and Herzegovina\\n\\nBosnia and Herzegovina has produced many athletes. The most important international [sporting event](/wiki/Sport \"Sport\") in the [history of Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/History_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina \"History of Bosnia and Herzegovina\") were the [14th Winter Olympics](/wiki/1984_Winter_Olympics \"1984 Winter Olympics\"), held in [Sarajevo](/wiki/Sarajevo \"Sarajevo\") from 7 to 19 February 1984.[[259]](#cite_note-262)\\n\\nThe [Borac](/wiki/RK_Borac_Banja_Luka \"RK Borac Banja Luka\") [handball](/wiki/Handball \"Handball\") club has won seven [Yugoslav Handball Championships](/wiki/Yugoslav_Handball_Championship \"Yugoslav Handball Championship\"), as well as the [European Cup](/wiki/EHF_Champions_League \"EHF Champions League\") in [1976](/wiki/1975%E2%80%9376_European_Cup_(handball) \"1975–76 European Cup (handball)\") and the [International Handball Federation Cup](/wiki/EHF_European_League \"EHF European League\") in 1991.[[260]](#cite_note-263)\\n\\n[Amel Mekić](/wiki/Amel_Meki%C4%87 \"Amel Mekić\"), Bosnian judoka, became [European champion](/wiki/2011_European_Judo_Championships \"2011 European Judo Championships\") in 2011. Track and field athlete [Amel Tuka](/wiki/Amel_Tuka \"Amel Tuka\") won bronze and silver medals in 800 metres at the [2015](/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics \"2015 World Championships in Athletics\") and [2019 IAAF World Athletics Championships](/wiki/2019_IAAF_World_Athletics_Championships \"2019 IAAF World Athletics Championships\")[[261]](#cite_note-264) and [Hamza Alić](/wiki/Hamza_Ali%C4%87 \"Hamza Alić\") won the silver medal in [shot put](/wiki/2013_European_Athletics_Indoor_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_shot_put \"2013 European Athletics Indoor Championships – Men\\'s shot put\") at the [2013 European Indoor Championships](/wiki/2013_European_Athletics_Indoor_Championships \"2013 European Athletics Indoor Championships\").\\n\\nThe [Bosna Royal](/wiki/KK_Bosna_Royal \"KK Bosna Royal\") [basketball](/wiki/Basketball \"Basketball\") club from Sarajevo were [European Champions](/wiki/Euroleague_Basketball \"Euroleague Basketball\") in [1979](/wiki/1978%E2%80%9379_FIBA_European_Champions_Cup \"1978–79 FIBA European Champions Cup\"). The [Yugoslavia men\\'s national basketball team](/wiki/Yugoslavia_men%27s_national_basketball_team \"Yugoslavia men\\'s national basketball team\"), which won medals in every world championship from 1963 through 1990, included Bosnian players such as [FIBA Hall of Famers](/wiki/FIBA_Hall_of_Fame \"FIBA Hall of Fame\") [Dražen Dalipagić](/wiki/Dra%C5%BEen_Dalipagi%C4%87 \"Dražen Dalipagić\") and [Mirza Delibašić](/wiki/Mirza_Deliba%C5%A1i%C4%87 \"Mirza Delibašić\"). Bosnia and Herzegovina regularly qualifies for the [European Championship in Basketball](/wiki/EuroBasket \"EuroBasket\"), with players including [Mirza Teletović](/wiki/Mirza_Teletovi%C4%87 \"Mirza Teletović\"), [Nihad Đedović](/wiki/Nihad_%C4%90edovi%C4%87 \"Nihad Đedović\") and [Jusuf Nurkić](/wiki/Jusuf_Nurki%C4%87 \"Jusuf Nurkić\"). The [Bosnia and Herzegovina national under-16 team](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_men%27s_national_under-16_and_under-17_basketball_team \"Bosnia and Herzegovina men\\'s national under-16 and under-17 basketball team\") won two gold medals in 2015, winning both [2015 European Youth Summer Olympic Festival](/wiki/Basketball_at_the_2015_European_Youth_Summer_Olympic_Festival \"Basketball at the 2015 European Youth Summer Olympic Festival\") as well as the [2015 FIBA Europe Under-16 Championship](/wiki/2015_FIBA_Europe_Under-16_Championship \"2015 FIBA Europe Under-16 Championship\").\\n\\nWomen\\'s basketball club [Jedinstvo Aida](/wiki/%C5%BDKK_Jedinstvo_Tuzla \"ŽKK Jedinstvo Tuzla\") from [Tuzla](/wiki/Tuzla \"Tuzla\") won the [Women\\'s European Club Championship](/wiki/EuroLeague_Women \"EuroLeague Women\") in 1989 and went to the [Ronchetti Cup](/wiki/Ronchetti_Cup \"Ronchetti Cup\") final in 1990, led by [Razija Mujanović](/wiki/Razija_Mujanovi%C4%87 \"Razija Mujanović\").[[262]](#cite_note-265)\\n\\nThe Bosnian [chess](/wiki/Chess \"Chess\") team was [Champion of Yugoslavia](/wiki/Yugoslav_Chess_Championship \"Yugoslav Chess Championship\") seven times, in addition to club [ŠK Bosna](/wiki/%C5%A0K_Bosna \"ŠK Bosna\") winning four [European Chess Club Cups](/wiki/European_Chess_Club_Cup \"European Chess Club Cup\"). Chess grandmaster [Borki Predojević](/wiki/Borki_Predojevi%C4%87 \"Borki Predojević\") has also won two European Championships. The most impressive success of Bosnian Chess was a runner-up position at the [31st Chess Olympiad](/wiki/31st_Chess_Olympiad \"31st Chess Olympiad\") in 1994 in [Moscow](/wiki/Moscow \"Moscow\"), featuring Grandmasters [Predrag Nikolić](/wiki/Predrag_Nikoli%C4%87 \"Predrag Nikolić\"), [Ivan Sokolov](/wiki/Ivan_Sokolov_(chess_player) \"Ivan Sokolov (chess player)\") and [Bojan Kurajica](/wiki/Bojan_Kurajica \"Bojan Kurajica\").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nMiddle-weight [boxer](/wiki/Boxing \"Boxing\") [Marijan Beneš](/wiki/Marijan_Bene%C5%A1 \"Marijan Beneš\") has won several Championships of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Yugoslav Championships and the [European Championship](/wiki/European_Amateur_Boxing_Championships \"European Amateur Boxing Championships\").[[263]](#cite_note-nezavisne-266) In 1978, he won the World Title against [Elisha Obed](/wiki/Elisha_Obed \"Elisha Obed\") from [The Bahamas](/wiki/The_Bahamas \"The Bahamas\").\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/20150331_2219_AUT_BIH_2704.jpg/250px-20150331_2219_AUT_BIH_2704.jpg)](/wiki/File:20150331_2219_AUT_BIH_2704.jpg)\\n\\n[Edin Džeko](/wiki/Edin_D%C5%BEeko \"Edin Džeko\") playing for [Bosnia and Herzegovina](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_national_football_team \"Bosnia and Herzegovina national football team\") in 2015\\n\\n[Association football](/wiki/Association_football \"Association football\") is the most popular sport in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It dates from 1903, but its popularity grew significantly after [World War I](/wiki/World_War_I \"World War I\"). Bosnian clubs [FK Sarajevo](/wiki/FK_Sarajevo \"FK Sarajevo\") and [Željezničar](/wiki/FK_%C5%BDeljezni%C4%8Dar_Sarajevo \"FK Željezničar Sarajevo\") won the [Yugoslav Championship](/wiki/Yugoslav_First_League \"Yugoslav First League\"), while the [Yugoslav national football team](/wiki/Yugoslavia_national_football_team \"Yugoslavia national football team\") included Bosnian players of all ethnic backgrounds and generations, such as [Safet Sušić](/wiki/Safet_Su%C5%A1i%C4%87 \"Safet Sušić\"), [Zlatko Vujović](/wiki/Zlatko_Vujovi%C4%87 \"Zlatko Vujović\"), [Mehmed Baždarević](/wiki/Mehmed_Ba%C5%BEdarevi%C4%87 \"Mehmed Baždarević\"), [Davor Jozić](/wiki/Davor_Jozi%C4%87 \"Davor Jozić\"), [Faruk Hadžibegić](/wiki/Faruk_Had%C5%BEibegi%C4%87 \"Faruk Hadžibegić\"), [Predrag Pašić](/wiki/Predrag_Pa%C5%A1i%C4%87 \"Predrag Pašić\"), [Blaž Slišković](/wiki/Bla%C5%BE_Sli%C5%A1kovi%C4%87 \"Blaž Slišković\"), [Vahid Halilhodžić](/wiki/Vahid_Halilhod%C5%BEi%C4%87 \"Vahid Halilhodžić\"), [Dušan Bajević](/wiki/Du%C5%A1an_Bajevi%C4%87 \"Dušan Bajević\"), [Ivica Osim](/wiki/Ivica_Osim \"Ivica Osim\"), [Josip others.\\n\\nThe [Bosnia and Herzegovina national football team](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_national_football_team \"Bosnia and Herzegovina national football team\") played at the [2014 FIFA World such as then and now captains [Emir Spahić](/wiki/Emir_Spahi%C4%87 \"Emir Spahić\"), [Zvjezdan Misimović](/wiki/Zvjezdan_Misimovi%C4%87 \"Zvjezdan Misimović\") and [Edin Džeko](/wiki/Edin_D%C5%BEeko \"Edin Džeko\"), defenders like [Ognjen Vranješ](/wiki/Ognjen_Vranje%C5%A1 \"Ognjen Vranješ\"), [Sead Kolašinac](/wiki/Sead_Kola%C5%A1inac \"Sead Kolašinac\") and [Toni Šunjić](/wiki/Toni_%C5%A0unji%C4%87 \"Toni Šunjić\"), midfielders like [Miralem Pjanić](/wiki/Miralem_Pjani%C4%87 \"Miralem Pjanić\") and [Senad Lulić](/wiki/Senad_Luli%C4%87 \"Senad Lulić\"), striker [Vedad Ibišević](/wiki/Vedad_Ibi%C5%A1evi%C4%87 \"Vedad Ibišević\"), etc. Former Bosnian footballers include [Hasan Salihamidžić](/wiki/Hasan_Salihamid%C5%BEi%C4%87 \"Hasan Salihamidžić\"), who became only the second Bosnian to ever win a [UEFA Champions League](/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League \"UEFA Champions League\") trophy, after [Elvir Baljić](/wiki/Elvir_Balji%C4%87 \"Elvir Baljić\"). He made 234 appearances and scored 31 goals for German club [FC Bayern Munich](/wiki/FC_Bayern_Munich \"FC Bayern Munich\"). [Sergej Barbarez](/wiki/Sergej_Barbarez \"Sergej Barbarez\"), who played for several clubs in the German [Bundesliga](/wiki/Bundesliga \"Bundesliga\"). including [Borussia Dortmund](/wiki/Borussia_Dortmund \"Borussia Dortmund\"), [Hamburger SV](/wiki/Hamburger_SV \"Hamburger SV\") and [Bayer Leverkusen](/wiki/Bayer_04_Leverkusen \"Bayer 04 Leverkusen\") was joint-top scorer in the [2000–01 Bundesliga](/wiki/2000%E2%80%9301_Bundesliga \"2000–01 Bundesliga\") season with 22 goals. [Meho Kodro](/wiki/Meho_Kodro \"Meho Kodro\") spent most of his career playing in Spain, most notably with [Real Sociedad](/wiki/Real_Sociedad \"Real Sociedad\") and [FC Barcelona](/wiki/FC_Barcelona \"FC Barcelona\"). [Elvir Rahimić](/wiki/Elvir_Rahimi%C4%87 \"Elvir Rahimić\") made 302 appearances for Russian club [CSKA Moscow](/wiki/PFC_CSKA_Moscow \"PFC CSKA Moscow\") with whom he won the [UEFA Cup](/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League \"UEFA Europa League\") in [2005](/wiki/2005_UEFA_Cup_Final \"2005 UEFA Cup Final\").\\n[Milena Nikolić](/wiki/Milena_Nikoli%C4%87 \"Milena Nikolić\"), member of the [women\\'s national team](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_women%27s_national_football_team \"Bosnia and Herzegovina women\\'s national football team\"), was the [2013–14 UEFA Women\\'s Champions League](/wiki/2013%E2%80%9314_UEFA_Women%27s_Champions_League \"2013–14 UEFA Women\\'s Champions League\") [top scorer](/wiki/UEFA_Women%27s_Champions_League#Top_scorers_by_tournament \"UEFA Women\\'s Champions League\").[[265]](#cite_note-uefa.com-nikolic-scorer-268)\\n\\nBosnia and Herzegovina was the world champion of [volleyball at the 2004 Summer Paralympics](/wiki/Volleyball_at_the_2004_Summer_Paralympics \"Volleyball at the 2004 Summer Paralympics\") and [volleyball at the 2012 Summer Paralympics](/wiki/Volleyball_at_the_2012_Summer_Paralympics \"Volleyball at the 2012 Summer Paralympics\"). Many among those on the team lost their legs in the [Bosnian War](/wiki/Bosnian_War \"Bosnian War\"). Its [national sitting volleyball team](/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_national_sitting_volleyball_team \"Bosnia and Herzegovina national sitting volleyball team\") is one of the dominant forces in [the sport](/wiki/Sitting_volleyball \"Sitting volleyball\") worldwide, winning nine European Championships, three World Championships and two [Paralympic](/wiki/Volleyball_at_the_Summer_Paralympics \"Volleyball at the Summer Paralympics\") gold medals.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\n[Tennis](/wiki/Tennis \"Tennis\") is also gaining a lot of popularity after the recent successes of [Damir Džumhur](/wiki/Damir_D%C5%BEumhur \"Damir Džumhur\") and [Mirza Bašić](/wiki/Mirza_Ba%C5%A1i%C4%87 \"Mirza Bašić\") at [Grand Slam](/wiki/Grand_Slam_(tennis) \"Grand Slam (tennis)\") level.
